area: What is being estimated, and from what
title: What is being estimated, and from what
intro: This section covers the quantities wooldid reports and the data they come from. It covers the four averages of treatment effects, the reference period and the comparison group, and how the sample is formed. It also covers how controls, continuous treatments and subgroups enter, and the tables that show the effect in each cell. The changes share one aim. Every reported number should be a clearly defined average of effects the data can identify. wooldid should also say so whenever it changes what is being estimated or leaves out something it cannot estimate. Most changes add checks or disclosure. Each item says whether it moves reported numbers.

items.heading: The four estimands are presented as four weightings of the same cell effects
items.what_changed: The definitions of the four estimands are unchanged from version 1.3. The guide now shows them side by side. att weights each treated observation by its sample weight. att_it gives each treated cohort-by-period cell equal weight. In wooldid a cohort is one value of the panel identifier i. att_i gives each cohort equal weight. att_itime gives each cohort equal weight, and within a cohort gives each period equal weight. The help and the guide also list in one paragraph every option that treats the three cell-weighted estimands differently from att.
items.why: A cell is one cohort in one calendar period. wooldid estimates one treatment effect for each treated cell and then averages those effects. So choosing an estimand means choosing weights, and the regression stays the same. The weights matter only when effects differ across cells. att gives the effect for the average treated observation. att_i gives the effect for the typical cohort. Some options cannot honour a weighting set at the level of cells. The Bayesian bootstrap draws random weights for whole clusters, which are groups of rows whose errors may be related. It never resamples a treatment cell. For att_it, att_i and att_itime its standard errors would then leave out the variation that comes from sampling cells. That is why it is refused for them. Unconditional standard errors are refused for the same three estimands because they were judged unreliable there. The records give no mechanism for that judgment. impvalues replaces every estimand with the mean over clusters, each cluster weighted equally. A split subgroup changes what att_i and att_itime weight.
items.decision: The author kept the four estimands and their definitions. The restrictions were gathered in one place, so users see them all at once. They no longer find them one error at a time. One restriction on the list is new. By his ruling, bootstrap(bayes) is now refused for these estimands even under safety(off).
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. A run that combines bootstrap(bayes) with one of these estimands under safety(off) now stops with an error. The estimand section of the help ends with a paragraph on what unconditionalse, bootstrap(bayes), makecfxplots and a split subgroup do to att_it, att_i and att_itime. The guide's version of that paragraph adds impvalues. The guide also has a table of the four weightings, each with a note on when to use it.

items.heading: The help explains that the reference period sets the comparison group, and the pooled reference stays the default
items.what_changed: By default wooldid compares each treated cohort's treated periods with all of its untreated periods taken together. This is the pooled reference. With esfixedbaseperiod it compares them with one pre-treatment period instead. By default that is the period just before onset. The help now explains that this choice also changes which rows serve as controls. It therefore changes which parallel-trends assumption the estimate relies on. The help's sentence on when pooling does harm has been corrected. The help also now says what the pretreatment row reports under esfixedbaseperiod. It averages every pre-treatment period that can be estimated. The default is unchanged.
items.why: Parallel trends means that, without treatment, the treated and comparison groups would have followed the same path over time. Under the pooled reference every untreated row is a control. That includes never-treated cohorts and cohorts treated after the sample ends. It also includes the pre-treatment periods of cohorts treated later. Parallel trends must then hold across all of those periods. Under the fixed reference, each treated cohort's other pre-treatment periods get their own indicators. They then stop informing the period effects. The comparison rests only on never-treated cohorts and cohorts treated after the sample. Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021) use this comparison. The pooled version corresponds to the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024). In a test, distorting one later-treated cohort's early pre-period moved the pooled att from 1.8456 to 1.895. The fixed-reference att did not move at all. The old help said pooling does harm whenever the outcome changes over the pre-period. That was wrong. The period fixed effects absorb any trend that all cohorts share. The real risk to pooling is a pre-trend that differs between treated and comparison cohorts. The pooled baseline averages over the whole pre-period, so such a trend carries into every estimate. A baseline set at the last pre-period limits the damage at short horizons. Under the fixed reference, the pretreatment row averages every estimated pre-period effect. Under parallel trends each of those should be near zero. So the row works as a placebo check, a test on periods where the true effect should be zero.
items.decision: Four changes were put to the author. One was to make the fixed reference at period -1 the default. The others were to print a note on pooled runs, to relabel the plot, and to refuse to pass pooled event-study results to honestdid. honestdid is a tool that measures how sensitive results are to pre-trends. He kept the pooled reference as the default and left it unlabelled. The record gives the ruling and not his reasons. Two points in the default's favour had been noted when the change was proposed. Pooling uses more data, and it is the approach wooldid shares with did_imputation and jwdid. For the pretreatment row, the alternative was to limit it to the window the user requested. He kept the row as it is and had it documented as a placebo over the whole history.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. The event-study section of the help has a new paragraph on the comparison group. The esfixedbaseperiod entry says the pretreatment row covers every pre-treatment period that can be estimated. The joint pre-trend test covers only the window you requested.

items.heading: Event-study windows count periods, and a widened window is always announced
items.what_changed: A horizon is a number of periods since onset. esprelength() and espostlength() set how many horizons the event study reports before and after onset. They count consecutive relative periods, whether or not each period appears in the data. The help now says so. Sometimes subgroups() is combined with pre-treatment horizons and no post-treatment horizon. wooldid then raises espostlength() to 1. Version 1.3 did this silently under safety(off). The caution now prints every time. A related caution stays silent under safety(off), as in version 1.3. It concerns a unit with too few pre-periods. That unit's first observed period is forced into its pooled reference. Other cohorts may report that same period as a horizon.
items.why: Counting periods keeps the window arithmetic simple. On panels without gaps it gives the same answer as counting observed horizons. Take a panel observed every two years. A request for four pre-periods then reaches only two observed horizons, so users have to ask for more. Raising espostlength() changes what is estimated, because the run reports a horizon the user did not request. safety(off) switches off protective checks. It is not meant to hide a change in the quantity being estimated, so the announcement now prints either way. The forced reference is a change of the same kind. A period reported as an effect for one cohort becomes part of another cohort's baseline.
items.decision: Defining windows by observed horizons was proposed and turned down. The author chose to document the counting rule. He also ruled that a set of small fixes be taken, and this was one of them. A change to the estimation window is announced whatever safety() says. Silently changing what is estimated is not a safety check. For the forced reference, it was recommended that the caution also print under safety(off). He instead kept the test that records the current silent behaviour as expected. The silence therefore stands as a recorded choice.
items.what_you_notice: Under safety(off) the caution "espostlength set to 1" now appears. It comes without the advice lines that follow it by default. On panels with gaps, the help tells you to widen the window until it reaches the horizons you want.
sources: wooldid.ado lines 5617-5627 (the raise and its comment); v1.3 ado lines 245-249

items.heading: New option anticipation(#) moves the effective onset earlier
items.what_changed: anticipation(#) moves the effective treatment onset # periods before the recorded onset ttre. The result is identical to replacing ttre with ttre minus # by hand. did_imputation's shift() option follows the same convention. The shift also moves the rule that decides which late-treated cohorts count as untreated controls. That applies under oostreatedcontrols() and inside permute() as well. Negative values are refused. Two cautions come with it. One reports units dropped because the shift left them with no usable pre-period. The other reports shifted onsets that fall on periods missing from the data.
items.why: Difference-in-differences assumes no anticipation. That means outcomes before onset are untreated outcomes. Suppose units react before the recorded onset. Those periods then enter the baseline. That pulls the estimate toward zero and creates a false pre-trend. In tests, effects started one, two and three periods early. The default call then understated the true effect by about 22, 44 and 66 percent. It also rejected parallel pre-trends at p near 1e-90. With a fixed reference at -1 the att fell to about zero. The standard remedy is to redefine the onset. Shifting only the onset value would still leave anticipating late cohorts in the control pool. In testing, that alone biased the att by 12 percent.
items.decision: Before this option, users edited ttre by hand. The author asked for a named option. The hand edit leaves no record of the shift, while an option documents itself. The option stores the shift in e(anticipation). It keeps subgroups(ttre) labels at the recorded onsets. Every number is identical to the hand edit. A negative value would mean treatment started later than recorded. It is refused because it would move treated periods into the control pool. The help advises the smallest value you can defend, checked with an event study. A value that is too small shows up as a pre-trend just before the effective onset. A value that is too large keeps the pre-trends clean. The first post-treatment horizons then read near zero, and the pooled estimate shrinks.
items.what_you_notice: There is a new option, anticipation(#), and the shift is stored in e(anticipation). Relative period 0 is now # periods before the recorded onset. To keep the same number of real post-treatment horizons, raise espostlength() by #.
sources: wooldid.ado lines 987-995 (the shift), wooldid_anticgrid (6274), wooldid_anticesf (6292), reltime caution (13581)

items.heading: Malformed timing data is refused early, and rows the if() rule drops are counted
items.what_changed: wooldid now checks the timing variables before it estimates anything. The onset ttre must be constant within each i, with no mix of missing and non-missing values. ttre must lie on the same grid as t, so that t minus ttre is a whole number. i must not exceed 2,147,483,647 on treated units. The customweightmultiplier() variable must not be negative. Each failure stops the run with an error that names the problem. safety(off) lifts all of these except the limit on i. The help also states rules that users had relied on without being told. Some cohort must be never-treated or first treated after the window. t may be zero, negative or have gaps. The exception is where t enters as a factor variable, a set of indicators that Stata builds from a whole-number variable. wooldid keeps only rows where the if() expression equals exactly 1. It now counts and announces rows where the expression is nonzero but not 1. Rows where it is missing are excluded as before and are not in that count.
items.why: wooldid builds each row's position relative to onset from ttre. A unit whose onset differs across its rows is silently split, and part of it becomes its own control. A common cause is recording the onset only from the onset period onward. In tests, three such rows moved one horizon estimate by 41 percent. They also created a pre-trend with the wrong sign. Another layout got past the check that there is a control group and gave an att biased by 20 percent. An onset off t's grid labelled the onset period as pre-treatment. These are data errors that change what is estimated. They are not modelling choices, so the run should stop early and say what is wrong. The exactly-1 rule keeps a flag variable's missing values out of the sample. Stata's own if treats a missing value as true.
items.decision: A simple check on the raw onset variable was rejected. It fires falsely when missing values are coded in different ways. The check reads wooldid's internal onset on the screened sample instead. A hard check on the values of t was also rejected. Tests showed that zero, negative, fractional and very large values of t give identical results on the default path. The help was rewritten instead. For very large i, the author first ruled for an internal recoding. He switched to a refusal once its cost was known. On the if() rule he kept the exactly-1 rule and fixed the reporting. The alternative was to switch to Stata's nonzero convention.
items.what_you_notice: Some do-files that ran before now stop with a named error. A new caution counts the rows the exactly-1 rule excludes. It suggests writing if <var> != 0 to get Stata's usual behaviour. Those rows now count in the dropped-observation total, which used to show zero.

items.heading: The help now recommends onset cohorts as i, with unit fixed effects
items.what_changed: The help no longer claims that the estimator is most efficient when i is set at the level of clustering. It now advises against setting i at the finest level by default. Instead, set i to onset cohorts and put unit fixed effects in fe(). An onset cohort is the group of units that start treatment in the same period. The guide adds a section on this choice. It covers what is gained and lost. It also covers the cases where a unit-level i is still right.
items.why: i decides how many separate cell effects the model estimates. With a unit-level i, each treated cell holds a single observation. The cell's own indicator then fits that observation exactly and leaves a residual of zero. A cluster-robust variance measures uncertainty from the residuals summed within each cluster. So it cannot see that cell's noise, and the standard errors of the att are understated. Under contreat() the dose slope in such a cell cannot be estimated at all. Onset cohorts with unit fixed effects keep the permanent differences between units in the model. They also let several units, and several clusters, share each cell. The guide adds one caveat. With unit fixed effects, a coarse cell weights its units by how their rows split between untreated and treated periods. It does not weight them by their number of treated rows. So it matches the unit-level estimate only in two cases. One is a balanced panel, where every unit is observed in every period. The other is when effects are the same across a cohort's units. A unit-level i is still right for small panels and for an estimand defined at the unit level. It is also right for reproducing did_imputation. The same holds for Ibragimov-Muller inference, which tests across separate estimates for each unit.
items.decision: The author was offered three options for the efficiency claim. He could narrow it to point estimates, add a measured range for how far the standard errors are understated, or leave it alone. He had it removed. He also asked for three pieces of advice. First, choose i by where treatment effects may differ, and not by where you want fixed effects. Second, prefer onset cohorts. Third, cluster below the level of i. Later work added that the cluster must also be at or above the level at which treatment is assigned. That is why the help now says both.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. The i entry in the help gives the new advice. The guide has a section called "The finest-i trap". Runs with a coarser i are much faster.

items.heading: The help states exactly when wooldid matches did_imputation and csdid
items.what_changed: The help's comparison section now gives fuller conditions for an exact match. To match did_imputation, the run must also request no pre-treatment horizons. In addition, i must identify single units, or every unit within an i must be observed in the same periods. A new paragraph covers csdid and xthdidregress. The cell effects returned by gteffects are group-time effects, meaning the effect for one onset group in one period. Under the default pooled reference they differ from csdid's numbers. They equal csdid's long2 table under esfixedbaseperiod at period -1, with a balanced panel and no controls. The long2 table measures each effect against a single base period.
items.why: Users often run wooldid next to these tools. They need to know whether a difference points to a bug or to different definitions. The pooled reference is built from the horizons the run requests. Asking for pre-treatment horizons takes those periods out of the baseline. That shifts every post-treatment estimate. On one test panel the shift was 0.048 for every post estimate. did_imputation's post estimates do not move in the same case. The condition on i follows from how fixed effects are removed. did_imputation uses unit fixed effects. Cohort indicators reproduce those only when the units within an i are observed in the same periods. The csdid paragraph is needed because the two defaults differ. wooldid's default uses not-yet-treated controls and a pooled baseline. csdid's default uses never-treated cohorts and differences from one base period.
items.decision: No code changed. A first draft of the condition on i required a fully balanced panel. Testing showed that balance within each i is enough, and the wording follows that. The condition on pre-treatment horizons was treated as a plain documentation fix that needed no ruling.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. The Comparison section lists the conditions for each tool. Adding the unit to fe() does not restore the match with did_imputation when a coarse i is observed unevenly.

items.heading: Choices kept on purpose where wooldid differs from common practice
items.what_changed: No code changed. Four points were put to the author as departures from common applied practice. He kept each one. First, the run still stops when every unit is treated inside the window. wooldid needs a never-treated cohort or one first treated after the window. csdid and jwdid fall back on not-yet-treated units instead. safety(off) lifts the refusal, as before. Second, covariates enter only through the outcome regression. There is no doubly robust or inverse-probability-weighted version. Those estimators also weight by the estimated chance of being treated. Third, estimands are fixed at estimation time. There is no re-aggregation after estimation and no calendar-time aggregate. Fourth, the word cohort keeps its meaning of the panel identifier i. The onset timing is ttre.
items.why: The records give his decisions but not his reasons. These are the considerations put to him. Under a fixed reference, a panel with no never-treated or late cohort is not identified, and the fit fails. Under pooling, wooldid drops every calendar period that has no untreated row. The run could then go ahead on a shortened window. That is what happens today when safety(off) lifts the refusal. wooldid gives each cohort-by-period cell its own effect. So within a cell the outcome model is close to fully flexible. Doubly robust weighting adds most when covariates vary within cells. Re-aggregation after estimation would need its own inference. gteffects already provides each cell's exact weights for building a custom average.
items.decision: For the missing control group, the proposal was a caution in place of the refusal under pooling. The refusal would stay under a fixed reference. For covariates, it was either a paragraph stating the position or a full inverse-probability or doubly robust estimator. For aggregation, the options were cohort labels on the histogram, a calendar-time aggregate, or a menu for re-aggregating after estimation. For the vocabulary, it was a box that maps i and ttre onto other packages' terms. He declined all of them and left each behaviour as it was.
items.what_you_notice: No results change. The ttre entry in the help now states that some cohort must be never-treated or first treated after the estimation window.

items.heading: Coarse cohort controls are now centred, so each cell reports its average effect
items.what_changed: coarsecohortcontrols() and ccc_absorb() give each treated cell its own slope on each control. The reference period and the control group still share one pooled slope. What changed is how the cell slopes are built. Each cell slope now multiplies the control minus its weighted mean in that cell. This copy is zero on reference rows. A categorical control, entered as a factor variable, is centred category by category. Under ccc_absorb() the pooled slope enters the regression directly. Only the centred cell slopes are absorbed, meaning the fixed-effects solver handles them without reporting them. The model fits the data exactly as before. Every coarsecohortcontrols() and ccc_absorb() estimate changes from version 1.3. The exception is controls that already had a mean of zero in every cell.
items.why: Suppose a treated cell has its own slope on an uncentred control. The cell's indicator then measures the effect at a control value of zero. That point can be far outside the data. For a categorical control, it is the effect in the base category only. So the old reported effect moved when a constant was added to the control. It also moved when the control's units changed or a different base category was chosen. In a test with a true att of 2.00, the old build reported -0.53 with the control as given. It reported -49.4 with 100 added to the control, and 0.97 with a categorical control. The intended quantity is the cell's average outcome minus the untreated outcome predicted for the same units. That is the imputation idea of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024). Wooldridge (2025) centres covariates inside the cohort-by-time terms for the same reason. Centring at the cell mean gives that quantity, so the level and units of the control no longer matter. After the change the same test returned 1.930, and did_imputation also returned 1.930. The two agree to three decimals but are not identical. The treated rows' variation within a cell still informs the unit fixed effects and the pooled slope. So the help does not claim the two methods are equivalent.
items.decision: The author had four options. He could build the centred model, which moves every estimate. He could document that the effect is at a control value of zero and leave centring to users. He could refuse uncentred controls. Or he could leave things as they were. He chose to build the centred model, including on the poisson path. Under ccc_absorb() the pooled slope had to become an explicit regressor. In version 1.3 the reference cell's slope inside the absorbed term stood in for it. The centred copy is zero on reference rows, so that column no longer exists. The pooled slope enters as one column per variable. That keeps the memory saving the option exists for.
items.what_you_notice: Numbers change for every run with coarsecohortcontrols() or ccc_absorb(). Adding a constant to a control, rescaling it, or changing its base category no longer changes the reported effect. A ccc_absorb() variable that is constant within cells used to absorb the treatment terms. The run then stopped with an error. That variable's centred copy is now zero everywhere and is left out, so the run completes.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s5 item 1, s8, s9 G1

items.heading: interactivecontrols() no longer gives the reference period its own slope
items.what_changed: interactivecontrols() lets treatment effects vary with a control. It is built as a set of slopes on the control, one per cell, after the cohort mean has been subtracted. In version 1.3 those slopes also covered the pooled reference cell. They now cover treated cells only, so the reference-period effect is zero by construction. Results change wherever the demeaned control does not average to zero over the reference rows. That happens when the control varies over time within a cohort, when the data are weighted, or when the panel is unbalanced. A new caution fires when the control has no variation within cells. The option also turns off the cell collapse, the shortcut described later in this section.
items.why: The reference cell's slope could be built exactly by adding and subtracting other terms in the model. Those were the time-by-control terms and the treated-cell slopes. So the solver had to drop one of those columns, and its choice decided the reported numbers. Reordering the terms, or switching from reghdfe to regress, moved horizons and the att by up to 0.10. It moved a joint pre-trend p-value from 0.051 to 0.639. On a panel with a trending control, the old build reported a false pre-trend with p of 1.9e-38. Its att was 2.6 times too large. A number that depends on an arbitrary choice by the solver does not estimate anything. With slopes on treated cells only, the horizons are well defined. They do not depend on term order or on the regression command. The reference period is again a true zero, which joint tests, honestdid and the plots all assume. Sometimes a control does not vary within cells. The run then equals one that includes the control interacted with time. It gives no variation in effects, and the new caution says so.
items.decision: The first idea was to fix only the joint tests. It was rejected, because every reported row, the plots and the honestdid export would still be wrong. Subtracting the reference effect afterwards was also rejected, because the needed shift differs by horizon. The author had asked for the mechanism to be settled before anything was fixed. He then ordered the model itself corrected.
items.what_you_notice: Numbers change for most interactivecontrols() runs. Horizons and p-values no longer depend on term order or on the regression command. A caution names a control that does not vary within cells. The help now cites Wooldridge (2025).

items.heading: Under contreat(), treated cells whose dose never varies are dropped from the sample
items.what_changed: contreat() names a continuous treatment, a dose, in place of a yes-or-no treatment. wooldid now finds treated cells in which the dose takes a single nonzero value on every row. It drops those cells from the estimation sample and prints a caution with their count. The att and the average marginal effect of the dose are then estimated on the remaining cells. The average marginal effect, or ame, is the average effect of a small increase in the dose. The count is stored in e(contreat_ndropcells). Cells whose dose is zero throughout are never dropped. If no post-onset cell has dose variation, nothing is dropped at all. The older check then reports the ame as missing. If post-onset cells vary but no pre-onset cell does, the pre-onset block is kept whole. safety(off) silences the caution but still drops the cells.
items.why: A cell with one dose value carries no information about how the effect changes with the dose. The regression drops that cell's slope. The step that averages the cell effects then reads the missing slope as zero, at the cell's full weight. That pulls the ame toward zero in proportion to those cells' share. In a test with a true effect of 1.00, the old build reported 0.72. It gave a p-value near zero and only a generic message about a dropped term. A slope that cannot be estimated should not enter an average as zero. Dropping the cells redefines the estimand as the average over the cells where the dose effect can be learned. The caution says so.
items.decision: Three options were put to the author. The first voided the whole ame family, as already happens when no cell varies. The second rescaled the average over the cells that have a slope and reported the share left out. The third only documented the problem. He chose a fourth route, dropping the cells from the sample. Applied literally, that ruling broke a design the help recommends, a dose set to zero before onset. So the exemption for all-zero cells was widened to every contreatcontrols() type. The pre-onset block is also kept whole when none of it varies. This departure from the literal ruling is recorded for him to confirm.
items.what_you_notice: Numbers change for contreat() runs where some treated cells have a constant dose. A caution counts the dropped cells. e(contreat_ndropcells) and e(N_dropped) record them.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s5 item 2, s8, s9 G2

items.heading: Under contreatcontrols(untreatedZero), a treated cell's dose slope that cannot be estimated now stops the run
items.what_changed: contreatcontrols() sets how the model controls for the dose outside treated cells. The type untreatedZero is for doses that are zero, or undefined, outside treated cells. It fits no baseline dose slope. The ame then comes only from dose variation inside treated cells. The option was rebuilt. It no longer adds the dose terms of the other control types. Each power of the dose now enters as one term interacted with the treated cells. Sometimes a treated cell with a nonzero dose loses its dose slope. The run now stops with error r(322), where it used to continue with a generic caution. Dose terms that are zero by design, such as a pre-onset dose under this option, do not trigger the error. A dose that is constant within every treated cohort is refused for the same reason. Under the other control types that case reports the ame as missing and continues. safety(off) lifts the refusal. Some numbers move on runs that use explicit fixed-effect indicators, as customvce() and unconditionalse do.
items.why: Under untreatedZero the treated cells' dose slopes are the only source of the ame. A slope that cannot be estimated would enter the average as zero and pull it toward zero. Two ways of fitting the same model had also given different answers. In one test with a linear dose term, the ame was 0.26 with explicit fixed-effect indicators. It was 30.23 on the default path. With squared and cubed terms the two paths disagreed widely. The rebuild removed the extra terms behind the gap, so both paths now fit the same model. The explicit path now gives 30.23 as well, and the default path did not move. With squared and cubed terms they now agree to within 1e-10 and 2e-8. The option also rests on a premise. If the dose is not in fact zero outside treated cells, the model leaves out a dose effect it needs. The estimates are then biased, however precise they look.
items.decision: The author accepted the rebuild. He chose to bring the explicit path into line with the default path, including its refusals. He later kept the refusal of a dose that is constant within cohorts, although other control types report the ame as missing there. The help now states this difference. He also declined a check that the dose really is zero outside treated cells. The help states the premise and the bias that follows when it fails.
items.what_you_notice: Some untreatedZero runs that used to finish now stop with r(322). A dose that is constant within cohorts is refused under untreatedZero, and the help says so. Numbers change on the explicit-indicator path, which now matches the default path.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s5 item 7, s8 (CT-9 not built)

items.heading: The baseline dose slope must be identified, and a nearly unidentified one draws a caution
items.what_changed: Every contreatcontrols() type except untreatedZero fits a baseline dose slope. That slope is the dose effect in untreated rows. basic fits one slope for the whole sample. byTreated fits one for the treatment group and one for the control group. byTtre fits one per onset group, byCohort one per cohort, and byTime one per calendar period. Each baseline slope is identified only by dose variation among its group's reference rows. wooldid now refuses a run where any group lacks that variation, with error r(459). Lacking variation here means a spread at or below 1/100000 of the dose's standard deviation in the sample. safety(off) cannot lift the refusal, and it also applies under contreatwithin. A group whose spread lies between 1/100000 and 1/1000 of that standard deviation draws a caution instead. byCohort already had a check of this kind. Under byTime the refusal fires whenever never-treated units carry a zero or constant dose in the periods after the last onset.
items.why: The treated cells' dose slopes are measured against the baseline slope. If the baseline slope cannot be estimated, the solver drops a term, and the reported effects rest on an arbitrary choice. Near that edge the answer can be badly wrong, and the standard errors do not show it. In one test with byTime, the never-treated units' dose spread was only 4.4e-4 of the sample standard deviation. The run reported an att of -150.3 and an ame of -72.7, with p of .00013. The true values were 2.56 and 1. No caution printed. The check also runs in every replication of bootstrap() and permute(). A resampled dataset can lose variation that the observed data have.
items.decision: The author ruled a hard refusal for basic, byTreated, byTtre and byTime. It follows the existing byCohort check, which safety(off) cannot lift. It applies under contreatwithin too, because contreatwithin does not supply the missing variation. He set the cut at 1/100000, measured relative to the dose's spread so that it does not depend on units. That value is his ruling. Tests confirmed that the rule behaves the same way on three designs. They did not show that the cut sits where estimates turn from wrong to right. He later added the caution for the band up to 1/1000, as byCohort already had, and approved its wording.
items.what_you_notice: Runs whose reference rows carry no dose variation for some group now stop with r(459). Under byTime the message names the calendar periods involved and two remedies. A caution names each control type with a group in the fragile band. Runs that pass the check give the same numbers as before.
sources: wooldid.ado ccref screen and fragility band (~lines 14620-14715)
wooldid.sthlp contreatcontrols() paragraph on reference-period variation (~lines 783-786)

items.heading: Under lattice(), a bin with a single dose value borrows another bin's slope, and a caution now says so
items.what_changed: lattice() splits each treated cell into bins of a variable the user chooses. Each bin within each cell gets its own dose slope. Call one bin inside one cell a piece. If a piece has only one dose value, its own slope cannot be estimated. The help used to say such pieces were dropped, and that the ame averaged only the pieces that remained. That was wrong. The piece takes the slope of another bin in the same cell, and the ame includes that borrowed slope. The help now says so. A new caution, printed by default, counts these pieces. The help also corrects when standard errors are understated. That happens when a piece has no more rows than parameters and is fitted exactly. The code that estimates the model is unchanged.
items.why: Each bin's slope enters the model as a difference from a reference slope for the cell. When a piece has no dose variation, the solver drops its difference term. The piece then carries the reference slope, and the averaging step still counts its rows. In one test the true bin slopes were 1, 3 and 5. One cohort's piece in bin 3 had a single dose value. That piece's implied slope was 1.008. The ame for bin 3 read 3.80 against a truth of 5. The headline ame was 2.48 against a truth of 2.90. Leaving the piece out would have given 2.65. No caution printed. A user reading the old help would have believed the ame left the piece out.
items.decision: The author had earlier declined a check for such pieces. He asked instead for a help warning not to over-saturate the model with lattice bins. That warning is his. The wrong description after it was corrected under his request that econometric errors in the help be fixed. He then approved a default caution in his own wording. It suggests a coarser lattice or dropping the affected cells.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. A caution counts the pieces whose slopes are borrowed and suggests coarsening the lattice. The help's lattice paragraph describes the borrowed slope.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s5 item 7, s8 (CT-2 text approved)

items.heading: The help now names the assumption the ame needs to be read as causal
items.what_changed: No code changed. The continuous-treatment section of the help has a new paragraph on what the ame measures. Within a treated cell, the ame compares units that received different doses. The paragraph says this comparison measures the effect of a dose increase only under strong parallel trends. The same holds for differences in att across the bins of the continuous-treatment plots. Under contreatwithin with no untreated group, the att is close to the ame summed over doses from zero. So it needs the same condition.
items.why: Ordinary parallel trends says that, without treatment, units at different doses would have followed the same outcome path. That identifies the att, and the att within each dose bin. It does not identify how the effect changes with the dose. For that, units at different doses must also have gained the same from treatment at any given dose. This is the strong parallel trends assumption of Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024). Without it, the ame also carries selection bias. The units that took higher doses may simply be those that gain more from treatment.
items.decision: No ruling was taken. The paragraph was added under the author's request that econometric errors in the help be corrected. It changes no number. It changes how the ame should be read.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. The help has a new paragraph, "What the ame Measures", in the continuous-treatment section.

items.heading: Under contreatwithin, the att in periods with no untreated rows is now flagged
items.what_changed: contreatwithin estimates dose effects from variation inside treated cohorts. As in version 1.3, it keeps calendar periods that have no untreated observations. What is new is a caution that names those periods. It says that the att there depends on an arbitrary normalisation. It points users to the ame. The help describes the att in those periods the same way.
items.why: Take a period where every unit is treated. The cell indicators for that period then add up to the period's own indicator. The solver silently sets one cell's level to zero and measures the other cells against it. So the att in that period depends on which cell was dropped. A test gave an att of 1.472 under one labelling of cohorts. The same data relabelled gave 3.304. The ame stayed at 1.001 in both. The ame comes from dose variation within cells and is still identified. The level effect is not.
items.decision: The starting point was to document the issue only. The author chose to add a caution, and he approved its wording.
items.what_you_notice: A new caution lists the periods with no untreated reference rows and points you to the ame results. No numbers change.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s5 item 7, s8, s9 G4
wooldid.ado caution at line 13454; calendar-support check gated on contreatwithin (~line 13673)

items.heading: The triple-difference recipe now uses att_it, with i defined as onset cohort by group
items.what_changed: Version 1.3 said to put the two groups in subgroups() with group-by-period fixed effects. The triple difference was then the difference of the two estimates. It named no estimand and no definition of i. The help and the guide now give a fuller recipe. Define i as the onset cohort crossed with the group. Use att_it. Make sure both groups appear in every treated cell. The code is unchanged.
items.why: A triple difference should remove shocks that hit both groups in the same treated cohort and period. It does that only if the two groups' estimates average the same cells with the same weights. Under att, each group weights a cell by its own share of observations. So the contrast keeps each shared shock, multiplied by the gap between the two groups' weights on that cell. With staggered adoption those shares rarely match, so shared shocks leak into the estimate. In a noiseless test with a true effect of 1, att returned 3.84. That is the leakage the formula predicts. att_it returned 1. att_it gives every cell equal weight in both groups, so the shared shocks cancel cell by cell. This result follows from the algebra of the weights alone. Olden and Moen (2022) is the reference on the triple-difference estimator.
items.decision: Leaving the old sentence was considered. It is true if a triple difference simply means the difference of the two estimates. It was changed because readers take it as a recipe for a valid triple difference. No option was put to the author for a ruling. The change was made under his request that econometric errors in the help be corrected.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. The help and the guide give a new recipe, and the guide's worked example uses att_it.

items.heading: Subgroups must be made of whole units, and split or partly labelled units are refused
items.what_changed: Version 1.3 said a cohort cannot be split across subgroups but never checked it. wooldid now refuses three cases, each with an error. The first is a subgroup that varies within a cohort-by-period cell. The second is a unit that changes subgroup over time. The third is a treated unit labelled on some rows and missing on others. A unit missing on all its rows is still simply left out of every subgroup. Under safety(off) the run proceeds outside permute(). A split unit then enters each subgroup weighted by its share of sample weight there. Under permute() none of these refusals can be lifted.
items.why: Subgroups do not enter the regression. They only choose which rows the averaging step uses. So every subgroup shares the same cell effects. If a subgroup varies within a cell, its estimate just reweights those shared effects. The contrast then measures a difference in who is in each subgroup, and says nothing about a difference in effects. In testing, a true threefold difference was reported as exactly zero. A split or partly labelled unit also gets the wrong weight under att_i, att_it and att_itime. Those estimands divide by totals built from all of the unit's rows. The averaging step rescales within the subgroup, so the unit counts as a fraction of a unit. permute() reassigns onset across whole clusters. That is not defined for a unit spread over several subgroups.
items.decision: The first version refused only the within-cell case. It gave just a caution for units split over time. The author then ruled that split units be refused outright, with share weighting kept only as the safety(off) route. Next he added the check on partly labelled units, so they could not pass with a silent share weight. The next day he asked for share weighting to be deleted. It turned out not to be a separate feature. It was only the arithmetic that follows from letting a split unit through. He then kept the safety(off) route outside permute(). He made every refusal under permute() impossible to lift, the partial-labelling one included.
items.what_you_notice: Subgroup variables that split units now stop the run with an error. The error suggests defining i at the finer level. The help warns that with safety(off), att_i and att_itime no longer weight units equally.
sources: wooldid.sthlp subgroups() entry and containment paragraph (~lines 652-679)

items.heading: Subgroup horizons that cannot be estimated are dropped with a caution
items.what_changed: Sometimes a subgroup's effect at one horizon cannot be estimated. For example, the subgroup may have no treated cells there. Version 1.3 then either stopped with an obscure error after estimation, or reported a zero with a missing standard error. wooldid now drops that horizon from that subgroup's event study. It names the horizon in a caution and continues. A subgroup that loses every horizon has its event study skipped. A later fix stops one subgroup with no pre-treatment cells from removing the pre-treatment row of every other subgroup.
items.why: Subgroups need not share every relative period, so uneven subgroups are legitimate. margins, the Stata command that does the averaging, can return a number for a combination it cannot estimate. That number is not an estimate. Showing it as zero invites misreading. Dropping it with a caution keeps all the other results.
items.decision: The alternative was to refuse the run. The author ruled that the run should proceed. He also holds that heavy effort should not go into data too thin to give good results.
items.what_you_notice: Runs with uneven subgroups complete. A caution lists the horizons dropped for each subgroup. The adversarial test is skipped for a subgroup that lost a horizon.

items.heading: suppresssgprimaryeffects removed
items.what_changed: The option skipped the per-subgroup estimates. It reported only the subgroup contrasts and the test of equality across subgroups. It has been deleted. A do-file that names it stops with error r(198). The same call without the option returns everything the old call did and more.
items.why: It existed for speed. It still saved time, making subgroup runs with an event-study window about 1.8 times faster. But it saved far less than it once did. The subgroup estimates now come from the same margins pass that builds the contrasts. So the option skipped only the per-subgroup event-study, marginal-effect and composition passes. It also cost maintenance, and it had already disabled a safeguard without any sign. Showing the subgroup estimates next to the contrasts also lets users see what each contrast is a difference of.
items.decision: The author was asked whether to keep it or delete it. He deleted it, judging the cost of keeping it higher than its value.
items.what_you_notice: The option is gone. Subgroup runs always report the per-subgroup estimates.

items.heading: New option gteffects returns the cohort-by-period effects behind every average
items.what_changed: gteffects returns a table, e(gteffects). It has one row per estimated cohort-by-relative-period cell, taken directly from the regression. Each row gives the estimate, its standard error and its interval. It also gives the cell's total weight under each estimand. Averaging the estimates with one of those weight columns reproduces the main result exactly. The option is refused under contreat(). Two safeguards come with it. Cells with no identified variance get a missing standard error. A caution counts cells whose standard errors are understated. That happens when the whole cell lies inside one cluster, or holds a single observation under a robust variance.
items.why: Every wooldid estimand is an average of these cell effects, so showing them makes the estimator transparent. It also lets users build their own averages, for example by calendar time, without running the model again. When i is the onset cohort, the cells are the group-time effects users know from csdid. Under contreat() the cell coefficients are intercepts at a dose of zero. They are not treatment effects, hence the refusal. The standard-error caution matters because a cluster-robust variance is built from residuals summed within each cluster. A cell whose indicator fits it inside one cluster makes those sums zero. The cell's own noise then never reaches the variance. Only a cluster() finer than the cells fixes this. bootstrap() resamples such a cell whole, so its standard error stays understated there too.
items.decision: A menu that would re-aggregate this table after estimation, with its own inference, was proposed. The author ruled that estimands stay fixed at estimation time. There is no re-aggregation and no calendar-time aggregate. The table's weight columns remain the route to a custom average, which the help describes. For cells with no identified variance, he chose to blank the standard error. The alternative was to print rounding noise as if it were a result.
items.what_you_notice: There is a new option, gteffects. The table prints when it has up to 200 rows. e(gt_ncontained) and e(gt_ndegen) count the flagged cells.

items.heading: New event-study composition table e(escomp)
items.what_changed: Every run with an event study now stores e(escomp). It has one row per reported horizon. Each row gives the number of cohorts, units, clusters and observations that contribute. It also gives each horizon's share of the treated weight under att and under att_it. There are versions for each subgroup, and scalars that describe the reference pool. The table is displayed with summarystats.
items.why: An event study averages different cohorts at different horizons. Late horizons, for example, come only from cohorts treated early. So a jump or a trend in the profile can reflect a change in which cohorts are averaged. It need not reflect any change in effects. In the project's own test data, a pre-trend that seemed to worsen, with p of .021, was a change in which cohorts were present. Both weight shares are shown because they reveal different breaks. In one test with attrition, the att share moved by 83 percent and the att_it share by 33 percent.
items.decision: Adding columns to the event-study matrix was rejected, because other code relies on that matrix's layout. The table is on by default. No separate ruling was found.
items.what_you_notice: There is a new stored matrix, e(escomp), and summarystats displays it.

items.heading: impvalues reports a mean that weights clusters equally, and refuses clusters finer than i
items.what_changed: The help now states the rule directly. Under impvalues the reported estimate is the simple mean of the estimates for each cluster, whatever estimand was requested. With clustering at the cohort level, att therefore gives the same numbers as att_i. A cluster() finer than i, or one that cuts across it, is now refused with an error. safety(off) cannot lift that refusal.
items.why: The method of Ibragimov and Muller runs a t-test on the mean of independent cluster estimates. That justifies a t reference distribution with the number of clusters minus one degrees of freedom. It holds even with few clusters of unequal variance. Reweighting the mean to reproduce att would recover att's weights but lose that justification. So the change of estimand is the price of the method. When clusters sit inside a cell, the cluster estimates are not independent draws. They are reweightings of the same coefficients, and the standard error is far too small.
items.decision: Recomputing the estimand weights under impvalues was first proposed and then withdrawn. The author judged that the method cannot be reweighted. For the finer cluster, the problem first drew a caution. He then ruled it an error, and later ruled that safety(off) could not lift it.
items.what_you_notice: Runs with impvalues and a cluster finer than i now stop with an error. The help says att under impvalues is the mean that weights clusters equally.

items.heading: semielasticity removed
items.what_changed: Version 1.3 could report effects as percentage changes through the semielasticity option. That option has been removed. So have poisexpresults and the eydx and eyex forms of contreatelasticitytype(). Effects are now reported in levels, or in the dyex form. Under poisson every effect is on the log scale of the linear index. A do-file that names a removed option stops with error r(198).
items.why: A percentage change divides by the model's prediction, so it needs the full prediction. reghdfe's prediction leaves out the absorbed fixed effects. So these effects were computed against the wrong denominator. They differed from a run with explicit fixed-effect indicators by 7 to 15 percent. The level and dyex forms never divide by the prediction and were not affected.
items.decision: A repair was built and confirmed. The author chose removal over repair. He also accepted that stored estimates from older versions replay under a plain header.
items.what_you_notice: The option is gone. Do-files that used it stop with error r(198).

items.heading: The averaging step runs on one row per cell by default
items.what_changed: The regression still runs on the full data, so the coefficients, the variance and the clustering are unchanged. The averaging step uses Stata's margins command, and it takes most of a run's time. It is now evaluated on one row per cohort-by-period-by-treatment cell. That row carries the cell's summed weight. This is the cell collapse. It now covers yes-or-no and continuous treatments, poisson, subgroups, impvalues, lattice() and customvce(). It also runs inside bootstrap() and permute() replications. It is skipped for interactivecontrols(), for contreatpoly() above 1, when the dose appears among the controls, and for unconditionalse.
items.why: Suppose no model term makes the treatment effect vary within a cell. Every row in that cell then has the same effect. Averaging over the rows or over one weighted row gives the same number. With a dose, the effect in a cell is a straight line in the dose. So the cell's weighted mean dose reproduces the average exactly. A higher power of the dose does not, which is why contreatpoly() above 1 is excluded. A lattice bin or a cluster that splits a cell simply becomes part of the key that defines the collapsed row. The gain grows with the number of rows per cell. On a 30,000-row panel it cut total run time by 35 to 60 percent. Under contreat() runs became 2 to 4 times faster.
items.decision: The collapse started as an option users had to turn on. The author made it the default the same day, with a way to turn it off. Each extension was measured before he allowed it. The original proposal assumed only contreat() broke the collapse. Measurement found that interactivecontrols() gave errors of 23 to 37 percent, so that case was excluded. For subgroups he chose to collapse and then check each subgroup result for a numerically singular direction. When one appears, the run is repeated on the full data. The alternative was to leave subgroups uncollapsed. customvce() was allowed after measurement showed that its differences were margins' own numerical noise.
items.what_you_notice: Runs are faster, most of all with many rows per cell. Results agree with an uncollapsed run to margins' own accuracy. Hidden e() entries record whether the collapse ran.

items.heading: One switch turns the collapse off, and a skipped collapse is announced
items.what_changed: The collapse used to have three settings spread over two options. The default ran it when possible. fastcollapse raised an error if the request was not eligible. fullprecisionslow turned the collapse off. These are now one option, nofastcollapse. The old two were removed with no alias. When a request is not eligible, a caution names the option responsible. The run then continues on the full data. The help's statement on accuracy was also corrected. Agreement is typically at machine precision. It can reach about 1e-6 relative on standard errors with sampling weights, controls and an event-study window.
items.why: On an eligible request fastcollapse did nothing. Its only effect was to turn a silent skip into an error. What users needed from it was to know when the collapse had not run. A caution gives that without an extra option. The accuracy correction comes from measurement. The remaining difference comes from margins' own numerical derivatives, which uncollapsed runs share. So neither run is the exact answer.
items.decision: Three alternatives were considered. One kept all three settings. One renamed them as the pair fastcollapse and nofastcollapse, which would falsely suggest opposites. One kept fullprecisionslow as a hidden alias. The author chose a clean break with no alias. He regarded the resulting error as an honest signal to update old do-files.
items.what_you_notice: Do-files that name fastcollapse or fullprecisionslow stop with error r(198). nofastcollapse turns the collapse off. A caution explains when the collapse was skipped and which option caused it.

area: Analytic standard errors and what they can and cannot see
title: Analytic standard errors and what they can and cannot see
intro: This section covers the standard errors wooldid computes from the regression itself, without resampling. It also covers the variance matrix wooldid stores for other commands to read. A few terms recur. A treated cell is the set of treated rows that share an onset cohort and a calendar period. The att is the average effect of treatment on the treated. The ame is the average marginal effect of the dose when treatment is continuous. The variable i names the groups that get their own treatment dummies, usually the unit or the onset cohort. A cluster-robust variance allows errors to be correlated within a cluster, and it adds up residuals cluster by cluster. Most of the changes follow from one feature of the design. wooldid gives every treated cell its own dummy, and that dummy forces the cell's residuals to sum to zero. A variance built from residuals can then be blind to the cell's own noise. The program now says where that blind spot lies. It withholds numbers that fall inside it, and it labels the stored variance for what it is.

items.heading: The default variance is stated, and the examples carry a warning
items.what_changed: The help now says what variance a run gets when neither cluster() nor robust is given. On the linear path it is the conventional OLS variance. That variance assumes the errors are independent and share one variance. Under poisson or with pweights, which are sampling weights, the default is robust, which stays valid when error variances differ. Examples 1 to 10 now open with a line saying they leave out cluster() only for brevity. The line adds that cluster() belongs at the level where treatment is assigned. The default itself is unchanged.
items.why: In a panel, the same unit's outcomes are correlated from one period to the next. A variance that treats every row as a separate draw counts the same information many times. Its standard errors are then too small. Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan (2004) showed that this makes difference-in-differences tests reject far too often. None of the three defaults allows for that correlation. Nine of the fifteen examples in the old help ran without cluster() and said nothing about it. That taught the habit the literature warns against.
items.decision: On 2026-09-07 the author ruled to leave the default as it was. He also kept the header, which does not name the default variance. On 2026-09-25 the help and the guide were found to say nothing about the variance a run gets without cluster() or robust. Nine of the fifteen examples also ran unclustered with no remark. Both gaps were corrected as documentation omissions, which needed no ruling. The one question put to him was whether to keep example 0 in its rewritten form. It now uses cluster(unit) fe(unit) att with i set to the onset cohort, and he kept it. The help now states the default plainly and asks the user to choose the cluster level on purpose.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. The robust entry states the default and its limits. The examples carry a one-line warning. Example 0 now clusters by unit.

items.heading: The stored variance labels use Stata's usual names and describe the variance actually used
items.what_changed: Stata keeps a command's results in named stored slots, such as e(vce). Every run now fills Stata's usual slots e(N_clust), e(clustvar), e(vce) and e(vcetype). They sit beside wooldid's own e(Nclus) and e(wdid_vcespec). Under poisson on the default ppmlhdfe path, the labels now read robust. The same holds under pweights with no variance option. Before, they read oim or ols. Under unconditionalse they read unconditional, and the first-stage variance type moves to e(vce_stage1). When no e(V) was posted, e(vce) and e(vcetype) stay empty. e(clustvar) still names the design in that case.
items.why: Table tools such as esttab and estout read these slots to print the cluster count and the variance type. Without them, a wooldid table silently lost that information. The labels also have to be true. ppmlhdfe, the poisson command wooldid calls, always computes a robust variance. That variance stays valid when the poisson variance assumption is wrong. A regression with pweights also computes a robust variance. The oim label tells a reader the standard errors rest on a correct likelihood. The ols label tells a reader they rest on independent errors with one shared variance. Neither was true. Under unconditionalse the standard errors come from the unconditional variance that Stata's margins command computes. They do not come from the first-stage regression, so the first-stage label would misdescribe them.
items.decision: The author approved the usual names as a pure addition. For poisson and pweights he was offered two choices. One was to post robust, which changes only the label. The other was to keep the old label. He chose robust. An oim label now appears only when the user asks for it through customvce(oim). customvce() lets the user name any variance Stata offers.
items.what_you_notice: No estimate or standard error moves. esttab footers show the cluster count, and a Robust or Unconditional label where it applies. On poisson and pweighted runs, the header's Standard Errors field names vce(robust).
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s.5 item 3, s.8, s.9 G3 (POIS-1/SEB-05)

items.heading: The advice on where to cluster was reversed
items.what_changed: The old help said the estimator was most efficient when i is set at the level you cluster at. Its first example clustered on i. That sentence is gone, and the advice now runs the other way. Set i to the treatment onset cohort, and put unit fixed effects in fe(). Then cluster below i, but at or above the level where treatment is assigned. Example 0 now reads cluster(unit) fe(unit) att, with i the onset cohort. Sometimes no level is both finer than the cells and at or above the assignment level. The help then sends users to bootstrap() or permute(). bootstrap() resamples whole clusters. permute() compares the estimate with estimates from reshuffled treatment assignments.
items.why: A cluster-robust variance is built from the sum of residuals within each cluster. Each treated cell's own dummy forces that cell's residuals to sum to zero. If a whole cell sits inside one cluster, the cell adds exactly zero to that cluster's sum. The variance then cannot see the cell's own noise. It counts only the noise on the control side. MacKinnon and Webb describe the same failure when only one cluster is treated. The package ran a 500-draw simulation with 40 clusters. With i set to the unit and clustering on the unit, pooled att standard errors were 0.66 to 0.80 of the true spread. Nominal 95 percent intervals covered only 79 to 88 percent of the time. csdid and did_imputation give the same point estimates on those draws, and they covered 93 to 94 percent. With i set to the onset cohort, wooldid covered 93 to 95 percent. The second condition is the standard one. Clusters finer than the level of assignment ignore the correlation that a shared assignment creates. Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2023) set this out.
items.decision: The author removed the efficiency sentence outright on 2026-09-13, saying he was skeptical of it. He could have narrowed it to the point estimates or added a measured range. He did neither. At his instruction the 500-draw simulation ran the next day, at 40 clusters only, and it confirmed the removal. He then had the i entry recommend treatment onset cohorts. He kept the rewritten example 0 when offered a revert. Earlier he had ruled that the cluster() entry carry a note, and only a note, on what goes wrong at or above i. That note says no simple correction exists. At that clustering the analytic covariance measures the wrong thing, so rescaling it would not help. The remedies it names are a finer cluster(), bootstrap() or permute().
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. The i, cluster() and robust entries state the two conditions. So does a new discussion of what level to cluster at. Example 0 and the guide show the recommended layout.
sources: v1.3 wooldid.sthlp line 62 (removed sentence) and example 0 line 712

items.heading: No number is given for how many clusters each cell needs
items.what_changed: A finer cluster() is offered as the remedy in three places. These are the joint tests, the adversarial line test and the subgroup comparisons. The adversarial line test asks whether all event-study estimates could lie on one straight line through the reference period. Wherever the remedy is offered, the text adds a condition. The finer cluster works only when it leaves many clusters inside each treated cell. No number is given anywhere, and none is checked when the program runs.
items.why: A finer cluster helps only through the number of distinct clusters it leaves inside each treated cell. The package measured the size of the line test, meaning how often it rejects when the null is true. With six or more clusters per cell, it rejected close to the nominal 5 percent. With two, it rejected about three times as often. With one, it rejected about ten times as often. The cut-off moves with the design. A single number would imply a calibration that nobody has.
items.decision: A numeric rule with its own caution was proposed. The author ruled it out and chose a statement with no number. The condition is left off the remedy for the continuous-treatment standard errors on purpose. Those concern a different statistic.
items.what_you_notice: The help entries and cautions for jointtests, adversarial and subgroup contrasts say the finer cluster must leave many clusters inside each cell. No count of clusters per cell is printed.

items.heading: The att rows carry no caution when clustering is at or above i, by design
items.what_changed: When cluster() sits at the level of i or coarser, the analytic standard errors of the binary att rows are understated. wooldid prints no caution for this, and the help and guide say so openly. Other results do get a caution or have their inference withheld. These are the continuous-treatment rows, the joint tests, the per-cell table from gteffects and the analytic band.
items.why: The pooled att averages over many cells, and the noise on the control side is still counted. So the understatement is milder than for a single cell. It is real, as the simulation in the item above shows. But the most common binary call meets the condition. That call is i equal to the unit with cluster(unit). A caution would fire on almost every ordinary run and would soon be ignored.
items.decision: The author ruled that standard binary runs get no caution. His judgment was that the remaining exposure falls mostly where clustered standard errors are known to be fragile anyway. Few clusters is the main example. A targeted simulation of the binary rows was offered to him, and he declined it. That ruling came before the 40-cluster simulation. The response to the simulation was a new recommended design, with i the onset cohort and a finer cluster. No caution was added. A proposed caution in pretrendpower() for single-row cells was dropped for the same reason. It would have cautioned a large share of ordinary runs.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing prints on the att rows. The help's discussion of what level to cluster at states the understatement, and so does the guide's rule 3.

items.heading: Continuous-treatment standard errors are withheld when a treated cell sits inside one cluster
items.what_changed: contreat() is the continuous-treatment option. Under contreat() with a clustered variance, wooldid checks each treated cell that has two or more rows. If any such cell lies wholly inside one cluster, the ame inference is withheld. Every standard error, test statistic, p-value and interval for the ame is reported as missing. That covers the main row, the event-study horizons, the subgroup rows and the subgroup contrasts. The ame joint and line tests are skipped, and the ame event-study covariance is not posted. The ame point estimates and all att results still post. A caution gives the number of cells and names the alternatives. These are bootstrap, randomization inference, a finer cluster, or Ibragimov-Muller p-values, which test the spread of separate estimates from each cluster. safety(off), the switch that lifts most of wooldid's refusals, does not lift this one.
items.why: The ame is learned from how outcomes move with the dose inside each treated cell. Each cell has its own dummy. When a cell also lies inside one cluster, the cluster-robust variance cannot see that within-cell variation. What it reports is essentially the variance of the baseline dose control that the model absorbs. That same value repeats across every ame quantity. It looks like a standard error, yet it does not measure how the ame estimate varies from sample to sample. A single-row cell is different. Its own dummy fits it exactly, and its dose slope is dropped as collinear. So it adds nothing to the variance. Counting such cells had withheld valid standard errors from runs that did not have the problem.
items.decision: The author chose a check on how the treated cells sit in clusters. The alternative was a check on the matrix itself, such as a test of its rank. A rank test asks whether some combination of the estimates has no measured variance. It would miss this problem. On some specifications the matrix has full rank and is still blind to within-cell noise. The check fires if any cell is contained, because one contained cell is enough to contaminate the matrix. Bootstrap standard errors were not an option when this was decided, since the package had no bootstrap engine yet. The author later ruled that single-row cells should not count.
items.what_you_notice: On an affected contreat() run the ame rows print point estimates with blank inference columns, and a caution explains why. Runs that failed the check only because of single-row cells report ame standard errors again.

items.heading: wooldid reports a destroyed covariance and no longer tries to repair it
items.what_changed: Stata sometimes replaces a variance matrix it judges non-symmetric or highly singular with a matrix of zeros. The quiet estimation call hides its warning. An earlier version responded by refitting the whole model, with the fixed effects written out as dummies, to recover the att variances. That refit is gone. wooldid now detects a matrix of zeros. It also detects a matrix that is only rounding residue. The residue check compares the square root of the largest covariance entry with the largest coefficient. It fires when that ratio falls below one part in a trillion. A caution then says that no standard error in the run is identified. The point estimates still post. A second check applies under a clustered variance. It cautions when three or more reported standard errors agree to about twelve digits while their estimates differ. When the ame containment caution of the item above has fired, its message takes precedence.
items.why: The refit recovered some standard errors from a specification whose containment had already made the ame inference invalid. It cost a solve over hundreds of redundant dummy columns. It also delayed the moment the user learned the specification was broken. The two checks catch unknown routes to the same failure by its symptom. A matrix of zeros does not measure sampling variability. Neither does a matrix that repeats one value across different quantities. The repeated-value check runs only on clustered runs. Balanced designs without clustering can legitimately give identical standard errors.
items.decision: The refit had been approved as part of a larger package. When its cost was put to the author on its own, he ruled to remove it. Three other fallbacks of a different kind were kept, among them the poisson retry. For the checks, the author capped the general-purpose guards at two. He made both of them cautions, which let the run finish. Guards based on matrix rank or eigenvalues were rejected. A matrix can pass them and still be meaningless. The residue check came later. The zero test had stayed silent on a two-cluster design that reported standard errors of 4e-16. The author ruled to add a floor with a conservative margin. The margin was set by measurement. The nearest healthy fit in the package's tests sat eight orders of magnitude above the floor.
items.what_you_notice: A run whose covariance is exactly zero prints point estimates, missing standard errors and a caution naming the alternatives. There is no long refit. A run whose covariance is only residue prints standard errors near 1e-15 and p-values near 1e-45, and its caution says to read none of them. An event-study family is the set of horizons for one estimand, such as att. A family whose covariance is wholly unidentified posts e(b_es_*) and e(numpre_*) without e(V_es_*).

items.heading: The zero-covariance caution names the cause that applied and leads with resampling
items.what_changed: The caution for a zero or residue covariance used to assume one cause. It blamed clustering at a high level and pointed every reader to the ame containment caution. It now names the cause that applied on the run. lattice() lets the dose effect vary across groups inside a cell. With robust and no cluster(), lattice() can also zero the covariance, and the caution now says so on such runs. It points to the containment caution only when that caution actually printed. bootstrap() and permute() now lead the list of alternatives. Conditional robust standard errors, which treat the covariates as fixed, are offered only to a run that has not already asked for a conditional variance. impvalues is offered only when cluster() is set, since it refuses to run without one. Under poisson on ppmlhdfe, robust standard errors are no longer offered, since that path already computes them.
items.why: A caution that names the wrong cause sends the user to the wrong fix. On contreat runs with robust alone, the old text pointed to a caution that had never printed. It then offered a finer cluster to a user who had not clustered at all. It offered robust standard errors to a user who had just asked for them. The new order of remedies follows a measurement. A simulation held the design fixed and redrew only the noise. On the design that prints this caution, customvce(robust) still reports a standard error. It was 0.017 of the estimator's own sampling spread on that design, about 58 times too small. So the remedies that resample the data come first.
items.decision: The text changes moved no number and were made without a ruling. The poisson part followed a ruling of 2026-09-25. The author ruled that poisson runs get their own arm in the cell containment check. The same ruling had the list of remedies stop offering robust standard errors to a run that already has them.
items.what_you_notice: The caution names the cause that applied to the run. It lists bootstrap() and permute() first. It no longer offers an option the run already uses or cannot use.

items.heading: gteffects cells inside one cluster are counted, and bootstrap is no longer named as a cure
items.what_changed: The gteffects option reports a separate estimate for each treated cohort and each period relative to onset. wooldid now counts the cells of that table that lie wholly inside one cluster. Under a robust variance, pweights, a robust customvce() or poisson on ppmlhdfe, it counts single-row cells instead. The count is posted as e(gt_ncontained). A caution says those cells' standard errors, p-values and intervals are understated. The caution and the help say that bootstrap() does not repair this. Only a finer cluster() does. Under a plain OLS variance there is no count.
items.why: A single cell has no averaging to hide behind. If it lies inside one cluster, the cluster-robust variance sees none of its own noise, and its interval badly under-covers. A cluster bootstrap cannot fix this. It resamples whole clusters, so a cell inside one cluster is drawn whole or not at all. Its own noise never varies across replications. In a test with no true effect, the bootstrap cell standard errors were 0.19 to 0.32 against a true spread of 1.12. Some cells printed a p-value of 0. Under a robust variance the same blind spot appears on a single-row cell, whose own dummy sets its residual to zero. The conventional OLS variance does not share it, because it pools residual variance across all cells. Over 400 simulated datasets its cell standard errors matched the true spread at a ratio of 0.999. The robust ones on the same data sat at 0.549.
items.decision: The count and caution were added without a ruling, because they change no number. The author ruled to add the poisson arm, since ppmlhdfe is robust even when not asked. He also ruled to extend the count to the plain OLS variance. That extension was measured first and not built, because it would have cautioned about cells whose standard errors are correct. That ruling still stands on paper, and withdrawing it is open to him. The earlier text that named bootstrap as a cure was corrected.
items.what_you_notice: gteffects runs print a count of affected cells and a caution, and e(gt_ncontained) holds the count. The caution no longer suggests bootstrap(). Poisson runs without cluster() now get the single-row count.
