items.heading: gteffects cells whose variance is only residue are left blank
items.what_changed: Some gteffects cells get a variance that is cancellation residue, or one that comes from an exact fit. wooldid now reports their standard error, p-value and interval as missing. The point estimates stay. Two floors decide which cells qualify. A cell fails if its standard error is below one ten-billionth of its estimate. It also fails if its variance is below one trillionth of the largest cell variance. Both floors are ratios, so multiplying the outcome by 1000 flags the same cells. The count is posted as e(gt_ndegen). A caution gives the count on analytic runs and under boottstat. Under a plain bootstrap() or permute() no caution prints, because the replications supply those columns. Under boottstat, the bootstrap mode that divides each replication's estimate by its standard error, the blanking also moves the p-values of the healthy cells.
items.why: Cancellation residue arises when a variance is the difference of nearly equal numbers. What is left is rounding error, near 1e-15. Before this change such cells printed as ordinary rows. They showed p-values near 1e-45 and intervals of zero width. On a test design with 40 states, 10 of 39 cells were of this kind. The smallest real standard error on that design was 0.0157. The two kinds of number sit about thirteen orders of magnitude apart, so the floors separate them cleanly. Under boottstat the residue values had been the divisors in every replication. Once those replications stop counting, the reference distribution for every cell changes.
items.decision: The author ruled to blank these cells. The first version also printed a note above the table, and on 2026-09-21 he had that note removed. The caution and e(gt_ndegen) remain. Under permute() no caution prints, since permute() already blanks those columns.
items.what_you_notice: Analytic gteffects runs with residue cells show blank inference columns on those rows. A caution gives the count, and e(gt_ndegen) holds it on every path. Under boottstat, p-values on the other cells can shift too.

items.heading: The zero-residual blind spot comes from the design, and robust does not escape it
items.what_changed: The help and guide now say that robust standard errors do not escape the problem when i is the unit. With one row per unit and period, each treated cell is a single row. Its own dummy drives its residual to zero. The att standard errors are then understated under robust, just as under cluster() at i. The entry for the stored event-study covariance lists two design conditions. Every user of that matrix inherits them. That includes honestdid, the Rambachan and Roth sensitivity analysis, and pretrendpower(), Roth's pre-trend power analysis. Sometimes pretrendpower() finds a pre-period block with less than full rank, meaning some combination of pre-period estimates has no measured variance. Its caution now says whether a design with single-row cells is the cause.
items.why: The zero residual comes from the cell dummies. The variance estimator does not cause it. Any robust variance built from residuals inherits it. The conventional OLS variance does not, because it pools residual variance across all cells. The guide had said robust avoids the problem. A simulation showed otherwise, with a robust att standard error of 0.212 against a true spread of 0.257. The conditions are spelled out because nothing in the matrix itself shows the problem.
items.decision: A caution on every design with single-row cells was considered and dropped. i equal to the unit is the ordinary call, so the caution would fire on a large share of runs. The explanation is attached instead to the existing rank caution in pretrendpower(). That caution fires only when the pre-period block actually lacks full rank. The correction to the guide was a documentation fix.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. The guide's advice on robust is reversed, and the e(V_es_*) entry carries the two conditions. When pretrendpower() finds a pre-period block without full rank, it prints a second line naming the likely cause. When that caution fires, the largest treated cell size it found is kept in the hidden e(roth_cellmax_*).

items.heading: Joint pre-trend tests under coarse clustering are computed with a caution
items.what_changed: The joint pre-trend test asks whether all pre-treatment estimates are zero together. Suppose i is nested in the cluster variable, so each level of i lies inside one cluster. jointtests and pretrendpower() still compute the test in that case. They now print a caution that its p-value is not calibrated, meaning it does not reject at the stated rate when the null is true. The caution names the valid alternatives. These are permute(), bootstrap(), or a cluster strictly finer than the cells that leaves many clusters in each. The nesting is judged on treated rows only. The adversarial line test carries the same warning in its help entry. It has no run-time check of how clusters sit relative to cells.
items.why: A joint test needs the covariance between horizons. With each cell inside one cluster, the cell's residuals sum to zero within that cluster. The cluster-robust variance then cannot capture how the cell's horizons move together. Measured rejection rates were 11 to 66 percent at a nominal 5 percent, and they did not improve with more cohorts or larger cells. The check reads treated rows because a common coding puts all never-treated units into one value of i. That value sits in every cluster. It would otherwise hide a design in which every treated cohort is nested.
items.decision: This was first a hard error that safety(off) could lift. The author downgraded it to a caution. Comparable packages run the same tests at panel-level clustering without any gate. wooldid's own help then recommended the clustering that tripped the error. So a refusal left users at a dead end. An earlier decision suppressed the test only inside pretrendpower(). It was replaced by one rule for both places the statistic appears. For the adversarial test the author chose documentation only.
items.what_you_notice: Compared with v1.3, the joint test prints the same number but now carries a caution under clustering at or above i. The caution names whichever option asked for the test.

items.heading: The adversarial line test says when its covariance has lost rank
items.what_changed: Sometimes the event-study covariance behind the adversarial line test has less than full rank. Some combination of the estimates then has no measured variance. The test now runs on the combinations a generalized inverse keeps. A generalized inverse stands in for the inverse of a matrix that has none. Without bootstrap() or permute(), a caution gives the rank and the degrees of freedom the test used. Here the degrees of freedom count the independent restrictions the test checked. They are stored in e(adversarial_df_att) and its twins for the other estimands and subgroups.
items.why: A test on a covariance that has lost rank checks fewer restrictions than the user asked for. Its p-value comes from a smaller reference distribution. Without the rank and the degrees of freedom, a reader cannot tell how much of the event-study evidence the test used.
items.decision: The author approved this caution and its wording on 2026-09-25. The caution states the degrees of freedom the test used, which is one fewer than the rank it keeps.
items.what_you_notice: An adversarial test on a covariance without full rank prints a caution with the rank and the degrees of freedom. e(adversarial_df_att) and its twins hold the degrees of freedom.

items.heading: Subgroup contrasts whose standard error is only rounding residue are blanked
items.what_changed: wooldid checks each pairwise subgroup contrast on the analytic path. It computes the implied correlation between the two subgroups' estimates. When that correlation exceeds 0.99, the contrast's standard error, statistic, p-value and interval are reported as missing. So is any equality test across subgroups that uses it. The point estimate stays, and a caution gives the count and the largest correlation. safety(off) prints the caution but keeps the numbers. permtstat and permanalyticse show the analytic standard error beside the permutation results. Under permute() with either option, the same check runs but nothing is blanked. The permutation p-values are built from differences in the estimates and do not use this standard error. The caution then counts the rows whose analytic standard error is residue.
items.why: A contrast's variance is the sum of the two variances minus twice their covariance. When the cells sit inside their clusters, the two subgroups' standard errors can agree to several digits. The contrast's standard error is then only what is left after they cancel. It is rounding residue, and it estimates nothing. On a test dataset the clustered contrast standard errors were 1/44 and 1/20 of their robust counterparts. The withheld equality p-values went as low as 3.3e-88. That is false certainty.
items.decision: The author ruled to blank the rows with a caution instead of printing them. The cut at a correlation of 0.99 was a judgment he confirmed. A cut at 0.999 was tried first. It caught only one of the two degenerate rows, whose correlations were 0.9994 and 0.9972. A healthy design sits near 0.5. On 2026-09-23 he ruled that permute() runs reuse the same check as a disclosure only, with the first sentence of the existing caution.
items.what_you_notice: Subgroup contrast rows that fail the check print a point estimate with blank inference columns and a caution. The matching equality test is stored as missing. Under permute() the rows keep their permutation inference, and a caution counts the residue analytic standard errors.

items.heading: Redundant absorbed copies of the dose no longer cost degrees of freedom
items.what_changed: Under contreat() with contreatcontrols(), wooldid adds exact copies of the dose. They control which column the collinearity check drops. reghdfe, the regression command wooldid calls by default, absorbs fixed effects without reporting them. It counted those absorbed copies as parameters, which cut the residual degrees of freedom. Now only the finest set is absorbed. e(df_r) and every standard error, t, p and interval now match the same model fitted without absorbing. Paths that enter these terms as ordinary regressors are unchanged. No point estimate moves.
items.why: A column that exactly copies one already in the model adds no information. It should not cost a degree of freedom. The small-sample correction should count only real parameters. The old count inflated every att standard error by the square root of the ratio of the two residual degrees of freedom. That was about 0.14 to 0.25 percent on the package's lattice test designs. On a plain run with one redundant copy it was a few hundredths of a percent. It grows only when residual degrees of freedom are few, reaching about 5 percent on a tiny test dataset with nine. The new standard error equals the one from the non-absorbing fit to all sixteen digits.
items.decision: The alternatives were to accept the extra count as built, since the effect is small, or to accept it and pin it in the tests. The author chose to count correctly.
items.what_you_notice: On contreat() runs with contreatcontrols() on the default reghdfe path, att standard errors fall slightly. The drop is about a quarter of one percent on the package's lattice test designs. e(df_r) rises. Point estimates do not change.

items.heading: The degrees-of-freedom rule is stated for every path
items.what_changed: The help now names the reference distribution on each path. Under cluster() it is t with one less than the number of clusters. Under clustering on several variables it is one less than the smallest count. Otherwise it is the residual degrees of freedom. Under poisson, p-values come from the normal. Under bootstrap() the rule follows bootdf(). Under impvalues it is the Ibragimov-Muller minimum. The recipe for testing across event-study horizons now posts the matrix with dof(e(df_r)). test and lincom then match the printed table.
items.why: With few clusters the gap between t with G minus 1 degrees of freedom and the normal is material, where G is the number of clusters. The t reference is the standard few-cluster recommendation, as Cameron and Miller (2015) summarise. A user who re-posts the event-study matrix without dof() gets the normal and chi-squared laws, whose intervals are narrower than the table's. v1.3 said only 'the residual degrees of freedom', which is not what reghdfe uses under clustering.
items.decision: Naming the reference distribution on each path was a documentation correction made on 2026-09-25, and it needed no ruling. A separate ruling of 2026-09-07 concerned a difference between the regression engines. The default reghdfe path and the regress-based paths used by customvce() and unconditionalse count fixed effects nested inside the cluster variable differently. So the same specification can return slightly different standard errors depending on the path. The author chose to document that difference and not rescale one path onto the other. The regress path is the conservative side. That note now lives in the guide's cluster() entry. The help's copy was removed when the help was shortened on 2026-09-21.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. The help lists each path's degrees of freedom, and the stored-results recipe carries dof(). The guide's cluster() entry notes the difference between engines.

items.heading: impvalues posts its own degrees of freedom and names the method
items.what_changed: impvalues replaces the analytic standard errors with Ibragimov-Muller inference. Each row's statistic and interval use t with q minus 1 degrees of freedom. Here q is the number of clusters that contribute an estimate to that row. e(df_r) is now the smallest of these. It used to be the first-stage regression's residual degrees of freedom. The range is posted in e(imdf_min) and e(imdf_max), and a note prints when rows differ. The header now reads Ibragimov-Muller p-values over the cluster variable, t on G minus 1 degrees of freedom. Before, it named a cluster-robust variance the run did not use.
items.why: The old e(df_r) was always larger than what the table used, for example 79 against 49. So esttab, lincom and test run on the stored results gave smaller p-values and narrower intervals than wooldid's own table. Posting the minimum makes a test run by hand conservative for every row.
items.decision: The options were the maximum, the minimum or a missing value. A missing value would push test and lincom to the normal, which gives intervals too narrow for every row. The author chose the Ibragimov-Muller degrees of freedom, posted as the minimum. He also had the header name the method, as the bootstrap and permutation paths already do.
items.what_you_notice: Under impvalues e(df_r) falls, tests run by hand widen to match the table, and the header names Ibragimov-Muller inference.

items.heading: impvalues refuses a cluster finer than i or one that cuts across it
items.what_changed: impvalues now stops with an error when the treated levels of i are split across more cluster groups than there are levels. That happens when cluster() is finer than i or crosses it. The check counts treated rows only, so pooling all never-treated units into one i does not trip it. safety(off) does not lift the error.
items.why: The Ibragimov and Muller method computes a separate estimate in each cluster and t-tests their spread. Its validity needs those estimates to be independent. In wooldid they are read off one fitted model. When several clusters share a level of i, their estimates are re-weightings of the same coefficients. They are not independent draws. The standard error then shrinks as cluster labels are added, even when no new information comes with them. Nominal 95 percent intervals covered 38 percent of the time for a nested cluster and 25 percent for a crossing one. This is the opposite layout from what the analytic path wants. So a design that needs a cluster below i should use bootstrap() or permute().
items.decision: It was first a caution. The author escalated it to an error, and later ruled that safety(off) should not lift it either. The guide notes that the check can refuse more than it needs to. A panel where a few units change cluster partway through is refused too, although its inference is barely affected.
items.what_you_notice: impvalues with a cluster finer than i, or one crossing it, now stops with an error. In v1.3 it ran and reported intervals far too narrow.

items.heading: impvalues always reports the equally weighted mean over clusters
items.what_changed: The impvalues entry now leads with the general rule. The method averages the cluster estimates with equal weight. So what it reports is the mean over clusters with each cluster weighted equally, whatever estimand was requested. att_i is the simple average of the cohort effects. cluster() at i with att_i is named as the pairing that fits by construction. wooldid does not refuse or caution about other estimands under impvalues. The help is the only safeguard.
items.why: Ibragimov and Muller's result needs the cluster estimates to be independent, roughly normal and to share a common mean. Their variances may differ. It is the t-statistic of the equally weighted mean that earns the conservative t reference with q minus 1 degrees of freedom when q is small. Reweighting the cluster estimates to match att's weights would recover the requested estimand. It would also give up that small-sample robustness, which is the reason to use the method at all.
items.decision: Reweighting the cluster estimates was proposed, and the author rejected it on this reasoning. A refusal of the combinations that do not fit, or a caution at the table, were then offered. He declined both and chose documentation only.
items.what_you_notice: No behaviour changes. The help states the equal weighting as the rule, and no longer presents it as a special case of cohort-level clustering.

items.heading: Conditional and unconditional standard errors differ when effects vary, whatever the sample size
items.what_changed: The help no longer says conditional and unconditional standard errors should be similar whenever samples are large. It says they are similar when effects vary little across cells, covariate values and doses. Where effects differ, the unconditional ones are larger. The ratio between them does not shrink as the sample grows. The conditional ones describe the effect averaged over the treated units in the sample. The unconditional ones describe the population average. The unconditionalse entry now also lists its constraints in full.
items.why: Both variances shrink at the same rate as the sample grows. The extra unconditional term is the spread of the unit-level effects across the treated sample. Those effects are the ones implied by covariates and cell membership. So the extra term measures how much effects vary, and it does not fade in large samples. With cohort effects of 0 and 4, the unconditional-to-conditional ratio was 2.23 at 60 units and 2.29 at 600. The choice is about the target, either the sample's treated units or the population they came from. Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2020) set this out. Sample size does not decide it.
items.decision: This corrected a factual error in the help and needed no ruling. The same entry reflects an earlier ruling of 2026-09-07. The author chose to document how fe() behaves on this path instead of changing it. reghdfe absorbs a bare fe() variable as a set of categories. regress and poisson read it as a single continuous variable and fit a linear term in the identifier. wooldid cautions and enters the variable as written. So the help tells users to put unit effects into controls() with their own i. prefixes on this path.
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. The guide no longer suggests that a large sample is a reason to skip unconditionalse.

items.heading: customvce() runs use the default cell collapse
items.what_changed: customvce() runs now use the default cell collapse. The collapse evaluates margins on one row per cell instead of on every row. The help had claimed the collapse matches an uncollapsed run to machine precision, and that was corrected. It matches to the accuracy of margins itself. That is usually machine precision, but up to about one part in a million on standard errors with weights, controls and an event-study window.
items.why: The collapse is exact because the treatment derivative is constant within a cell. margins reads only the coefficients and their variance. Neither fact depends on which command produced the variance. Holding customvce() out made every such run pay the full cost of margins with no gain in accuracy. The remaining differences come from the numerical derivatives margins takes, which the uncollapsed run shares.
items.decision: customvce() had been held out until it could be measured. The author asked for the measurement first. He then lifted the hold-out and had the help corrected.
items.what_you_notice: customvce() runs are faster. On weighted designs with controls, their standard errors can differ from an uncollapsed run around the sixth significant digit. nofastcollapse restores the old behaviour.

items.heading: The full event-study covariance is returned
items.what_changed: Each event-study family now returns three things. These are its coefficient vector labelled pre and post, its full covariance matrix, and the number of pre-periods. The covariance carries the true terms between horizons. This holds for att, att_it, ame and ame_it, and for each subgroup. After ereturn post with dof(e(df_r)) these work with lincom, test and honestdid. fastnose, the fast mode that skips variance estimation, posts the coefficient vector only. impvalues posts neither. The help lists the conditions honestdid needs to read the vector by position. It names e(es_ndegen_*) as the guard for rows whose variance is zero or missing.
items.why: All horizons of a family come from one margins call, so that call's covariance is their exact joint covariance. v1.3 computed it and threw it away. That blocked the Rambachan and Roth sensitivity analysis for parallel trends. It also blocked Roth's pre-trend power analysis and any test across horizons. The guard matters because honestdid does not reliably refuse a matrix with such rows. It can silently return a changed interval, or an identical one, with no warning.
items.decision: The author listed this feature from the outset. For rows with zero or missing variance he chose a help sentence naming e(es_ndegen_*). The alternatives were withholding e(numpre_*) or adding a run-time caution. For fastnose he had the command post the coefficient vector, so that the help's claim became true. The alternative was to correct the help.
items.what_you_notice: New stored results e(b_es_*), e(V_es_*) and e(numpre_*). Example 10 shows the handoff to honestdid.

items.heading: What e(V) now holds
items.what_changed: In v1.3 e(V) was a diagonal matrix of squared standard errors meant for display only. Now each event-study family's covariance block is placed into e(V), so test and lincom across horizons of one family are valid on the posted matrix. Every other term off the diagonal stays zero. A hidden marker, e(wdid_vcvstate), says what e(V) holds on the run. When only some standard errors are unidentified, e(V) is still posted. The missing entries carry a large negative placeholder, which Stata displays as a missing standard error. A caution gives the count.
items.why: Within one family the zeros were an accounting gap, because the joint covariance already existed. Across families, and between a family and a pooled estimate, the covariance is truly unavailable on several paths. A pooled effect is also a combination of its own horizons, so a full matrix would be singular by construction. Stata refuses to post a matrix with any missing diagonal entry. Before the placeholder, one unidentified standard error cost every other estimate its variance. A far horizon reached by a single cluster is a typical case. The placeholder had to avoid inventing a number anywhere it is read.
items.decision: The author was skeptical about posting a real covariance at all and asked for a feasibility study first. He then chose event-study blocks only, a stored marker and help text. He chose on purpose to print no footer under the table. A zero placeholder was rejected, because it gives zero-width intervals in esttab and falsely confident lincom results. A large positive one breaks the way test drops constraints. He had ruled that the placeholder's row and column be zeroed. The build zeroed only the terms off the diagonal, since zeroing the diagonal would turn a missing standard error into a printed zero. He ruled to keep it that way.
items.what_you_notice: test and lincom across horizons of one event-study family work on e(V) directly. Unidentified standard errors show as missing, and the rest of the table keeps its variance. Code that reads e(V) directly should treat a negative diagonal entry as not identified.

items.heading: The analytic simultaneous band uses a t law and has no floor
items.what_changed: simultaneousbands, off by default, builds a band that covers every horizon of an event study at once with the stated probability. Without bootstrap() it is simulated from the analytic event-study covariance. Where the regression reports degrees of freedom, the simulation uses the same t distribution as the pointwise intervals. Under poisson, which reports none, it uses the normal. No floor is applied, so on some designs the band can sit inside the pointwise intervals. With cluster() at or above i, a caution says the analytic band is too narrow and that bootstrap() gives a valid band.
items.why: A simultaneous band widens pointwise intervals so they hold jointly. It uses the sup-t form that Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2019) describe. Its critical value comes from the largest t-statistic across horizons. The band is scaled by the analytic standard errors. When those are understated because cells sit inside clusters, the band inherits the understatement. The t law keeps the band consistent with the pointwise intervals it is meant to widen. A normal law had made the band narrower than the pointwise interval at few clusters, covering 88 percent at a nominal 95.
items.decision: The author chose the multivariate t with the regression's degrees of freedom. A floor at the pointwise quantile was built and removed the same day. In his words, 'Better users see the SB approach isn't working as expected than a more sensible but fundamentally different type of result.' On 2026-09-25 he approved the caution for the analytic band at coarse clustering, along with its wording. The caution fires on the common design with i the unit and cluster(unit), as the jointtests caution already does. He was told this after it was built.
items.what_you_notice: A new option, simultaneousbands, with band endpoints in e(esband_*) and a dashed pair of lines on the plots. A caution prints when the analytic band is built with clustering at or above i.

title: The bootstrap engine
intro: This part covers bootstrap(). A bootstrap run fits the whole model again many times, each time on a resampled copy of the data. It then reports inference from the spread of those estimates. Version 1.3 had no bootstrap. Three themes run through the changes. A bootstrap run shows only bootstrap inference. The engine was checked draw by draw against Stata's own commands. Where a construction cannot be made right for an estimand or a design, the program refuses it or says so. It does not print an approximation in its place.

items.heading: A bootstrap of its own that replaces the analytic inference
items.what_changed: bootstrap(standard) or bootstrap(bayes), together with reps(), fits the full model again in every replication. A replication is one fit on one resampled data set. The printed standard errors, p-values, confidence intervals, joint tests and subgroup contrasts all become bootstrap quantities. So do the event study plots, the gteffects cells and the continuous treatment cells. Point estimates never change. The analytic covariance is the formula based one that version 1.3 printed. It is kept out of sight as e(V_analytic).
items.why: The analytic cluster robust standard errors are least reliable in the designs wooldid is built for. A cluster is a group of observations whose errors may be correlated, such as all rows from one state. Suppose cluster() sits at or above the cohort variable i. Then every treated cell of one cohort in one period lies inside a single cluster. The cluster robust formula has no variation inside that cluster from which to learn the cell's noise. In a simulation with 24 clusters above the unit level, the analytic standard error came out at 0.87 of the true sampling spread. The cluster bootstrap came out at 0.97. Resampling whole clusters and running the estimator again measures the spread directly.
items.decision: The author chose to replace the analytic numbers instead of printing a bootstrap block beside them. That way no analytic p-value can be read off a bootstrap run. His rule is that a bootstrap run never presents any other kind of p-value. He extended the rule to the plots after one case where the table's interval included zero and the plot's analytic band excluded it. He would have preferred to build on Stata's bootstrap prefix and on bayesboot. He accepted an engine written inside wooldid on one condition. It had to be shown to match them. The engine was needed for three reasons. The prefix refuses weighted commands. bayesboot cannot drive wooldid at all. The prefix also discards any replication in which an event study horizon disappears. With the same seed, the engine's replications match the prefix to 14 decimal places. Its Bayesian draws match the random number generator behind bayesboot exactly.
items.what_you_notice: A new family of options appears. It is bootstrap(), reps(), bootdisplay(), bootdf(), boottstat and bootsave(). The tables hold bootstrap numbers, and a footer names the method. Unless boottstat is asked for, replications skip variance estimation, since only their point estimates are needed. Only histogramcohorteffects is untouched, because it draws point estimates.

items.heading: The standard mode is the pairs cluster bootstrap
items.what_changed: bootstrap(standard) draws whole cluster() groups with replacement. With replacement means one cluster can be drawn more than once and another not at all. With no cluster(), it draws single observations. This is called the pairs cluster bootstrap, because each drawn cluster brings its outcomes and regressors along together. For att and ame without boottstat, a cluster drawn twice is carried as a weight of 2 on its original rows. Its rows are not copied. The estimands that weight cells equally copy the rows instead, and so does boottstat under cluster(). The draws come from Stata's own bsample command. So a run with a given seed uses random numbers in the same order as the official bootstrap prefix.
items.why: Resampling whole clusters keeps the dependence inside each cluster intact. That is what makes the spread of the replications a valid standard error when errors are correlated within clusters. Consider an estimand that averages over observations. Weighting a cluster by the number of times it was drawn gives the same estimate as copying it. The two agreed to 15 decimal places, the limit of machine precision. Weighting costs much less.
items.decision: Drawing with bsample lets every replication be checked against Stata's official bootstrap. That check was the author's condition for writing the engine inside wooldid. One check looked at a panel run without cluster(). There, the bootstrap standard error that resampled whole units was 1.5 times the one that resampled single observations. The author chose not to add a caution for this. The footer instead names the run an observation level bootstrap.
items.what_you_notice: The footer says cluster bootstrap or observation level bootstrap. Without cluster(), nothing warns that panel rows are being resampled one at a time. So give cluster() at the level where treatment is assigned.

items.heading: Replications are counted estimate by estimate
items.what_changed: Replications are stored by coefficient name. So a resample in which an event study horizon or a subgroup disappears still counts for every other estimate. Each standard error uses the replications in which that estimate exists. That count is recorded in e(boot_navail). A caution names any estimate available in fewer than half of the completed replications. A replication that fails is dropped and counted in e(boot_failed). No minimum share of replications has to complete. The ame is the average marginal effect of a continuous dose. A replication can return an exact 0 for it because the resample lost all dose variation in some cells. That 0 is treated as missing for that estimate.
items.why: Stata's prefix drops any replication whose set of coefficients shrank. It keeps only the draws in which every horizon survived. That understates the spread of exactly the horizons most at risk of disappearing. The zero rule exists because a hard 0 from a resample with no dose variation is not an estimate. Counting it would make the ame look far more precise than it is.
items.decision: The author chose no completion floor for the bootstrap, unlike permute(). Counting per estimate and the zero rule were adopted as part of the engine's design.
items.what_you_notice: Cautions list failed replications, excluded zero cells and estimates with low availability. e(boot_navail) gives the count behind each standard error. Treated cells with no dose variation inside the cell are now dropped from every fit, replications included. So the zero rule catches only the cases that screen misses.

items.heading: att_i, att_it and att_itime resample whole cells, under a rule that respects how i and cluster() relate
items.what_changed: These three estimands give each treated cell equal weight. A cell is one value of i in one period. When one of them is requested, each replication copies the drawn clusters. Suppose cluster() nests i, meaning each unit of i lies wholly inside one cluster. Then every copy gets a fresh unit code. The fresh code replaces i wherever i appears in fe(), controls(), interactivecontrols(), coarsecohortcontrols() or ccc_absorb(). Now suppose cluster() is finer than i or cuts across it. Then units keep their identity. A cluster drawn twice arrives as duplicate rows inside its unit's cells. Two earlier refusals are gone. One refused a cluster that does not nest i. The other refused these estimands without cluster().
items.why: A weight that is constant within a cluster cancels out of an average within a cell. So weighting alone would hold the set of cells fixed. It would miss the variance that comes from which cells were drawn. The standard errors would then be too small when effects vary across clusters. Copying clusters with fresh codes restores that part of the variance. Fresh codes are wrong when a unit spans two clusters. They would split that unit in two in every replication. Unit fixed effects would turn into unit by cluster effects. Covariates that name i must follow the fresh code too. Otherwise the two copies of a cluster share one unit effect. The replication would then fit a different model from the one being resampled. This matters most under boottstat, which uses each replication's standard errors.
items.decision: The author chose separate paths for estimands that weight observations and estimands that weight cells. He rejected refusing the cell weighted ones. He also rejected running them on weights with a caution. His principle is that i says which cohorts the effects average over. cluster() is a claim about dependence and about how treatment was assigned. So a cluster finer than i is legitimate and should run. The choice between the two rules is one switch for the whole run. A single unit that straddles two clusters puts every unit under the rule that keeps identities. He chose to disclose that instead of handling each unit separately. The geometry is rare and is usually a specification mistake. He also asked that unit codes inside covariates be rewritten instead of warned about.
items.what_you_notice: Runs with a cluster finer than i now work. Some units may straddle two clusters in a run with a cell weighted estimand. Then a caution says the att_i, att_it and att_itime standard errors can be too small. It suggests egen newi = group(i clus), missing, or a cluster that nests i. In one measured case, a single straddling unit out of 96 cut the att_i standard error by 20 to 29 percent. e(boot_nstraddle), e(boot_reid) and e(boot_covsub) record what happened. A variable that encodes i under another name keeps its original codes. A simulation checked coverage, which is the share of simulated data sets whose interval contains the true value. Its pass rule was written down before it ran. With a cluster finer than i, the att_i interval covered 94.7 percent at a stated 95. With cluster() equal to i, it covered 99.3 percent, so that interval is too wide. That conservatism was there before this change. It was reported to the author and left in place.

items.heading: The Bayesian bootstrap has one convention, and it is refused for the estimands that weight cells equally
items.what_changed: bootstrap(bayes) is the Bayesian bootstrap. It never drops a cluster. Instead, each replication gives every cluster a random positive weight. The weights come from a flat Dirichlet distribution, so they sum to one and every way of splitting the total is equally likely. Every row of the cluster, and any user weight, is multiplied by its cluster's weight. A cluster's total weight stays proportional to its size. The bootalpha() option, which chose another convention, is gone. bootstrap(bayes) with att_it, att_i or att_itime stops with an error under every safety() setting.
items.why: This is the Bayesian bootstrap of Rubin (1981), with clusters as the units being drawn. It is centred on the same estimand as the point estimate. Its weights match those of the pairs cluster bootstrap in mean. They match in variance up to a factor of G over G plus 1, where G is the number of clusters. Two earlier forms were measured wrong. bayesboot's convention sets each cluster's Dirichlet parameter to its row count. That treats panel rows as independent evidence. In a simulation its standard errors came out at 0.28 to 0.39 of the true spread. The first build of the kept convention divided each cluster's draw by the cluster's weight total. So every cluster carried the same expected mass whatever its size. On unequal clusters the replications centred near 0.80 while the estimate was 1.69. The default interval excluded the estimate. The kept convention still gives slightly small standard errors. In the same simulation they ran 6 to 10 percent below those of the pairs bootstrap. A later simulation on clusters of equal size agreed in direction. Measured against the analytic standard error, bayes gave 0.94 and the pairs bootstrap 1.04. So bootstrap(standard) is the better calibrated choice where it is available. The estimands that weight cells equally raise a separate problem. Reweighting never adds or removes a cell. A weight constant within a cluster cancels out of an average that gives cells equal weight. So the part of the variance that comes from sampling cells is missed.
items.decision: The author adopted bayesboot's convention as the default. He reversed it the same day on the simulation evidence and kept it only as bootalpha(size). He chose to fix the kept convention's centring error once it was shown. The size convention had its own centring error on weighted data. There the draws sat 9.4 bootstrap standard deviations off centre. That error was fixed, and then it went away with the option. He deleted bootalpha() because its only other value existed to reproduce another command's number. On panel data that value could only mislead. For the estimands that weight cells equally, he first allowed a run under safety(off) with a caution. He then removed that exception. The standard errors would be too small with nothing in the output to show it.
items.what_you_notice: Naming bootalpha() is an error, and e(boot_alpha) is not posted. bayes results do not change, since the kept convention was already the default. bootstrap(bayes) with att_i, att_it or att_itime stops with an error that points to bootstrap(standard).

items.heading: Four ways to read the draws, with percentile as the default and one standard error for all four
items.what_changed: bootdisplay() picks the p-value and interval the tables print. percentile, the default, reads them off the ranks of the draws. bc shifts the percentiles to correct for median bias. Median bias means more than half the draws fall on one side of the estimate. bca is described below. wald uses a normal or t approximation built on the bootstrap standard error. All except bca are computed and stored on every run. Without boottstat, the standard error column is always the standard deviation of the bootstrap draws. So the estimate plus or minus a critical value times that standard error need not reproduce the printed percentile interval. Stata's own bootstrap behaves the same way. Under the displays that rank the draws, the statistic column is labelled t_wald or z_wald.
items.why: Percentile intervals keep the asymmetry of the sampling distribution. A symmetric interval hides it. The standard deviation of the draws is the standard error users expect from other software. The ratio of the estimate to its standard error belongs to a different test from a p-value read off ranks. Printing the two side by side without a label invites reading them as one test.
items.decision: The author first preferred a standard error backed out of the percentile interval. After consulting others, he chose the common convention over his own preference. He also judged that a number backed out of an interval is not a standard error. Making wald the default was considered and declined. Stata's prefix, csdid and did_multiplegt all use it as their default. Relabelling the statistic column was chosen over blanking it.
items.what_you_notice: By default, intervals can be asymmetric and p-values are percentile p-values. The statistic column is marked t_wald or z_wald. A footer explains that a test run by hand on e(V) gives the wald numbers, which differ from the printed ones.

items.heading: A p-value for the bias corrected intervals
items.what_changed: The bc and bca displays print a p-value. It is the smallest significance level at which the bias corrected interval excludes zero. With no median bias it equals the percentile p-value. It does not move in steps of 2 over n, where n is the number of replications. It can be exactly 0 when every draw falls on one side of zero.
items.why: The author chose never to back a standard error out of an interval. That left the bias corrected family with an interval but no p-value. Defining the p-value from the interval makes the two tell the same story. The interval at any level excludes zero exactly when the p-value is below one minus that level.
items.decision: Stata's estat bootstrap reports bias corrected intervals without p-values. So there was no convention to copy. The construction follows directly from the display choice above.
items.what_you_notice: A p-value column appears under bc and bca. Stata's own bootstrap shows none there.

items.heading: Bias corrected and accelerated intervals from a jackknife over clusters
items.what_changed: bootdisplay(bca) gives bias corrected and accelerated intervals, known as BCa. The acceleration term comes from a jackknife. The jackknife drops one cluster at a time and fits the model again. That adds G fast fits after the replications. bca requires cluster() and is computed only when asked for. Under bca, the gteffects and continuous treatment cells show the bc family.
items.why: Efron's BCa interval adjusts the percentile interval for two things. One is median bias. The other is skewness that changes with the size of the parameter, which the acceleration term measures. Without cluster(), the jackknife would need one fit per observation.
items.decision: The author chose to build it, since Stata's own prefix offers it too. A separate jackknife for each cell was judged not worth its run time. So the cells keep the bc family.
items.what_you_notice: A bca run ends with G extra fits. Asking for bca without cluster() is an error. The cells carry the bc family.

items.heading: Which p-values add one, and what a p-value of 0 means
items.what_changed: A percentile p-value is the plain two sided share of draws beyond the null. It is twice the smaller of the two tail counts, divided by the number of replications. It can print exactly 0. Studentized p-values come from boottstat, described below. They add one to the tail count and one to the number of replications, so they cannot print 0. Joint, equality and adversarial tests use a one sided share, also with one added. Their smallest possible value is 1 over n plus 1, where n is the number of replications. reps() is required and has no minimum. A caution says when the smallest attainable p-value is above .05. A p-value of 0 stays 0, with a line under the table giving the resolution.
items.why: Adding one treats the observed statistic as one more draw from the reference set under the null. For permutation draws that is exact. Under the null, the observed assignment is just as likely as any permuted one. The studentized and joint test bootstrap draws are recentred to mimic the null. For them, adding one is the usual convention for Monte Carlo tests. It errs on the conservative side by one rank step. It also removed a measured problem. On the studentized tail, the plain share rejected 6 percent of the time at a stated 5 percent with 99 replications. Percentile draws are centred at the estimate. Adding one there would only be a choice to be conservative, with no such argument behind it. Measured, the plain share disagreed with the percentile interval in 6 of 35,646 cases. The add one form disagreed in 36. A p-value of 0 means no replication reached the far side of the null. That says more about resolution than about the strength of the evidence.
items.decision: One convention everywhere was considered. The author chose the split. He had the reasoning published in the help and the companion guide. He refused a minimum number of replications, because small runs are useful for timing a specification. He added the resolution caution instead. He first asked for the table to print a zero as less than 2 over n. The numeric table cannot carry that sign, so the resolution line was printed under the table instead. He then ruled that the 0 stays in the cell and in e(). Under bc and bca, the resolution line and caution are skipped. Those p-values do not move in steps of 2 over n.
items.what_you_notice: Leaving out reps() is an error. At low reps() a caution names the smallest p-value the run can produce. Percentile p-values of 0 come with a resolution note. Studentized p-values are never 0.

items.heading: The wald family uses t with G minus 1 degrees of freedom when clustered
items.what_changed: bootdf() sets the reference distribution for the wald family and for its joint test F statistic. With cluster(), the default is a t distribution with G minus 1 degrees of freedom. G is the number of clusters in the estimation sample. Without cluster(), the default is the normal. bootdf(clusters) without cluster() is refused. A number sets the degrees of freedom directly. e(df_r) follows the choice. So test and lincom on e(V) reproduce the wald family. G now counts only clusters that contribute rows to the fit. Some rows are dropped by the fit, such as rows with missing values or fixed effect groups of one observation. They no longer create clusters to draw from. On one test design with a wholly dropped cohort, this moved the bootstrap standard error by about 5 percent.
items.why: With a few dozen clusters, the bootstrap standard error is itself noisy. So an interval of 1.96 standard errors either side covers too rarely, even when the standard error is right on average. In a simulation such an interval covered 81 percent at a stated 95. A t critical value with G minus 1 degrees of freedom recovers some of that. At 24 clusters it is 2.069, about 5.6 percent wider. Without clusters, G minus 1 would be the number of observations minus 1. That is the normal in practice. A cluster with no rows in the fit cannot change any replication. Counting it made G too large and let empty clusters be drawn in place of live ones.
items.decision: Stata's prefix uses the normal, and so did wooldid at first. The author made the t reference a choice, and then the default whenever cluster() is given. He refused to let bootdf(clusters) fall back silently to t with the number of observations minus 1 as its degrees of freedom. A reference built from the replications themselves is left as a possible later value.
items.what_you_notice: Clustered runs print t statistics and slightly wider wald intervals than a normal reference would give. Percentile, bc, bca and studentized results do not depend on bootdf(). On runs where the fit drops whole clusters, the bootstrap standard errors and degrees of freedom change.

items.heading: boottstat, an optional studentized bootstrap
items.what_changed: boottstat bootstraps the t statistic instead of the coefficient. This is called a studentized, or percentile t, bootstrap. In each replication, the estimate is centred at the observed one. It is then divided by that replication's own analytic standard error. The p-value and interval come from the ranks of those t statistics. The standard error column then shows the analytic standard error, labelled se_analytic. The statistic is labelled t_pt. It covers every coefficient, the gteffects and continuous treatment cells, and the subgroup contrasts. It also covers the joint, equality and adversarial tests. It is refused with poisson, with bootstrap(bayes), with fastnose, and with the wald, bc and bca displays.
items.why: A percentile t bootstrap is valid only under one condition. Each replication's standard error must use the same calculation on the resampled data as the observed one uses on the original data. Suppose a cluster drawn twice were carried as one cluster with weight 2. The cluster robust formula would square its contribution. Replication standard errors would then come out about 1.4 times too large. The reference distribution would be too narrow, and the test would reject far more often than its stated level. So under cluster(), a duplicated cluster is copied and given its own code. Each replication clusters on those codes. Poisson replications run on sampling weights. The Bayesian bootstrap uses continuous weights. Neither can be turned into literal copies. Studentizing them would give intervals that are too narrow.
items.decision: The author asked for bootstrapped t statistics, but not as the default. Every replication must then estimate its own variance, and the run is much slower. He wanted the interval shown with its asymmetry. So a symmetric interval built from absolute t values was rejected. The help promises only that the replication standard error is the same calculation as the observed one. It does not promise calibrated coverage. The one simulation run so far covered the true value in 10 of 10 data sets, too few to establish a rate. He also ruled on a caution about subgroup contrasts, described below. It prints only when the problem actually occurs, instead of on every clustered run with subgroups.
items.what_you_notice: Columns are labelled se_analytic and t_pt. The interval is not symmetric about the estimate. A run is several times slower than a plain bootstrap. Suppose cluster() sits at or above i. Then the analytic standard errors of pairwise subgroup contrasts can be degenerate, meaning zero or unusable. The studentized subgroup contrasts and the equality test may then be absent, with a caution. Cell containment means each treated cell lies inside one cluster. Under it, the ame rows have no analytic standard error to divide by. So use bootstrap() without boottstat there. On a boottstat run, e(boot_ci_percentile), e(boot_ci_bc), e(boot_p_percentile) and e(boot_p_bc) hold the families built from the coefficient draws. They do not hold the studentized results printed in the table.

items.heading: No bias corrected studentized interval
items.what_changed: A bias corrected studentized interval was built at first. It has been withdrawn. bootdisplay(bc) and bootdisplay(bca) are refused with boottstat. Only the percentile display exists there.
items.why: The construction applied the bias correction shift to the quantiles of centred t draws and then reflected them. That moves the interval against the bias. It undoes the correction that percentile t already makes. In a test case its upper endpoint landed on the plain percentile endpoint that bias correction exists to repair. No such construction appears in Efron and Tibshirani (1993) or in Davison and Hinkley (1997). Percentile t is already second order accurate. That means its coverage error shrinks faster with sample size than that of a plain percentile interval.
items.decision: The author chose to refuse the combination. Repairing the direction of the shift was possible in principle. No verified correction was available, though. Keeping it as documented would have cost roughly 0.6 points of coverage.
items.what_you_notice: Combining bc or bca with boottstat is an error.

items.heading: Replications with no usable variance are left out and counted, never adjusted
items.what_changed: Under boottstat, a replication can return standard errors that are all tiny. The cut is a hundred millionth of the outcome's standard deviation. Such a replication keeps its point estimates. It is left out of every studentized p-value, interval, band and test. It is counted in e(boot_novar). Replications with any standard error below a hundred thousandth on the same scale are counted in e(boot_sesmall), with a caution. No standard error is ever raised to a floor or replaced.
items.why: A resample that draws too few distinct clusters can fit the data exactly. That gives a standard error near zero. Dividing by it makes the t statistic explode. One such replication once pushed a simultaneous band out to about 385 trillion.
items.decision: Substituting a floor value for tiny standard errors was proposed. The author refused any heuristic editing of a standard error. The honest options left were to exclude the draw and to say so. He chose both.
items.what_you_notice: Cautions give the counts. Studentized columns may rest on fewer replications than completed.

items.heading: Joint and equality tests are bootstrap rank tests, and the adversarial test needs boottstat
items.what_changed: Under bootstrap(), two kinds of joint test become bootstrap tests. One is the joint pretrend test, which asks whether the effects before treatment are all zero. The other asks whether effects are equal across subgroups. Without boottstat, each test measures the distance of the estimates from zero, scaled by the bootstrap covariance. It does the same for each replication, after centring the replications at the estimate. It then ranks the observed distance among them. With boottstat, each replication uses its own covariance. The adversarial pretrend test is bootstrapped only under boottstat. Without it the test is reported as absent, with a caution.
items.why: Centring the draws at the estimate makes them behave like draws taken when the null is true. Ranking the observed statistic among them needs no chi squared approximation. The permutation engine uses the same construction. With clustering at or above i, the analytic joint test is the part that fails. So this is where a bootstrap test matters most. The adversarial test needs each replication's own event study covariance. Only boottstat replications compute it.
items.decision: A chi squared Wald test on the bootstrap covariance was built first. That is what Stata's prefix does. The author's rule is that a bootstrap run never shows an analytic p-value. A test that cannot be bootstrapped is left absent. That rule led him to the rank test. For the adversarial test, he rejected two alternatives. One showed the analytic value. The other showed a fitted line without a p-value. Either invites reading it as a bootstrap result.
items.what_you_notice: Joint test p-values have a floor of 1 over n plus 1. A footer notes that a test run by hand on e(V) is a different test. e(boot_jt_absent), e(boot_sgjt_absent) and e(boot_adv_absent) flag withheld tests. In a simulation where the pretrends were truly parallel, neither version of the joint test rejected too often.
sources: wooldid.sthlp boottstat entry L409-410, adversarial entry L579-580

items.heading: Simultaneous event study bands from the replications
items.what_changed: With simultaneousbands, a bootstrap run builds a sup t band from the replications. A sup t band is meant to cover every event study horizon at once. For each replication, the program finds the largest standardized deviation across horizons. The band uses an upper quantile of those largest deviations. Under boottstat, each replication's deviations are divided by its own standard errors. The band is then a percentile t band, on the same scale as the intervals beside it. Replications with no usable variance are left out of it.
items.why: Reading many horizons at once needs a correction for multiple comparisons. A band built from the same draws covers every horizon together with the stated probability. The analytic band is too narrow when clustering is at or above i. So the help points to the bootstrap there.
items.decision: The author chose bands as the bootstrap's tool for many horizons. He left the step down procedure, which adjusts each horizon's p-value for the others, to permute(). Under boottstat he chose the percentile t form over a single construction that uses the standard deviation of the draws. That way the band matches the intervals beside it.
items.what_you_notice: Bootstrap plots show dashed band lines. e(esband_engine) reads bootstrap or bootstrap-studentized.

items.heading: What e(V), e(p) and the interval matrices hold after a bootstrap run
items.what_changed: e(V) is the full bootstrap covariance of the reported estimates. It is computed from the replications in which every estimate exists. Its diagonal is rescaled so the square roots equal the bootstrap standard deviations. Those are the printed standard errors, except under boottstat. There the table shows se_analytic, while e(V) still holds the bootstrap standard deviations. The event study blocks e(V_es_*) are rebuilt from the replications too. So honestdid and pretrendpower read bootstrap covariances. e(p), e(ci_l) and e(ci_u) carry the p-values and intervals of the displayed family.
items.why: A covariance built pair by pair from different subsets of replications can fail to be positive definite. Positive definite is the property a test needs to invert the matrix safely. When it fails, a test run by hand silently drops a restriction. It then returns a confident but wrong p-value. A covariance from replications complete in every estimate cannot fail that way. Rescaling the diagonal keeps every correlation. It also makes tests run by hand match the bootstrap standard deviations. Without e(p) and the interval matrices, esttab rebuilt the wald family from e(V). A paper's table could then disagree with the log it came from.
items.decision: Swapping e(V) back to the analytic covariance under boottstat was considered. The author chose to keep the bootstrap standard deviation covariance in e(V). The footer names the commands that read it, which are test, lincom, coefplot and honestdid. For esttab he chose to post the displayed family, as permute() already did.
items.what_you_notice: e(V) is a full matrix, so tests across estimands work. A caution with e(boot_V_shortfall) fires when e(V) rests on fewer than half the completed replications. esttab now shows the printed p-values and intervals. Its standard errors still come from e(V). So on a boottstat run, esttab shows the bootstrap standard deviations in place of the printed se_analytic. e(wdid_vcvstate) reads bootstrap.

items.heading: A caution when few clusters are treated, and no wild cluster bootstrap
items.what_changed: Sometimes fewer than 6 clusters in the estimation sample are ever treated. Then a caution says the bootstrap is badly sized there, meaning its tests reject at the wrong rate. It says boottstat does not cure this. It points to permute(), or to boottest on the underlying regression outside wooldid. The help says neither bootstrap mode is a remedy for few treated clusters. It also says no wild cluster bootstrap is offered. A wild cluster bootstrap keeps every cluster and flips the signs of each cluster's residuals at random.
items.why: With few treated clusters, many resamples draw no treated cluster at all. Those replications fail and are dropped. What remains is conditional on drawing at least one treated cluster. With 2 of 12 clusters treated, 11.5 percent of replications were dropped. MacKinnon and Webb find the pairs cluster bootstrap badly sized in this setting. The earlier caution counted all clusters, which misses the problem.
items.decision: The wild cluster bootstrap is the usual remedy in the literature. It would need the margins step fitted again in every replication, which amounts to a separate engine. So the author chose a caution naming the alternatives. He considered adding a sentence that the wild bootstrap is itself very conservative with very few treated clusters. He did not adopt it.
items.what_you_notice: A caution gives the number of treated clusters.

items.heading: What the bootstrap does not fix
items.what_changed: The help says when to use bootstrap(). The first case is when the analytic covariance cannot be trusted. That means cluster() at or above i, joint tests and subgroup contrasts there, and the ame under cell containment. Under cell containment, only bootstrap() without boottstat gives the ame rows inference, since their analytic standard errors are missing. The second condition is clusters numbering in the tens or more. The companion guide adds that reported inference needs several hundred replications. The percentile and bias corrected intervals need a thousand or more. The help also says the bootstrap does not repair gteffects cells that lie wholly inside one cluster. Only a cluster() strictly finer than the cells of one cohort in one period does that.
items.why: A cell inside one cluster is always resampled whole or not at all. So its own noise never varies across replications. Its bootstrap standard error is understated, just like the analytic one. In a check, such cell standard errors came out at .19 to .32 against a true 1.12. The att rows are fine, because resampling varies which treated units enter them. The same check put the att standard error at .249 against a simulated spread of .257.
items.decision: Earlier text listed bootstrap() and permute() as remedies for those cells. It was corrected once the mechanism was checked.
items.what_you_notice: The help's discussion of what level to cluster at now says this. The gteffects caution that counts such cells applies under the bootstrap as well.
sources: wooldid_agent_guide.md ch.5 'When and how', reps() L274, L286

items.heading: How the bootstrap constructions were checked by simulation
items.what_changed: The author ordered a coverage study of the bootstrap as built. Coverage is the share of simulated data sets whose interval contains the true effect. The study used two designs. One had 24 clusters of equal size. The other had 12 clusters of unequal size, with the effect growing with cluster size. Each cell of the study used between 10 and 29 simulated data sets. On the unequal design, the analytic clustered interval covered 82.8 percent at a stated 95. The bootstrap that copies clusters covered 96.4 percent on the same data sets. On the equal design, the percentile and bias corrected intervals covered 87.5 percent. The copying path gave standard errors about 5 percent wider than the weighting path. Neither version of the joint pretrend test rejected too often when pretrends were truly parallel.
items.why: The percentile default and the other families were chosen before any coverage was measured. A simulation is the only direct check that an interval covers at its stated rate. With so few data sets, each coverage figure carries a Monte Carlo standard error, the noise from simulating only a few data sets. At 24 data sets that noise is about 4 to 7 points. The unequal design is the setting where the help tells users to reach for the bootstrap. The study shows why. The analytic standard error there was about 30 percent too small, and the bootstrap closed the gap. The 5 percent gap between the copying and weighting paths runs in the direction the design predicts. Copying adds the variance from sampling cells.
items.decision: The author ordered the study after the percentile default was questioned for having no measured coverage. Apart from the analytic interval on the unequal design, no gap it found reached two Monte Carlo standard errors. The 5 percent gap between the two paths is correctly signed, but its size is not yet established.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing in the output. The study supports the help's advice to use bootstrap(standard) on unequal clusters when clustering is at or above i.
sources: review_process/research_2026-09-06/F058_bootstrap.md s1 (82.8 percent, n=29), s2 (87.5 percent, n=24), s6 (joint tests), s7 (96.4 percent, n=28; ratio 1.046), 'Surfaces off by more than 2 MC standard errors'

items.heading: pretrendpower() works under the bootstrap
items.what_changed: pretrendpower() used to be refused with bootstrap(). It now runs after the replications, on the bootstrap event study covariance. Roth's (2022) power diagnostics ask how likely a pretrend test was to detect a given violation of parallel trends. They and the pretrend slope now use that covariance. If the covariance cannot be built for a family, the diagnostic is skipped for that family. It is never computed on the analytic covariance instead.
items.why: The refusal existed only because the diagnostic ran before the bootstrap covariance existed. The Roth (2022) formulas take a covariance as input. Where the analytic one is unreliable, feeding them the bootstrap one is the natural choice.
items.decision: The author asked for the extension. He declined a power calculation simulated from the shape of the draws. He preferred to stay within Roth's normal formulas for a feature that cites him. The pretrend slope is estimated by generalized least squares, with the covariance supplying the weights. Under the bootstrap it is estimated again with the bootstrap covariance, so that diagnostic's slope moves. A variant that kept the analytic weights and bootstrapped only the slope's standard error was proposed. He ruled that the estimated again form stands, as documented.
items.what_you_notice: pretrendpower() now works with bootstrap(). The Roth slope and power figures differ from those of the analytic run. A caution names any family it skipped.

items.heading: latticeignoreweights forms the lattice again on each resample
items.what_changed: A lattice is a set of dose levels formed from quantiles of the treatment. With a generated lattice and latticeignoreweights, each bootstrap replication now forms its quantile bins on the resample. It drops the user's weight. It keeps the replication's own draw count or Dirichlet weight.
items.why: Before, the option dropped the whole weight. So which rows fed the bins depended on the internal path a replication took. On unweighted data the option does nothing analytically, yet it changed the bootstrap result. Forming the bins again on each resample is the ordinary bootstrap of a statistic whose bins are estimated from the data.
items.decision: The alternative put to the author was to read the option as ignoring the resample too. Each replication's bins would then stay on the unweighted drawn rows. Under the Bayesian bootstrap they would stay on the original sample. He chose to form the bins on the resample, accepting that bootstrap standard errors on those runs move.
items.what_you_notice: Lattice runs that use latticeignoreweights get different bootstrap standard errors.

items.heading: The draws are kept and every run can be replayed
items.what_changed: bootsave(name) writes every replication's estimates to name.dta. The file has a row for the observed estimates. Failed replications are kept as empty rows. Under boottstat the replication standard errors are saved too. One column per cluster holds its draw count or Dirichlet weight. The file records the seed and the state of the random number generator. Every run also stores that state in e(boot_rngstate). Above 10,000 replications the draw matrices are not posted in e(), and a caution says so. The file is written regardless. dots() prints a projected run time after the fifth replication.
items.why: Saving the draws lets users compute any statistic of them. They can check wooldid's inference by hand. They can replay a run exactly, even one run without a seed. They can see which clusters drove a result. A bootstrap costs the time of one run multiplied by reps(). An early projection helps a user decide whether to wait or to cut reps().
items.decision: The author asked for the saved draws. A failed write became a caution below the tables. It is not an error at the end of a full run. Problems with the file name are caught before the loop starts. The limit on matrix size had been silent. The author approved a caution so users do not look for a matrix that was never posted.
items.what_you_notice: There is a bootsave() option. e(boot_save_rc) records a failed write. A caution appears above 10,000 replications. The dots line carries a time estimate.

items.heading: What bootstrap() will not combine with
items.what_changed: bootstrap() is refused with permute(), impvalues, unconditionalse, customvce() and cluster() on more than one variable. It needs at least two clusters. fastnose with bootstrap() is now accepted, with a caution that it has no effect. It is still refused with boottstat. Several earlier refusals are gone. They covered pretrendpower(), a cluster that does not nest i, and the estimands that weight cells equally without cluster(). They also covered fastnose outside boottstat.

Clustering on more than one variable leaves no single unit to resample. fastnose only switches off variance estimation. Plain bootstrap replications already skip it. boottstat needs each replication's own standard errors.
items.decision: Each remaining refusal was checked and kept as a real conflict. The author chose to turn the fastnose error into a caution. Typing a speed option that is already in force should not stop a run.
items.what_you_notice: There are fewer refusals than before. fastnose with a plain bootstrap gives a caution instead of an error.
