title: Randomization inference: permute() and its companion options
intro: Version 1.3 had no randomization inference. wooldid now has a second way to compute p-values, built for designs with few treated clusters. It reassigns treatment onset dates across clusters and reruns the full estimator on each reassignment. It then ranks the observed estimates among the results. One rule guides every change in this section. Every number a permute() run reports comes from the same estimator, applied to reassigned onsets under the sharp null. The sharp null says treatment had no effect on any unit at any time. Anything that cannot be produced that way is left blank. The help states what the test assumes.

items.heading: A new way to get p-values: randomization inference over onset dates
items.what_changed: permute(shuffle) reassigns the observed onset dates across clusters. It keeps the number of clusters at each onset date fixed. Never treated counts as one more onset label. permute(probabilities) instead draws each cluster's onset from probabilities the user supplies. Each reassignment is a full wooldid run. The program then ranks the observed estimates among the results from the reassignments. permreps(#) sets how many reassignments to sample. permexact lists every possible reassignment instead.
items.why: This mode is for designs with very few treated clusters, such as a policy adopted by one state or a handful. Cluster-robust standard errors allow errors to be correlated within a cluster, and they rely on having many clusters. MacKinnon and Webb show that with few treated clusters these standard errors can reject a true null far too often or too seldom. The wild cluster bootstrap, a resampling method meant for few clusters, can fail the same way. A randomization test in the tradition of Fisher needs no large number of clusters. It holds each unit's outcomes fixed. It then asks where the observed estimate falls among the estimates that other onset assignments would have produced. That set of estimates is called the reference distribution. Suppose treatment affected no one. Then every reassignment is as likely as the one that happened. The rank of the observed estimate then gives an exact p-value. Each replication runs the full estimator. So the reference distribution comes from the same estimator that produced the reported number.
items.decision: The author specified the two designs. He also chose to offer both sampling and complete listing. He required that the number of possible assignments always be reported, and he asked for a t-ratio variant. The replication loop sits in the program's outer shell, after the observed run. Two other placements were set aside. One re-estimated inside a stripped-down loop that bypassed wooldid. That would have duplicated the weighting and margins code, and the copy could drift from the original. The other ran the loop inside the estimation routine, where it would collide with the program's shared state. The observed statistic comes from a refit of the true assignment, made the same way as every replication. By default that refit skips standard errors. Under permtstat it computes them. Either way the observed statistic sits exactly inside its own reference set. permute() is refused with impvalues, unconditionalse and bootstrap(). Each of those supplies its own kind of inference, and a run should report only one kind.
items.what_you_notice: New options permute(), permreps() and permexact, with example 12 in the help. Every run reports the number of distinct assignments in e(perm_npossible). A text version in e(perm_npossible_str) holds very large counts. Each run also reports how many replications were requested, completed and failed.

items.heading: The cluster is the unit that was randomized
items.what_changed: permute() needs a single cluster() variable. That variable names the unit whose onset is moved. Every cluster must have one onset date. Never treated is coded as plain missing. Each cluster must contain whole units of i, so the cluster sits at the level of i or coarser. The option permonsetcohorts relaxes this last rule. The check runs on every row the if expression keeps. So a specification that runs without permute() can be refused with it. Some onsets fall so late that the estimator treats the unit as never treated. Those onsets are now also permuted as never treated.
items.why: A randomization test is valid only if it reshuffles what was actually randomized. If whole states adopted a policy, the test should reshuffle states. Splitting a state would create assignments that could never have happened. A cluster that mixes onset dates has no single onset to move. A unit of i spread over two clusters could receive two onsets in one replication. The estimator cannot handle that. The late-onset change makes the reshuffle use the same definition of treatment as the estimator. Before, those late onsets were kept as a label of their own. That overstated the number of possible assignments. It also refused complete listing on designs that allow it. And it hid the caution about few treated clusters.
items.decision: The rule of one onset per cluster is the author's. The requirement that clusters contain whole units of i was added after a finer cluster was found to make every replication fail. One question was whether rows the estimator drops for a missing outcome or weight should also leave the design. It was left as it is, and the help tells users to restrict the sample with if. The author chose to recode late onsets as never treated instead of keeping them as their own label. He also approved the caution that reports the recode.
items.what_you_notice: A cluster() finer than i is refused before any replication runs. A cluster with mixed onsets stops with the message 'permute() requires each cluster have at most one treatment onset time period.' When late onsets are recoded, a caution counts the clusters affected. On such data the assignment count changes. So do the number of exact replications and the onset columns of permsave(). Shuffle p-values do not change.

items.heading: permonsetcohorts: a cluster finer than i when i is only the onset grouping
items.what_changed: permonsetcohorts lets the user state that i is simply the onset grouping. That means i has one level per onset date and one level for the never treated. The program checks this claim and stops if it fails. safety(off) does not lift the check. With the option, a cluster() finer than i is accepted. Each replication then rebuilds i from the onsets it drew. The option works with permstrata() and permute(probabilities). It does not work with subgroups().
items.why: The help recommends defining i as onset cohorts, the groups of units that start treatment at the same date. It also recommends clustering below that level. A cluster-robust standard error can see how noisy the treated clusters are only when several clusters sit in each treated cohort and period. Without this option, a user who followed that advice could not use permute(), because the cluster had to contain whole units of i. When i is only the onset grouping, the units that drew onset k form cohort k in every replication. So rebuilding i keeps the meaning of the estimate. Subgroups break this. A rebuilt cohort would pool clusters from different observed cohorts, and the subgroup label could vary inside it.
items.decision: wooldid cannot tell from the data whether i is an onset grouping or a real unit such as a firm. A wrong guess would quietly change what is estimated. So the author required the user to state it. He chose the option's name. He ruled against a display line announcing the rebuild, since rebuilding is the expected behaviour and needs no warning. Later, late onsets began to be permuted as never treated. He then ruled that the check keep its old form at cluster() equal to i, where nothing is rebuilt. There an onset after the last period is a level of i in its own right. Under a finer cluster(), such an onset belongs to the never-treated level. A screen for covariates that are constant within the original i but vary within the rebuilt one was judged too rare a case to build.
items.what_you_notice: A new option. e(perm_irebuilt) records whether i was rebuilt. At cluster() equal to i nothing is rebuilt.

items.heading: permstrata(): shuffle only within strata
items.what_changed: permstrata(varname) confines the shuffle to clusters in the same stratum. Every cluster must lie in one stratum, and the stratum variable may not be missing. The number of possible assignments becomes the product of the counts within each stratum. Sampling and complete listing both work.
items.why: The set of reassignments should match how onset was really assigned. Suppose large states were only ever at risk alongside other large states. A shuffle across size classes would then build the reference distribution partly from assignments that could not have happened. That can make the test reject a true null too often or too seldom. Shuffling within strata keeps the make-up of each onset group fixed, such as its share of large clusters.
items.decision: The author asked for stratified shuffling. It is a separate option, outside permute(), because Stata parses nested parentheses unreliably. It applies to the shuffle design only. Under the probabilities design, the user writes any strata into the probabilities themselves. A design where no stratum holds more than one onset has only one possible assignment, and it is refused.
items.what_you_notice: A new option, permstrata(). A stratified design with nothing to move is refused before any replication runs.

items.heading: permute(probabilities): a user-stated assignment design
items.what_changed: permute(probabilities) takes a permprobs() specification. It gives each cluster a probability for each onset level, with '.' standing for never treated. Each cluster's onset is drawn from its own row. Every cluster must appear once. Its probabilities must be nonnegative and sum to 1 within 1e-6. Rows within that tolerance are rescaled to sum to exactly 1. permreps() is required, and permexact is refused. A caution prints if the observed assignment has probability zero under the stated design.
items.why: Some designs are not a fair shuffle. A cluster may have been more likely to adopt early, or unable to adopt at some date. Drawing from the actual assignment probabilities gives the right reference distribution for such designs. The zero-probability caution matters because a randomization test is exact only when the observed assignment could have occurred. If it could not, the p-value is still a tail probability under the stated design. It is no longer a randomization test.
items.decision: The syntax, the required permreps() and the refusal of complete listing follow the author's specification. A tighter tolerance was considered and rejected. It would refuse realistic hand-rounded rows, such as .3333333 written three times. Duplicate levels and stray entries are refused.
items.what_you_notice: New options permute(probabilities) and permprobs(). The number of possible assignments is the product, over clusters, of the number of onsets each cluster can receive.

items.heading: Sampled draws: a floor of 20, a resolution caution, and a floor on completed draws
items.what_changed: permreps() must be at least 20. One caution prints when the smallest p-value the run can produce is above .05. Under the default p-value that means fewer than 39 replications. Another caution prints when permreps() exceeds 10 percent of the possible assignments. Replications that fail to estimate are dropped and counted. A sampled run is refused when too few replications complete. The floor is 20 or half the number requested, whichever is larger. A design with only one possible assignment is refused. A caution prints if every draw gives the same value.
items.why: With sampled draws the p-value can take only values on a grid set by the number of draws. At 20 replications the default p-value cannot go below .095. No result could reach 5 percent, whatever the data said. The caution tells users when a run cannot answer the question they most likely asked. Draws are made with replacement, so the same assignment can come up twice. As the number of draws nears the number of possible assignments, repeats become common. Complete listing is then the better tool. Some reassignments leave the estimator unable to fit, for example with no usable control group. Dropping those is unavoidable. But if many drop, the survivors may no longer represent all the possible assignments. The run then refuses to rest a p-value on a thin and possibly skewed set.
items.decision: A floor of 40 was considered. The author kept 20 and added the caution, which leaves users free to run a short check. The floor of 20 matches the completion rule, so a smaller request could only waste the run. The completion floor does not apply to complete listing. There each finished assignment is still a genuine member of the set.
items.what_you_notice: permreps() below 20 is refused. Runs with fewer than 39 replications print the resolution caution. e(perm_failed) counts failed draws. e(perm_n) shows how many draws each p-value rests on.

items.heading: Exact enumeration: a higher cap, and an exact share even when some assignments fail
items.what_changed: permexact lists every distinct shuffle, including shuffles within strata. A caution prints above 1,000 assignments. Listing is refused above 65,534 assignments, the most rows a Stata matrix can hold. Above 10,000, the matrices of draws are not stored in e(), and a caution points to permsave(). P-values are plain shares over the M listed assignments. The smallest possible p-value is 2/M. Some assignments may fail to estimate. Each p-value then stays the exact share over those that finished, and a caution reports the loss.
items.why: With few clusters every assignment can be listed. The p-value is then exact. It is no longer a Monte Carlo estimate, meaning an estimate from random draws that would change with more draws. The observed assignment is one of the listed ones, so the share needs no correction. If some other assignments fail, the observed one is still in the set, so the share stays exact. Losing assignments costs resolution and leaves validity intact. The earlier rule switched every p-value to the sampled form after a single failure. That doubled the smallest attainable p-value and counted the observed assignment twice.
items.decision: The cap had been 10,000, set by the first build with no recorded reason. The author first asked that the cap become a caution that safety(off) could lift. When the 65,534-row matrix limit was put to him, he ruled to use that limit instead. That made the cap a machine limit that nothing lifts, so the safety(off) route was not built. His confirmation that this is what he intended is still outstanding. On failures under complete listing, he ruled that the rule depend on membership. The exact share stays, with a caution, while the observed assignment is still in the completed set. Only a coefficient whose own observed value is missing from its reference set switches to the sampled form.
items.what_you_notice: Exact runs of up to 65,534 assignments now run. A caution prints whenever an exact run loses assignments, and it gives the new smallest p-value. Coefficients that fell back to the sampled form are listed in e(perm_addone).

items.heading: The default p-value: equal-tailed, with the observed assignment counted
items.what_changed: The default p-value is two-sided and equal-tailed. It is twice the smaller of the two one-sided tail shares, capped at 1. For sampled draws each tail share uses the add-one form. Its numerator is one plus the number of draws at or beyond the observed value. Its denominator is the number of draws plus one. So the smallest possible p-value is two divided by one more than permreps(). Under exact listing the tails are plain shares, and the smallest possible p-value is 2/M. The first version compared absolute values instead. The convention in force is stored in e(perm_pconv).
items.why: The null distribution is the spread of estimates across reassignments when treatment has no effect. An equal-tailed p-value does not assume that distribution is symmetric around zero. With staggered onsets and cohorts of unequal size it is often lopsided. An absolute-value p-value can then be too small or too large. The add-one form counts the observed assignment as a member of its own reference set. Under the null, the observed statistic and the draws are exchangeable, meaning every ordering of them is equally likely. The rank of the observed statistic is then uniform. So the add-one p-value rejects no more often than the nominal level, the level the user tests at, for any number of draws. On the grid of a sampled run it rejects slightly less often. With 99 draws the equal-tailed rule rejects 4 percent of the time at a nominal 5 percent. The plain share leaves the observed assignment out and rejects too often when draws are few. The same rule applied to the bootstrap's studentized tail was measured at about 6 percent at a nominal 5 percent with 99 replications. A side effect of the add-one form is that the p-value can never print as zero.
items.decision: The author chose the add-one form wherever exchangeability makes it exact. That covers every permutation p-value. The bootstrap percentile rows keep the plain share. Those draws are centred on the estimate instead of the null. Adding one there would only make the test more cautious, with no gain in exactness. Stata's own permute prefix uses the same equal-tailed shape. ritest reports an absolute-value share instead. The help explains how the two relate.
items.what_you_notice: Permutation p-values never fall below two divided by one more than permreps(), or 2/M under permexact. The help and guide include a map of which convention each part of the output uses.

items.heading: Other p-value conventions, and the precision of a sampled p-value
items.what_changed: permabsp reports the absolute-value p-value. That is the share of draws whose absolute value is at or above the observed one, in the add-one form. It also switches the intervals to the matching symmetric form. permside(left) or permside(right) reports a one-sided p-value and keeps the two-sided intervals. The two options cannot be combined. Every run stores both one-sided shares in e(perm_p_lo) and e(perm_p_hi). Sampled runs also store the Monte Carlo standard error of the p-value in e(perm_p_se). They store an exact binomial interval for it, the Clopper-Pearson interval, in e(perm_p_ci). permrawp printed the plain share with no add-one. It was added and later removed.
items.why: The absolute-value convention is what ritest and much applied work report. It halves the smallest attainable p-value, to one divided by one more than the number of draws. But it assumes the null distribution is symmetric. Tying the interval to it keeps two statements equivalent. The interval excludes zero exactly when the p-value is below the test level. A one-sided test has more power when theory predicts the sign of the effect. A sampled p-value is itself an estimate. A p-value of .04 from 199 draws is weaker evidence than .04 from 9,999 draws. The standard error and the binomial interval show how far it could move with more draws. The plain share added nothing. Under complete listing it equals the permabsp value. Otherwise it can be computed from that value and the draw count. It is also the version that rejects too often and can print zero.
items.decision: The author asked for the absolute-value option. The symmetric interval that goes with it was a design choice put to him. He asked for one-sided p-values and kept two-sided intervals under permside(). permrawp was his own request, a plain cross-check against the number ritest prints. When its removal was proposed, he removed it. He kept permside() even though the one-sided shares are always stored. The precision measures are left missing under complete listing, where the share has no sampling error.
items.what_you_notice: New options permabsp and permside(). A do-file that names permrawp now stops with a syntax error. e(perm_rawp*) is gone.

items.heading: Intervals are shift intervals, and the help says where they hold
items.what_changed: Each coefficient's interval is a shift interval. It is the estimate minus the upper and lower level() quantiles of the null draws. These quantiles are the points that cut off the top and bottom tails at the chosen confidence level. The first version followed the author's specification. It reported the 5th and 95th percentiles of the null draws, labelled as a null band. But it stored them under names that looked like interval endpoints. That null band is now stored under its own names, e(perm_nullband), e(perm_bandlo_*) and e(perm_bandhi_*). The old e(perm_lb_*) and e(perm_ub_*) names are gone. When the draws are not centred at zero, the interval is left blank and the p-value stands. The coefficient is then listed in e(perm_offcentre). The help says the interval widens as the true effect grows.
items.why: The percentiles of the null draws describe where the estimate would fall if there were no effect. They do not form an interval for the effect. A true interval would come from inverting the test. That means rerunning the whole permutation for every candidate effect size. It also means assuming the effect is the same for everyone, which is doubtful when effects differ across cohorts. The shift interval is a cheap approximation. It assumes the spread of the estimate does not depend on the true effect. That holds near zero. But the draws relabel outcomes that carry the real effect, so the spread grows with it. On a 12-cluster example the 95 percent width was 1.9, 4.7 and 18.3 at true effects of 0, 5 and 20. In one study the interval matched the test exactly at zero and still covered about right at an effect of one residual standard deviation. At three it was 1.6 to 2.4 times as wide as at zero. When the draws are off-centre, the approximation fails outright. The interval is then withheld so that a wrong one is never printed.
items.decision: The author asked for intervals built from the replications. An exact inversion was costed at about twice the run time for the pooled effect. Under permtstat or poisson it would cost 20 to 40 times as much. It was not built. The author ruled that the help say plainly that the interval is reliable only near a zero effect. An attribution to Conley and Taber was dropped. Their placebo draws come from untreated units, whose outcomes carry no effect. wooldid's draws carry the effect. He first kept the old interval-like names for the null band, with a note that they would be retired. He later removed them, since permute() had never been in a released version.
items.what_you_notice: Intervals follow level() instead of a fixed band from 5 to 95. e(perm_se_shift) holds an implied standard error. The help says it is not a sampling standard error. Code that read e(perm_lb_*) or e(perm_ub_*) must switch to e(perm_bandlo_*) and e(perm_bandhi_*).

items.heading: permtstat and permtci: randomizing on t-ratios, and when that helps
items.what_changed: permtstat ranks each replication's t-ratio instead of the raw estimate. The t-ratio is the estimate divided by its own analytic standard error. The run is slower because the replications compute standard errors, and fastnose is refused. The joint tests and subgroup contrasts stay based on coefficients in both modes. permtci adds an interval for the pooled estimands. It is the estimate plus or minus the observed standard error times the level() quantile of the permuted absolute t-ratios. permtci implies permtstat.
items.why: The t-ratio divides by a standard error that reflects each assignment's own noise. That makes the statistic less sensitive to treated clusters that are unusually noisy. MacKinnon and Webb recommend it for that reason. It works only if the standard error can see the treated clusters' variance. The regression has a separate term for each treated cohort and period. When one cluster makes up that whole cell, the term fits the cell's mean exactly. That cluster's residuals in the cell then sum to zero. A cluster-robust variance is built from those sums, so it has nothing to measure. permtstat therefore protects only where several clusters sit in each treated cell. Under permute() that needs permonsetcohorts with a finer cluster(). One simulation used 12 clusters, 3 of them treated, with errors three times as dispersed in the treated ones. cluster() was at i. A true null was rejected at 5 percent in 6 of 30 datasets with the coefficient, and in 7 of 30 with the t-ratio. About 1.5 would be expected.
items.decision: The author asked for both options. The help's statement of the condition was corrected to the direction above. An earlier text had it backwards. He kept the caution at cluster() equal to i. He did not widen it to every cluster that contains whole units of i. He ruled that the condition of several clusters stay qualitative, with no number attached. permtci is described as an approximation built from draws under a zero effect. It is not described as an inversion of the test. He kept permtci even though permtstat with permabsp gives the same interval.
items.what_you_notice: At cluster() equal to i, permtstat prints a caution that it gives no protection there. The permtci endpoints are in e(perm_tlb_*) and e(perm_tub_*). They now follow level().

items.heading: What the test assumes, stated plainly, with cautions of its own
items.what_changed: The help and guide say the p-value tests the sharp null, meaning no effect on any unit at any time. They say the test assumes onset was assigned exchangeably across clusters. That means any cluster could have received any onset. They say this is stronger than parallel trends, the usual assumption that treated and control groups would have moved alike without treatment. They also say the test rejects a true null too often or too seldom when treated clusters differ from the rest in size or error variance. permute() has its own cautions. One prints at cluster() equal to i, whichever statistic is used. Another prints when fewer than 6 clusters are ever treated.
items.why: The pairs cluster bootstrap and randomization inference rest on different assumptions. The pairs cluster bootstrap resamples whole clusters. It treats clusters as interchangeable random draws, and it fails with few or atypical treated clusters. Randomization inference treats clusters as interchangeable in who got treated. MacKinnon and Webb show it fails when treated clusters are noisier or quieter than the rest. Small or noisy treated clusters make the reference distribution too narrow, so the test rejects too often. Large or quiet ones make it too wide, so it rejects too seldom. Moving from the bootstrap to permute() because treated clusters are few therefore trades one assumption for another. Few treated clusters do not by themselves make the possible assignments few. For example, 5 treated among 30 clusters give 142,506 assignments. The concern is that the test's rate of false rejection then rests entirely on exchangeability.
items.decision: The author ruled that permute() get cautions suited to its own failure. It does not copy the bootstrap's few-cluster cautions. He also ruled that differences between the two engines be kept where they are justified. They are not removed just for the sake of matching. The help's account of the few-treated caution was corrected to name exchangeability as the concern. The caution's own text still says the number of distinct assignments is small. Its rewording is held for his choice among three options.
items.what_you_notice: Runs at cluster() equal to i print a caution even without permtstat. It says the coefficient statistic has no protection against a treated cluster with unusually dispersed errors. Runs with fewer than 6 ever-treated clusters print a caution.
sources: econ_review_2026-09-25.md PERM-2, PERM-3, PERM-5, PERM-7, s5 item 8, s8 and s9

items.heading: Fast mode by default, with permanalyticse to restore analytic standard errors
items.what_changed: Under permute(), the observed run and the replications skip analytic standard errors by default. The se_analytic column is blank. The covariance matrix e(V) is not posted, nor are e(b_es_*) and e(V_es_*). So honestdid, test and lincom are unavailable. permanalyticse computes the analytic standard errors for the observed run and shows them for reference. The p-values and intervals stay permutation-based.
items.why: A randomization test on coefficients uses only point estimates. Computing standard errors in every replication wastes time. Printing analytic p-values next to permutation ones would also invite confusion. In the few-cluster setting the analytic ones are often degenerate, meaning the formula breaks down and the number carries no information.
items.decision: The author made fast mode the default. He accepted that tools needing an analytic covariance, such as honestdid, would not work after permute(). He kept permanalyticse when its removal was proposed. Typing fastnose with permute() is accepted, since fast mode is already in force. fastnose with permtstat, permtci or permanalyticse is refused. Each of those needs the standard errors that fastnose turns off.
items.what_you_notice: permute() runs are fast by default, with a blank se_analytic column. permanalyticse or permtstat brings back e(V) and the analytic column.

items.heading: Every p-value and interval is a permutation quantity, or blank
items.what_changed: As first built, permute() covered only the pooled estimands, in a separate block. The main tables kept analytic p-values. Now every reported p-value and interval comes from the permutation draws. That includes the event-study horizons, which are the effects at each period relative to onset. It also includes the pretreatment rows, subgroup estimates and contrasts, continuous-treatment effects, the joint tests and the plots. Anything with no permutation distribution is left blank. That means the gteffects cells, and the continuous-treatment plot cells whose bins are defined by treatment status. pretrendpower() is refused.
items.why: The author's rule was that a permute() run shows only permutation p-values, never a mix. The analytic numbers are also often degenerate in exactly the few-cluster setting permute() is for. On one fixture an analytic run gave a pairwise subgroup standard error of 2.33e-10, with p = 6.5e-87. A permutation p-value needs a statistic defined the same way in every draw. The gteffects cells are indexed by onset date, and some plot bins by treatment status. Reassigning onset changes what those cells are, along with their values. So they have no reference distribution. pretrendpower() needs a sampling covariance of the event-study estimates. The permutation draws do give a covariance. But it describes the estimates under relabelling of onset, not their sampling error. A power calculation built on it would mean nothing. A blank is honest. An analytic number under a permutation heading would misstate where it came from.
items.decision: Seventeen specific cases were put to the author. The options included labelling analytic numbers instead of removing them. They included refusing joint tests or subgroups under permute(). They also included three ways to handle gteffects. He chose full coverage wherever a permutation distribution exists, and blanks elsewhere. Analytic numbers never fill the gaps. Under permtstat or permtci he chose to override cfxplotnose instead of leaving the plot cells blank. The t-ratio needs those cells' standard errors.
items.what_you_notice: Event-study, subgroup and continuous-treatment rows carry permutation p-values and intervals. The gteffects cells and the baseTreated, byTreated and byTtre plot cells have no inference under permute(). The caution 'cfxplotnose was dropped; permtstat needs the plot cells' standard errors.' prints when that override applies. pretrendpower() with permute() is an error.

items.heading: What a sharp-null test means when the effect is real
items.what_changed: Pretreatment rows, the joint pretrend tests, the subgroup equality tests and the pairwise subgroup contrasts all get permutation p-values. The output and help say each tests the sharp null of no effect at any horizon. The help warns about two consequences in staggered designs. The pre-period p-values rise toward 1 as the true effect grows. And a common nonzero effect alone can make the subgroup tests reject.
items.why: The draws reuse outcomes that carry the real effect. Suppose a cluster draws an onset later than its real one. Its truly treated periods then count as pretreatment in that draw. The reference distribution carries the effect, while the observed pre-period statistic does not. So the pre-period p-value drifts up. In one measurement at an effect of 30, a pre-period p-value moved from .49 to .69. A joint pretrend p-value moved from .88 to .98. That errs toward reassurance, the wrong direction for a check of whether the design is credible. With a single onset date the problem does not arise. The same logic applies to subgroups. These tests ask whether there is any effect at all. They do not ask whether subgroup effects are equal. A common effect can push the null off-centre when the shuffle moves treated clusters between subgroups. It can also widen the null when strata fix each subgroup's make-up. One run showed an equality p-value of 1.000 beside a contrast p-value of .010. That pair makes sense only once the null is named.
items.decision: For the pretreatment rows, the author chose to report them and state the null where the numbers print. One alternative was leaving them analytic with a label. Another was showing them only after the user acknowledged the caveat. A placebo test using only not-yet-treated units was set aside. It would be a second engine about as large as the first. For subgroups he chose to label the tests as sharp-null tests. He also chose to list off-centre contrasts in e(perm_offcentre).
items.what_you_notice: The subgroup equality lines read 'permutation p-value (sharp null of no effect at any horizon) for joint test that all SGs have the same ...'. A footer explains the pre-period caveat. e(perm_precaveat) is 1 when such rows were reported.
sources: changes_review_2026-09-22.md s2b (perm-sgeq-uncentred; equality test and pairwise contrasts)

items.heading: Joint tests become permutation tests on a fixed yardstick
items.what_changed: Under permute(), three joint tests become one-sided permutation tests of a quadratic form. They are the joint pretrend test, the subgroup equality test and the adversarial test. A quadratic form here is a weighted sum of squared coefficients. The weights come from the covariance of the permutation draws. That covariance is computed once and held fixed across draws. The tests are the same whether the run ranks coefficients or t-ratios. Draws and observed values are stored in e(perm_jointW), e(perm_sgW), e(perm_advW) and their Wobs twins. When a subgroup lost an event-study horizon, its adversarial test is skipped, as on an analytic run.
items.why: The analytic joint tests need an analytic covariance. Fast mode does not produce one. It is also degenerate when each treated cell is one cluster. A permutation test is exact for any statistic that is fixed in advance. The weights are computed from all the draws and the observed row together. So they treat every assignment alike and keep the test exact. A poor choice of weights then costs power and leaves validity intact. The adversarial test fits a line through the event-study horizons. A line fitted through an incomplete set of horizons means nothing. So that test is skipped instead of reported.
items.decision: The author's specification allowed the joint tests and the subgroup comparison tests to be skipped except under permtstat. Refusing them would have contradicted the package's own advice to use permute() for joint inference. So the fixed-yardstick construction was built and put to him as a design choice, and he accepted it. He ruled on the subgroup skip and on dropping a test that cannot be formed. Under permute() the adversarial test tests the sharp null. Its analytic version tests whether the effects lie on a line.
items.what_you_notice: jointtests and adversarial work on permute()'s default fast path. When the adversarial test cannot be formed, a caution says it failed with 'too few usable permutations', and no line is posted.

items.heading: Subgroups under permute(): screens over the whole sample, with no escape
items.what_changed: With subgroups() under permute(), the subgroup screens run over the whole sample, including untreated units. Three cases are refused whatever safety() says. One is a unit split across subgroups over time. Another is a unit labelled on some rows and missing on others. The third is a subgroup that varies within one cell of i and t.
items.why: Outside permute(), a treated unit that is split or partly labelled can enter each subgroup in proportion to its weight. Under reassignment, any unit can become treated. The replications would then split such units silently. The reference distribution would not be built the same way as the observed statistic. Refusing is the only way to keep the observed and permuted estimates the same function of the data.
items.decision: The author ruled that the partial-label screen cannot be lifted. A safety(off) escape on the within-cell screen was removed, because it led only to the split-unit refusal. He kept both screens even though one catches a subset of what the other catches.
items.what_you_notice: Subgroup designs that run under safety(off) without permute() are refused with it.

items.heading: Residue pairwise standard errors are disclosed and kept under permute()
items.what_changed: Under permute() with permtstat or permanalyticse, the analytic standard errors of the pairwise subgroup contrasts are computed. With cluster() at i or above, such a standard error can be pure rounding residue. That is a tiny number left over when two nearly equal terms cancel. An analytic run cautions on these contrasts and reports them without inference. Under permute() the program now runs the same check on the observed fit. It flags the affected rows and prints the first sentence of the analytic caution. It blanks nothing and leaves the equality tests alone. The replications skip the check.
items.why: Under permute() the contrasts are tested by permuting the coefficient differences themselves. Their p-values and intervals do not use the analytic standard error, so they stay valid. The analytic number shown beside them is still meaningless. Before this change nothing said so. An analytic run cautioned on the same number, and so did a boottstat bootstrap run.
items.decision: The author ruled that permute() reuse the analytic path's detection, for disclosure only. He approved the caution's first sentence alone as the text for this path. This keeps a justified difference between the two engines. An analytic run withholds inference because its p-value rests on the residue. A permutation run does not rest on it.
items.what_you_notice: With permtstat or permanalyticse and cluster() at or above i, a caution counts the pairwise rows whose se_analytic is residue. The contrasts keep their permutation p-values. e(wdid_sgdegen), e(wdid_sgdegenr) and e(wdid_sgdegenact) record the check, with the last set to perm. The fast default flags nothing.

items.heading: permstepdown: adjusting for many horizons at once
items.what_changed: permstepdown reports step-down adjusted p-values, following Romano and Wolf. It does so for each event-study family with two or more horizons, using the same replications. Post-treatment and pretreatment horizons form separate families. The option is opt-in. simultaneousbands is refused under permute(). The step-down is permute()'s tool for many comparisons instead.
items.why: Separate p-values per horizon do not control the chance of at least one false rejection across horizons. That chance is called the family-wise error rate. The step-down does control it. It costs no extra computing, because it reuses the draws. Pooling pre and post horizons would change the post-treatment adjusted p-values. The two families also answer different questions. The control holds under the sharp null of no effect anywhere. When some horizons have real effects, the reassigned onsets carry them into the other horizons' draws. Control over the remaining horizons is then not guaranteed. The guide says so. The help states the control under the sharp null.
items.decision: It was first built to run on every permute() run. The author made it opt-in because it added output nobody had asked for. He split pre and post horizons into separate families. He kept the step-down for permute() only. The bootstrap gets simultaneous bands instead.
items.what_you_notice: A new option. Adjusted p-values are in e(perm_stepdown*) and summarised in the footer.

items.heading: Continuous treatment: onset moves, the dose stays
items.what_changed: permute() works with contreat(). Only onset timing is reassigned. Each unit keeps its dose, the continuous amount of treatment it received. The continuous-treatment effects are permuted along with everything else. contreatcontrols(untreatedZero) and contreatwithin are refused.
items.why: The test is still a test of the sharp null of no effect. It is valid when onset timing was as good as random given each unit's dose. untreatedZero requires the dose to be zero outside treated periods. Moving onset while freezing the dose would break that in every replication and contaminate the reference distribution. contreatwithin has no comparison group to move onset against.
items.decision: Refusing contreat() under permute() was considered and not taken. Reassigning the dose itself was set aside for later. An early version left the continuous-treatment effects out of the draws. They were brought in because the package's own advice already sent users with that design to randomization inference.
items.what_you_notice: The ame rows, which hold the average marginal effects of the dose, carry permutation p-values and intervals under permute(). An off-centre ame interval is blanked and listed like any other. untreatedZero and contreatwithin with permute() are errors.

items.heading: esttab shows the permutation p-values and intervals
items.what_changed: Every permute() run posts e(p), e(ci_l) and e(ci_u) from the permutation results. So esttab, a widely used table command, prints the same p-values and intervals as wooldid's own table. No e(se) is posted. test, lincom and _se[] still refuse. Where e(V) exists, under permanalyticse or permtstat, esttab shows the analytic standard errors.
items.why: Under fast mode esttab used to fail silently. It printed the coefficient and an empty standard-error row. Its footer claimed standard errors were shown. It wrote all of that into .tex and .csv files. esttab reads posted p-values and intervals before anything derived from e(V). So posting the real permutation numbers fixes the table without inventing a variance.
items.decision: The author first named an all-zero covariance as the remedy, on condition that it worked. Tested outside the program, it made things worse. It gave zero-width intervals and printed zero standard errors, so it was never shipped. Posting e(perm_se_shift) as e(se) was rejected, because it is not a sampling standard error. The author first limited the posting to fast runs. He then extended it to every run. Under permanalyticse, esttab had switched silently to analytic p-values while wooldid showed permutation ones.
items.what_you_notice: esttab tables from permute() runs show permutation p-values and intervals. They have no standard-error row unless analytic standard errors were computed.

items.heading: Reproducing a run: rseed(), the random-number state, and permsave()
items.what_changed: rseed(#) is accepted under permute() and stored in e(perm_seed). The random-number state before the first draw is always stored in e(perm_rngstate), so any run can be replayed. permsave(name) writes name.dta with one row per replication. A row numbered 0 holds the observed estimates. The file has one column per coefficient and one column per cluster holding its drawn onset. Under permtstat it also holds the replication standard errors. The seed and state are saved in the file.
items.why: A sampled permutation p-value changes with the draws. Recording the seed lets anyone reproduce the exact number reported. The saved file lets users build their own summaries or check the reference distribution by hand. The onset columns make every p-value checkable. Unlike the draw matrices in e(), the file has no row limit.
items.decision: A separate seed option for permute() was offered and dropped in favour of the shared rseed(). The file name must be a plain name. Overwriting needs the separate replace option, as with bootsave(). A failed write was first fatal. The author made it a caution, so the run's results are kept when the file cannot be written.
items.what_you_notice: A new option, permsave(). permsave(name, replace) is refused before the replications run. A failed write leaves the run complete, with a caution and e(perm_save_rc).

title: Continuous treatments
intro: This section covers runs with contreat(), where each treated unit receives a dose of treatment. wooldid splits the treated rows into cells. A cell holds the rows that share an onset cohort and a calendar period. Each treated cell gets its own intercept and its own dose slope. The program reports two main results. The att is the average effect of being treated. The ame is the average marginal effect, meaning the effect of one more unit of dose, and it averages the cell slopes. A few terms recur below. Clustered standard errors allow the errors of rows in the same cluster, such as the same firm, to be correlated. The bootstrap measures uncertainty by refitting the model on many resamples of the data. Permutation refits it after reshuffling when units were treated. An event study reports the effect separately for each period counted from onset. A joint test checks several of those rows at once. A caution is a warning the program prints. The changes share one theme. A dose slope can only be learned from variation in the dose. Where the data cannot supply that variation, or the variance formula cannot see it, the program now says so or stops. Before, it printed a number that looked valid.

items.heading: Treated cells with no variation in the dose
items.what_changed: Sometimes no treated cell has any variation in the dose. For example, the dose may be constant within each cohort. wooldid then reports every ame result as missing and skips the ame tests. The att results are still reported. Sometimes only some treated cells lack dose variation. wooldid then drops those cells from the estimation sample and prints a caution with their count. It estimates both the att and the ame on the cells that remain. A cell whose dose is zero throughout is never dropped.
items.why: Inside a treated cell, the dose slope is learned only from rows that received different doses. If every row in the cell has the same dose, the slope cannot be told apart from the cell's intercept. The regression then removes the slope as redundant. This is called a drop for collinearity. The step that averages the slopes read the removed slope as a zero. In v1.3 that zero entered the ame at the cell's full weight. In one constructed example this pulled the ame to .72 against a true value of 1.00. The p value was near zero, and the only warning was a generic note about dropped terms. The att does not need dose variation inside a cell, so it stays valid when the ame does not. The same logic covers a panel where i, the unit variable, is the individual unit. Each treated cell then holds one row, so no cell has dose variation. The ame is then not identified at all, meaning the data cannot pin it down. No choice of clustering, bootstrap or permutation can repair that.
items.decision: Take first the case where every slope drops. The author chose to report the ame as missing instead of printing the zeros. He keyed the check on the dropped dose terms, because they mark the problem directly. Now take the case where only some cells lack variation. He was offered three routes. One was to report the whole ame as missing, as in the first case. Another was to average only the cells with live slopes and report the share left out. The third was to document the problem. He chose instead to drop those cells from the sample, so that the att and the ame describe the same set of cells. The built version departs from his ruling as worded in two ways, and both await his confirmation. First, cells with a zero dose throughout are exempt under every control type, while the ruling named only untreatedZero. Recording the dose as zero before onset is a design the help endorses, and without the exemption those runs stopped with an error. Second, cells before onset are dropped only when at least one of them has dose variation. When no cell after onset varies, nothing is dropped and the check for all slopes dropped takes over. One consequence follows. A cell after onset whose dose is zero throughout is kept, and its zero slope enters the ame. He also ruled that the check for all slopes dropped runs under contreatwithin. That option relaxes the need for an untreated group. It does not relax the need for dose variation.
items.what_you_notice: A new caution gives the number of treated cells dropped for having no variation in the dose. The count is stored in e(contreat_ndropcells), and the dropped rows are counted in e(N_dropped). The att and the ame can move on runs that had such cells. safety(off) silences the caution but still drops the cells. On a design where no cell varies, the ame rows show as missing where v1.3 printed zeros. Under safety(off) the zeros still show. Under contreatcontrols(untreatedZero) the partial check does not run, and a design with a constant dose in every cell is refused instead. The guide now says that when i is the individual unit, the ame is unidentified whatever the clustering. One case is untested. On some designs with one row per cell, the regression keeps the slopes and drops the intercepts. Each reported slope is then the cell's effect divided by its dose, and the check for all slopes dropped may not fire.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s3 (dose:CT-1, dose:CT-5), s5 item 2, s8, s9 G2

items.heading: Each baseline dose slope must be identified before the run proceeds
items.what_changed: The baseline dose slope is the relationship between dose and outcome in rows outside the treated cells. Treated cells' dose effects are measured against it. contreatcontrols() sets which groups get their own baseline slope. Before estimating, wooldid now checks every requested control type. For each group with its own baseline slope, it measures dose variation among that group's reference rows. Under basic the group is the whole sample. Under byTreated it is each treatment status group, and under byTtre each onset group. Under byTime it is each calendar period, and under byCohort each treated cohort. The variation is measured relative to the dose's standard deviation in the sample. At or below one part in 100,000, the run stops with error 459. Between that and one part in 1,000, a caution says the slope is nearly unidentified. safety(off) cannot lift the refusal. The check also runs inside every bootstrap and permutation replication.
items.why: Every treated cell has its own dose term. So a group's baseline slope is learned only from dose variation in that group's reference rows. With no variation, the slope is not identified. The solver then picks a value arbitrarily, and the ame comes out wrong with nothing to mark it. One measured case gave an ame of the wrong sign, with a standard error of zero to fifteen decimal places and no warning. Near zero variation is almost as bad. In one example the control type was byTime and the never treated doses were nearly constant, at 4.4 parts in 10,000 of the dose's spread. The run reported an att of -150.3 and an ame of -72.7. The true values were 2.56 and 1. A bootstrap or permutation draw can lack variation even when the observed sample has it, so every draw is checked.
items.decision: The author made this a refusal instead of a caution. Where the check fires, it fires on every draw, because it reflects a fixed feature of the panel. A test for exactly zero variation was rejected. On the one design where this was mapped, the estimate stayed at the wrong answer until the relative spread reached about one part in 100,000. A later sweep on three more designs could not reproduce that transition. The cut therefore ships as his chosen value, without confirming measurements. Every requested type is checked, and not only the most detailed one, because types combine. basic plus byTime can fail where basic alone is fine. The byCohort check came first. He ruled it on 2026-08-25, with both the refusal and a caution for the band up to one part in 1,000. The other four types got the same refusal on 2026-09-20. He asked for their band caution on 2026-09-23. He also ruled to keep refusing byTreated and byTtre when only the never treated group has a constant dose. That group's slope cannot change any treated cell's estimate, and v1.3 ran those designs. No reason was recorded.
items.what_you_notice: Error 459 on some designs that v1.3 ran. The most common case is byTime when never treated units carry a zero or constant dose in the periods after the last onset. A new caution appears for groups whose variation falls between one part in 100,000 and one part in 1,000 of the dose's spread. The check also runs under contreatwithin.
sources: wooldid.sthlp paragraph after the control types (~l.785-788)

items.heading: ame standard errors are withheld when a treated cell sits inside one cluster
items.what_changed: With contreat() and clustered standard errors, wooldid checks whether any treated cell with two or more rows lies wholly inside a single cluster. If one does, it prints a caution. It then reports every ame standard error, t statistic, p value and confidence interval as missing. It also skips the ame joint tests and the ame adversarial test, withholds e(V_es_ame*), and draws the ame plots without intervals. The ame point estimates and all att results are still reported. A second caution fires in a related case, when three or more reported standard errors under clustering are identical while their estimates differ. That pattern is the signature of the same failure.
items.why: A clustered variance adds up each cluster's scores. A score is a row's residual multiplied by its regressors. A treated cell has its own intercept and dose slope. Fitting them forces that cell's summed scores for those two terms to zero. When the whole cell sits inside one cluster, that cluster's sum for those terms is therefore zero. The formula then cannot see any of the cell's own noise. What remains is the uncertainty of the shared baseline dose slope. In the diagnosed case every ame standard error equalled the baseline slope's. In simulation the true sampling variance was about five times larger. The printed numbers looked like standard errors of the ame, yet they measured only the baseline slope. A cell with a single row is different. Its intercept fits it exactly, so its score is zero whatever the clustering. It cannot distort the variance.
items.decision: The author chose to withhold the ame standard errors and to list the routes to valid inference. They are bootstrap() without boottstat, permute(), impvalues, robust standard errors when errors are independent across rows, or clustering strictly finer than the cells. boottstat is the studentized bootstrap. It divides each replication's estimate by the analytic standard error, which is the number withheld, so it gives the ame rows nothing. A bootstrap built into the check was not pursued, because the package had no bootstrap at the time. bootstrap() now exists and is on the list. Withholding the att standard errors too was rejected. The same containment holds in the standard binary design, with i as the unit and clustering on i. The check would then fire on nearly every run. The help instead says the att standard errors are understated there. Tests on the rank of the covariance matrix were rejected. Under byTime the covariance has full rank and is still blind to the noise within cells. So any one contained cell triggers the check. At first, cells with a single row counted toward the check. He reversed that rule. Such cells cannot distort the variance, and counting them only withheld valid standard errors.
items.what_you_notice: A caution gives the number of treated cells that lie within a single cluster. The ame side shows missing standard errors, tests and intervals where v1.3 printed numbers. e(b_es_ame*) is still posted. The check does not run under fastnose, impvalues or unconditionalse.
sources: commit 1186f72 (INV-1 diagnosis: rank-1 e(V_es_ame) under cohort clustering)

items.heading: No rescue refit when the covariance comes back empty
items.what_changed: On the default path, Stata replaces a covariance matrix it judges not symmetric or highly singular with zeros. The quiet estimation call hides Stata's warning about this. On the poisson path, ppmlhdfe can post an all zero covariance of its own. When the covariance comes back all zero, or as rounding residue close to zero, wooldid prints a caution. The caution says that no standard error in the run is identified, and the point estimates are still reported. A fallback used to refit the model with every fixed effect written out as a dummy variable, to recover some att standard errors. A fixed effect is a separate intercept for each unit or period. That fallback was removed. The caution now lists bootstrap() and permute() first. It offers conditional robust standard errors, which treat the sample's covariate values as fixed, only to runs that have not already asked for a conditional variance. It offers impvalues or finer clustering only to clustered runs.
items.why: The empty covariance has more than one source. Under clustering it comes from the containment in the previous item, which already invalidates the ame inference. With no clustering at all, it usually comes from a lattice, which splits the dose into bins. The lattice cuts treated cells into pieces the model fits exactly, so a robust variance has no residual to work from. The caution names that cause when a lattice is present. A refit could only salvage some standard errors from a broken specification. It cost a solve over hundreds of redundant dummy columns. It delayed the user learning that the specification was the problem. It also moved some ame point estimates by large amounts. The order of remedies rests on a simulation that held the design fixed. On the design that prints this caution, the conditional robust standard error was 0.017 of the estimator's actual sampling spread. Listing it first would send users to a number far too small.
items.decision: The author ruled to remove the refit and keep the detection and the caution. He also ruled to extend the detection to near zero residue, with a conservative floor. The new order of remedies was set on the simulation evidence during the build. It was not put to him as a separate question, and it is recorded so it can be reversed.
items.what_you_notice: No refit. A caution says the covariance is all zero or residue, and the estimates are kept. On an all zero covariance the standard errors are missing. Under residue they print as numbers that are zero to about fifteen decimal places, and the caution says to read none of them.

items.heading: untreatedZero means no baseline dose effect on every engine
items.what_changed: Under contreatcontrols(untreatedZero), the dose now enters only through each treated cell's own slope terms, on every estimation engine. The poisson, customvce() and unconditionalse paths used to add a pooled dose control, meaning a single dose slope shared by all rows. That control is gone. Sometimes a treated cell with a nonzero dose loses its dose slope to collinearity. The run then stops with error 322, whatever lattice() or verbose say. A dose recorded as zero before onset does not trigger this. permute() refuses untreatedZero.
items.why: untreatedZero is for a dose that is truly zero outside treated cells. The model should then have no baseline dose effect. Some engines added a pooled dose column anyway. The dose is zero off the treated cells, so that column equals the sum of the cells' slope columns. The engine therefore dropped one cell's slope to make room. The att then lost the pooled slope. The ame became the mean slope minus the dropped cell's slope. With a linear dose, one engine reported 0.26 where the default engine reported 30.23 for the same model. Now suppose a treated cell with a nonzero dose loses its slope under untreatedZero. The engine keeps the slopes and drops the cell intercepts instead. The reported slope then becomes the cell's effect divided by its dose. In one case that gave 1.55 against a true 1.0. The number is wrong and nothing marks it, which is why the run stops. Under permute(), each replication moves onset dates while each unit's dose path stays fixed. Every replication would then put a nonzero dose where the model assumes zero.
items.decision: The author ruled that all engines follow the default engine's model. The pooled control is cleared inside the untreatedZero branch of the code. A later edit to the code that builds it therefore cannot bring it back. The refusal used to sit behind a display setting that limits repeated messages on lattice runs. He moved it out, because a hard stop should not depend on a display option. He also extended it to the cells' slopes on interacted controls. He declined a check that would flag a nonzero dose outside treated cells, and the help states the consequence instead. Another proposal was to report the ame as missing and continue, as basic does. It was not adopted, because it would reverse his ruling that the engines align.
items.what_you_notice: On poisson, customvce() and unconditionalse runs with untreatedZero, point estimates move and now match the default engine. On poisson, one example gives an ame of .31 against a truth of .30, where v1.3 gave .19. A dose constant within each cohort is refused with error 322, as in v1.3, and the help now says so. The help also says that using untreatedZero when the dose is not zero outside treated cells gives biased estimates, however precise they look. permute() with untreatedZero is an error.
sources: review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/RULINGS_LEDGER.md R5, 'R5 / DEF-2 scope correction', 'DEF-2 out of the anti-spam gate'
