items.heading: With a lattice, basic controls remove the baseline dose slope within each bin
items.what_changed: A lattice splits the dose into bins and lets the dose effect differ across them. With lattice() and contreatcontrols(basic), wooldid now always includes the baseline dose control, both pooled and within each bin. Before, the control was skipped whenever a lattice was present. The att point estimates do not move. Their standard errors shifted by a fraction of a percent through the degrees of freedom, until the next item corrected that. The ame rows can move a lot.
items.why: The event study and the joint tests assume the reference period's effect is set to zero. Without the baseline control, the average dose effect in the reference period was about 1.0. Every ame row was therefore measured from a nonzero anchor. The joint pretrend test checks whether the rows before onset are zero. It instead tested equality with that anchor. In one example this gave a p value of .146 where the correct test gave .615. Anyone passing the results to HonestDiD or pretrends inherited the wrong reference. basic promises that treated cells' dose effects are measured against the untreated dose slope. With a lattice, that must hold within each bin.
items.decision: The question was whether a nonzero reference effect was correct behaviour or a flaw in how the model was built. The author ruled it a flaw in building the model and had the control always included.
items.what_you_notice: ame rows move on lattice runs with basic. In one example the main ame went from 1.267 to 0.2475. The rows before onset went from 0.81 and 0.77 to -0.213 and -0.247. The help's lattice() entry says the baseline dose effect is removed within each lattice bin.

items.heading: No degrees of freedom charged for redundant copies of the dose
items.what_changed: To control which terms the regression drops, wooldid absorbs an exact copy of the dose. Absorbing means reghdfe handles it the way it handles a fixed effect, outside the list of regressors. wooldid now absorbs only the finest version of that copy the run asks for. reghdfe therefore no longer counts redundant slopes against the residual degrees of freedom. These are the rows left over after counting the estimated parameters, and they scale the standard errors. No point estimate moves.
items.why: The redundant copies add no information. The design keeps the same number of independent columns and the same residual sum of squares with or without them. Charging degrees of freedom for them shrank the residual degrees of freedom. That slightly inflated every standard error, including those of the att rows. After the change, the absorbing engine's standard error matches the other engine's for the same model to sixteen digits.
items.decision: Three options were put to the author. One was to accept the extra charge. Another was to skip the redundant copies only when a control for each group is present. The third was to accept the charge and pin the residual degrees of freedom of every affected test configuration, so the factor could not drift unnoticed. The recommendation was to accept, with the pins. He ruled to stop the overcounting. Paths that enter these terms as listed regressors keep the full set, because there the copies decide which term the engine drops.
items.what_you_notice: Slightly smaller standard errors and narrower intervals on lattice runs and on dose runs with a control for each group. The change is up to about a quarter of a percent.

items.heading: ccc_absorb() reports the effect at each cell's average control value
items.what_changed: ccc_absorb() gives each treated cell its own slope on a control variable. It now enters each control once as a pooled regressor. Each treated cell also gets a slope on a copy of the control centred at that cell's weighted mean. The copy is set to zero on reference rows. The reported effect for each cell is its att at the cell's average control value. It no longer changes when the control is shifted or rescaled. coarsecohortcontrols() changed the same way.
items.why: With uncentred cell slopes, each treated cell's intercept reads the effect at a control value of zero. The answer then depends on where zero happens to sit. In one example the true att was 2.00. The estimate was -0.53 with a control x, and -49.4 with x+100. Centring at the cell mean spans the same columns and gives the same fit. It also makes the cell intercept the average effect in the cell. In that example it gave 1.930. The imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) also gave 1.930.
items.decision: Four options were considered. One was to build the centred model. Another was to document that the effect is at a control value of zero and tell users to centre. A third was to refuse uncentred controls. The last was to leave it. The author chose to build the centred model, including the poisson path and its retry. In effect this retires his earlier ruling to keep a late error for controls constant within a cell under an event study window. Once centred, such a control has a copy equal to zero in that cell. It can no longer absorb the treatment terms, so the case the error existed for cannot arise. That consequence was not put to him separately.
items.what_you_notice: Estimates from runs with ccc_absorb() or coarsecohortcontrols() can move. They no longer depend on the control's units or origin. The help no longer warns that a control constant within a cell absorbs the treatment terms.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s5 item 1, s8, s9 G1

items.heading: Poisson with a dose: controls entered directly, and a warning when ppmlhdfe drops the dose slope
items.what_changed: ppmlhdfe, the poisson engine, cannot absorb some of the slope terms wooldid needs. Under plain contreatcontrols(basic), the pooled dose control and any ccc_absorb() controls now enter the poisson regression as ordinary regressors from the first fit. Before, every such run failed once, printed a four line caution and refitted. contreatpoly() fits a polynomial in the dose. When it is above 1 with a lattice or a control for each group, the dose controls also enter directly. ccc_absorb() of several variables is absorbed one variable per term. Both of these designs used to stop with error 3201. Sometimes ppmlhdfe drops the pooled dose slope as collinear with the fixed effects. wooldid now warns that the ame is then wrong and says to subtract the dose's mean and rerun.
items.why: Entering the controls directly fits the same model ppmlhdfe cannot absorb, so the numbers do not change. For a dose polynomial, the old approach absorbed separate slope sets on the dose and on its square. Within a bin these were correlated at .9998. The solver for the fixed effects then barely converged. Runs took from 19 seconds to 15 minutes. One returned an ame about 47 times the direct fit's. On the dropped slope, ppmlhdfe removes a regressor whose variation after the fixed effects is tiny next to its raw size. A dose with a large mean and a small spread trips that rule. The model then loses its baseline dose slope, and the ame is wrong. In one example it was .52 against .24, 6.5 standard errors off, with nothing printed.
items.decision: The author first asked whether any absorbed spelling worked. None was found that ppmlhdfe 2.3.0 accepts, so he ruled to enter the terms directly. For error 3201 he ruled to fix it while keeping terms absorbed wherever possible. For ccc_absorb() on plain basic, he first ruled to keep it absorbed. He reversed to direct entry the next day. By then the empty covariance behind that ruling had been traced to a rounding accident in how ppmlhdfe posts its results. For the dropped pooled slope, he chose to detect it and warn. The warning is skipped when the fixed effects genuinely carry the dose.
items.what_you_notice: Plain basic runs show no fallback caution and make half as many ppmlhdfe calls, with the same numbers. Runs that stopped with error 3201 now complete. A new caution appears when the pooled dose slope is dropped. The help notes that under dyex, subtracting the mean also changes the elasticity.
sources: review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md s4 rows on ppmlhdfe, v5, r(3201), ccc_absorb, dropped pooled slope; 'The v5 probe'
wooldid.sthlp poisson entry (~l.528-541), ccnoabsorb and ccc_absorb() entries

items.heading: Poisson dose effects use an exact derivative
items.what_changed: wooldid computes its dose results with Stata's margins command. For the standard errors, margins also needs how each result responds to each coefficient. For poisson dose runs it used to work that out by numerical approximation. It now uses the exact form, for dydx since 2026-08-31 and for dyex since 2026-09-06. Point estimates do not move. Standard errors change by about one part in 100 million, toward the exact value. Runs are much faster. poisson runs with dyex can now use the cell collapse described below.
items.why: On the scale wooldid reports under poisson, each of these results is a straight line in the coefficients. The exact response is therefore known, and a check confirms the new form to about 16 decimal places. The approximation missed it by up to about three parts in a billion, and its error passed into the reported variances. The approximation also cost a pass over the data for every coefficient. One poisson event study fell from 305 seconds to 5. The approximation did serve a purpose. It kept margins on the scale of the log of expected y. The exact form names the same scale, so that purpose survives. The collapse had been refused for poisson with dyex only because of the numerical form.
items.decision: The author approved the dydx change on 2026-08-31. For dyex he first asked for more research. The exact form had to pass the straight line check, and the collapse refusal would be lifted only if it did. It passed, and both were built on 2026-09-06. The ey forms kept the approximation, and they have since been removed, as a later item explains.
items.what_you_notice: Poisson dose runs are roughly 2 to 60 times faster. Standard errors differ from v1.3 only far past the displayed digits. poisson with dyex now takes the cell collapse.
sources: commit 32517df (analytic Jacobian on the poisson dydx sites, author-approved)

items.heading: Too many lattice bins: a help warning and a caution when a bin borrows a slope
items.what_changed: The help now warns against splitting a run into too many lattice bins. Each treated cell needs at least two distinct dose values within each bin it occupies. The rule of thumb is several times as many units per treated cell as there are bins. A new caution is printed by default. It counts the pieces, meaning a cell within one bin, that hold a single nonzero dose value while their cell still has a live dose slope. It says their slopes are borrowed from another bin of the same cell. It advises coarsening the lattice or dropping the cells. The verbose list of dropped terms no longer calls such drops likely harmless.
items.why: A lattice gives each cell a separate slope in each bin. Each slope is identified only by dose variation inside its own piece. A piece with one dose value cannot identify a slope. The collinearity drop then leaves it with a neighbouring bin's slope. The ame then averages in a slope estimated on another part of the dose distribution. Separately, a piece with no more rows than parameters is fitted exactly, with zero residuals. No variance built from residuals can see its noise. In one design this put the ame standard errors at 0.017 of the true sampling spread.
items.decision: A runtime check that counted exactly fitted pieces was built and measured. It separated the broken design from the healthy one it was written against. However, it also fired on another healthy design, with a dose in whole numbers, whose standard errors were sound. The author asked for a help warning instead. Checks based on which terms dropped were rejected for the same reason. A cut on relative spread missed the pieces with two rows that do the damage. For the borrowed slope, he approved a caution printed by default. It counts pieces in the data and ignores which terms dropped. The term that drops need not belong to the affected piece.
items.what_you_notice: The new caution on lattice runs with pieces that hold a single dose value, and a paragraph in the help on too many bins.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s3 (dose:CT-2), s4, s5 item 7, s8, s9 G4

items.heading: A generated lattice is rebuilt on each bootstrap resample
items.what_changed: wooldid can generate a lattice itself from quantiles of the dose. latticeignoreweights builds those bins without the sampling weights. Such a lattice is now rebuilt on each replication's resample under bootstrap() with resampling by counts. The same holds under bootstrap(bayes), the Bayesian bootstrap, which reweights rows at random instead of resampling them. The rebuild keeps how often each row was drawn and ignores the sampling weights. Bootstrap standard errors, p values and intervals move on these runs.
items.why: When wooldid generates the lattice, the bins come from quantiles of the dose. They are therefore part of the estimator, and each replication must rebuild them from its own data. Before, one resampling scheme binned only the distinct rows drawn. The Bayesian scheme binned the original sample. The bootstrap standard error then depended on which internal scheme the run used. On unweighted data, an option that does nothing to the point estimate changed the bootstrap answer.
items.decision: The alternative was to keep the bins fixed at the original sample's. The author ruled to rebuild them in each replication.
items.what_you_notice: Bootstrap results change on these runs. On unweighted data, latticeignoreweights now leaves the bootstrap results unchanged.

items.heading: contreatwithin no longer switches off every check
items.what_changed: contreatwithin allows dose designs with no untreated group. In v1.3 it switched off every safety check. It still sets the program's working safety level to off. That lifts the requirement for an untreated group, the removal of periods with no control unit, and the check that some unit is observed both before and after onset. It also lifts the checks that the requested event study window appears in the sample, the check for dropped treatment dummies, and the restriction of makecfxplots to the att. Every check that reads the user's own safety() setting now runs. These include the checks on data integrity, the checks of the i variable and the variable count, and the check for all dose slopes dropped. They also include the baseline dose slope checks and the caution for dropped dose cells. byTime is still refused unless safety(off) is given. permute() refuses contreatwithin.
items.why: contreatwithin exists to allow designs with no untreated group. That gives no reason to skip checks on the data or on whether the dose slopes are identified. A contreatwithin run whose every dose slope dropped printed meaningless zeros as the ame. basic with contreatwithin could report an ame of the wrong sign with a standard error of essentially zero and no caution. Permutation moves onset dates across clusters and needs a comparison group, which these designs lack.
items.decision: The author ruled to restore the check on the number of variables that contreatwithin had disabled. He ruled to run the baseline dose slope checks under it, and the check for all slopes dropped too. An early draft exempted contreatwithin from the baseline check. That was reversed, because contreatwithin does not rescue the misspecification. Keying the i variable check to the user's own safety() setting was done during the build. It was not put to him separately.
items.what_you_notice: Some contreatwithin runs that v1.3 completed now stop with an error or print a caution.

items.heading: contreatwithin: read the ame, and a caution where the att rests on an arbitrary choice
items.what_changed: v1.3's help said the att under contreatwithin should essentially be the integral of the ame, meaning the ame added up over doses from zero. The help now explains when that fails and says to rely on the ame results under contreatwithin. A new caution names the periods with no untreated reference rows. It says the att there depends on an arbitrary choice.
items.why: In a period with no untreated rows, the treated cell dummies of that period add up to the period dummy. Their levels are then identified only up to a choice the solver makes. It sets one cell's level effect to zero and measures the others against it. The att in that period depends on which cell was chosen. It can change when cohorts are relabelled, and it can take the wrong sign. So the att can jump at the last treatment onset for this reason alone. The dose slopes within cells do not depend on that choice, which is why the ame is the quantity to read. Even when fixed effects absorb every cohort and period level, the att equals the integral of the ame only by extending the slope down to a dose of zero.
items.decision: The help correction came first. The author then approved the caution and its wording.
items.what_you_notice: A caution under contreatwithin gives the number of periods with no untreated reference rows. It says one treated cell's level effect in each was set to zero, so the att there depends on that choice. It says to rely on the ame results. The help's contreatwithin paragraph is rewritten.
sources: review_process/econ_review_2026-09-25.md s3 (dose:CT-3), s4, s5 item 7, s8, s9 G4

items.heading: What the ame measures: strong parallel trends
items.what_changed: The help and the guide now state what the ame identifies. The chosen control type sets the parallel trends assumption. Parallel trends means treated and untreated units would have moved alike without treatment. It identifies the att and the att within each dose bin. The ame is the effect of a marginal increase in the dose only under a stronger condition. Units at different doses would also have to gain the same from treatment at any given dose.
items.why: Within a treated cell, the ame compares units that received different doses. Ordinary parallel trends says their outcomes would have moved alike without treatment. It says nothing about whether high dose units would have gained as much as low dose units at the same dose. Units may sort into doses by how much they stand to gain. The slope then mixes the causal dose response with that sorting. Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (2024) call the needed condition strong parallel trends.
items.decision: This corrected the documentation under the author's standing instruction to fix econometric statements. It was not put to him as a separate question. The alternative was to stay silent, as v1.3 did.
items.what_you_notice: No numbers change. The help has a new paragraph, and the guide's first decision rule for dose designs repeats it. The same caveat applies to the ame by bin, to differences in the att across bins, and to the att under contreatwithin with no untreated group.

items.heading: Only dydx and dyex remain, and poisson results carry their proper names
items.what_changed: contreatelasticitytype() now accepts only two forms. dydx, the default, is the change in y per unit of dose. dyex is the change in y per proportional change in dose. eyex, eydx, semielasticity and poisexpresults were removed. Under poisson, results are on the scale of the log of expected y. On that scale dydx is already the semielasticity, the proportional change in y per unit of dose. dyex is already the elasticity, the proportional change in y per proportional change in dose. The tables, plots and histograms are now titled that way.
items.why: The removed forms divide by the model's prediction of y. On the default reghdfe path that prediction leaves out the absorbed fixed effects, so it is not the fitted outcome. These elasticities differed by about 7 to 20 percent from the same model fitted with explicit dummies. Under poisson the scale is already the log of expected y, so an ey form took a log of a log. Multiplying y by ten changed the reported semielasticity, which a true semielasticity cannot do. dydx and dyex never divide by the prediction, and they agree across engines to the last digit a computer stores.
items.decision: The first step remapped the ey forms under poisson with a caution. A later repair of the default path was tried. Its standard errors disagreed with the fit using explicit dummies. They were 10 to 14 percent narrower on dense cells and up to six times wider on sparse ones, and part of the gap was unexplained. The author chose removal over repair and left dydx and dyex untouched. He approved the poisson titles and their wording.
items.what_you_notice: eyex, eydx, semielasticity and poisexpresults are no longer accepted. Under poisson the dydx results are titled Semi-elasticities and the dyex results Elasticities. They used to be titled Effects and Semi-elasticities.
sources: review_process/blue_sky_2026-09-18/RULINGS_LEDGER.md R2, R6 (ELAS mooted), 'Ruled: take no action' (clean margins operators)

items.heading: The cell collapse now covers dose runs
items.what_changed: After the regression, wooldid computes the att and the ame as averages with Stata's margins command. By default it computes them on one row per cell of cohort, period and treatment status, instead of on every observation. This collapse now covers contreat() runs. The surviving row carries the cell's weighted mean dose. The weights are the estimand weights, the ones that define the reported average, and the mean is stored in double precision. lattice() and makecfxplots are covered too, with the bin added to what defines a cell. The collapse is still skipped, with a caution, in two cases. One is contreatpoly() above 1. The other is when the dose also appears in controls(), coarsecohortcontrols(), fe() or ccc_absorb().
items.why: Every margins quantity wooldid reports is linear in the dose within a cell. One row carrying the cell's weighted mean dose therefore reproduces it exactly. Four conditions were each shown to be necessary. The weight must be the estimand weight, and a row count will not do. The mean must be written before the surviving row is picked. The cohort variable must help define the cell. And the mean must be stored in double precision. A polynomial in the dose, or the dose inside another control, makes the slope vary within the cell. One row cannot represent that.
items.decision: The author proposed the cell mean himself and ruled it in after an assessment. In the simpler form, the surviving row keeps its own dose. That form failed on all nine dose configurations tested, and six coefficients changed sign. He later ruled to admit lattice() and makecfxplots once the bin joined the cell definition. A guard for a customweightmultiplier() with negative values was built and not shipped, because he treats that option as use at your own risk.
items.what_you_notice: Dose runs are 2 to 4 times faster on larger panels. Results match the uncollapsed run to the accuracy of margins itself. nofastcollapse turns the collapse off.

items.heading: Event study ame rows that cannot be estimated are dropped
items.what_changed: subgroups() splits the sample so wooldid can report effects for each group. In dose event studies by subgroup, a horizon whose ame cannot be estimated is now dropped from the table and from e(b), with a caution. A horizon is a period counted from onset. A subgroup whose ame horizons all fail is skipped. Before, such horizons printed as rows of missing values with zeros in e(b), or the run stopped with an error. fastnose, the fast mode, skips standard errors to save time. It now drops the same rows as a full run.
items.why: A row with no estimate carries no information. Programs that export results read the zeros in e(b) as numbers. Dropping the rows matches how the binary event study already treats horizons that cannot be estimated. Fast mode could not see which rows margins would mark as not estimable, because that mark comes with the variance fast mode skips. It printed rows the full run drops, including a row after onset reported as exactly zero.
items.decision: Blank rows or dropped rows was a display choice. The author ruled on 2026-09-07 to drop them with a caution. He confirmed the drop for a related case on 2026-09-13. For fast mode he asked for a cheap way to find the same rows. Computing the variance for this purpose would add 16 to 60 seconds per run, paid again in every permutation replication. He ruled in a check that costs about a twentieth of a second. It drops a row only when its value is exactly zero and no cohort in that subgroup and horizon has a dose slope the regression kept. On 25 designs it matched the full run on all 487 rows tested.
items.what_you_notice: Fewer rows in some subgroup event study tables and in e(b), and a caution naming the dropped horizons. Fast mode now shows the same rows as the full run.

items.heading: Dose tests need many observations per cell
items.what_changed: The help's jointtests entry now says that under a continuous treatment the tests also need many observations per cell. The adversarial entry points to the same condition. There is no runtime check on cell size.
items.why: Each cell's dose slope is estimated from the rows inside it. With few rows those slopes are noisy. The covariance the test uses then has the wrong shape as well as the wrong scale, so the test rejects too often. In simulation the ame line test rejected 40.2 percent of the time at six observations per cell. At fifty observations it rejected 11.0 percent of the time. The nominal rate was 5 percent.
items.decision: The simulation study had a rule set in advance, and that rule said to withdraw the ame adversarial test. The study recommended a check on cell size instead. Neither was built. The author stopped the testing before a threshold was mapped. On 2026-09-14 he ruled to leave the cell size condition to the user's judgement instead of adding a runtime check. The help then carried the measured rates. That ruling is recorded in the commit that added them, 6ccceec, and not in the written rulings.
items.what_you_notice: No change in output. The help carries the warning. The measured rejection rates were later cut when the help was shortened.
sources: commit 6ccceec (ruling to leave the cell-size check to the user's judgement)

items.heading: How permutation, bootstrap and gteffects treat a dose
items.what_changed: permute() keeps each unit's dose path and reshuffles only onset timing. It refuses contreatwithin and untreatedZero. gteffects, new since v1.3, reports each cohort and period effect, and it is not available with contreat(). cfxplotnose skips standard errors for the dose plot cells. It is dropped with a caution under permute() with permtstat or permtci, and under bootstrap() with boottstat. Otherwise the dose plot cells keep their replication inference under both methods.
items.why: Permutation tests the sharp null, the hypothesis that treatment had no effect on anyone. With a dose, that test is valid when onset timing is as good as random given the dose. So only timing is shuffled. The items on contreatwithin and untreatedZero give the reasons for the two refusals. Under a dose, the cell coefficients gteffects would report are intercepts at a dose of zero, which are not the cell effects. Studentized replication methods divide each replication's estimate by its standard error. They therefore need a standard error for each plot cell, and they must override the option that skips them.
items.decision: For cfxplotnose, the author ruled against leaving the plot cells blank under permtstat. He extended the same exception to bootstrap() with boottstat. The permute() and gteffects refusals carry their reasons in the code, and no separate ruling on them is recorded.
items.what_you_notice: Errors for permute() with contreatwithin or untreatedZero, and for gteffects with contreat(). A caution when cfxplotnose is overridden.

area: Event studies, pre-trend tests and bands
title: Event studies, pre-trend tests and bands
intro: This section covers how wooldid reports event studies. An event study estimates a separate effect for each period relative to treatment onset. Each such period is called a horizon. wooldid builds its estimates from cohort-by-period cells, where a cell is one group of units in one calendar period. The variable i names those groups, and it can range from single units up to whole onset cohorts. Every horizon is measured against a reference period whose effect is set to zero. The section deals with how horizons are named and windowed, which reference anchors them, and the tests offered for pre-trends. A pre-trend is a difference between treated and comparison groups that already shows before treatment starts. The section also covers the bands and covariance matrices stored for inference across horizons. A covariance matrix records how much each estimate varies and how the estimates move together. The common theme is that each pre-trend statistic is either calibrated for the design it runs on or says plainly that it is not. A final item records the scale on which poisson results are reported.

items.heading: Event-study horizons are named by relative period, with one naming convention
items.what_changed: Each event-study coefficient is named for the relative period it measures. pre# is relative period minus #, and post# is relative period #. post0 is the onset period. The reference period has no column of its own. Under esfixedbaseperiod, every horizon is compared with one omitted reference period, relative period -1 by default. So under that option the pre-period names begin at pre2. The oldsyntax option is gone. It had renamed post0 to contemp.
items.why: Users refer to these coefficients by name in lincom, test and honestdid. lincom and test are Stata's commands for combinations of estimates and for joint tests. honestdid is the sensitivity package of Rambachan and Roth (2023). The names must therefore say which period each coefficient measures. The old help said the horizons were numbered outward from the reference period. The code never worked that way. Read literally, the old text reversed the order of the pre-period horizons. Under esrelativeto(-3) it would have sent a user to a horizon two periods away from the one intended. A second name for the onset row also had to be carried through the covariance matrix, the composition table and the bootstrap and permutation engines. Both engines refused it anyway.
items.decision: The author kept the names the code already produced and corrected the text to match them. He removed oldsyntax to simplify the program. Seven comparison runs without the option came out identical to the last digit. That covered estimates, variances, row names and printed output.
items.what_you_notice: A call that names oldsyntax now stops with an error. The onset period is always post0. The help's account of the names matches the output. No number changes.

items.heading: The window counts consecutive periods, and horizons the data cannot supply drop out silently
items.what_changed: esprelength() and espostlength() set how many pre-treatment and post-treatment horizons to report. They count consecutive whole-number relative periods, whether or not the data contain each one. A biennial panel, observed every second year, leaves some of those slots empty. The reported window then comes out shorter than requested. The help now says so. It tells users to widen the request until it reaches the horizons they want. A requested horizon with no data still drops out of the table with no message. Gaps in the panel can cause this. So can a horizon at the edge of the data. subgroups() asks for separate estimates for groups of units, and a subgroup's earliest period can be forced into its reference. That also drops horizons. The guide also states that the pooled main row averages every post-treatment period that can be estimated, whatever espostlength() is.
items.why: On a biennial panel, a request for two pre-treatment and three post-treatment horizons returns one and two. Under the default pooled reference, each treated cohort is compared with the pool of its own pre-treatment periods outside the window. The window therefore decides which pre-periods leave that pool. So the counting rule is part of the estimator, and changing it would change estimates. The window limits what the event study shows. It does not limit the periods the pooled estimate uses. A horizon with no cells has no estimate to report. A user who asked for more horizons than the panel supports sees the shorter table.
items.decision: The author chose to document the counting rule and leave it unchanged. He declined the whole proposed fix, which had two parts. One part would have built the window from the periods the data actually contain. On panels without gaps that gives exactly today's answer. The other part was a caution naming the requested relative periods that had no cells. A caution keyed on the whole-number range had also been proposed. It would not have fired on any of the cases shown, so it was never a real candidate. He ruled that horizons should keep dropping silently. He also declined to make the forced-reference caution print under safety(off), the option that silences cautions. The record gives these rulings without a reason.
items.what_you_notice: No result changes. The help entries for esprelength() and espostlength() explain the counting rule. The caution about a subgroup's earliest period being forced into its reference still prints. safety(off) still silences it.

items.heading: The pooled reference stays the default, and the help now says what each reference assumes
items.what_changed: The pooled reference remains the default, and no note prints to say so. Under it, each treated cohort is compared with the pool of its own pre-treatment periods. A new help paragraph explains that the choice of reference changes the comparison group. Under the pooled reference, every untreated observation serves as a control. That includes the pre-treatment periods of cohorts treated later. Under esfixedbaseperiod, each treated cohort's other pre-periods get their own indicators. The period effects then come only from never-treated cohorts and from cohorts treated after the sample ends.
items.why: The two references rest on different parallel-trends assumptions. Parallel trends means the treated and comparison groups would have moved alike without treatment. Under the pooled reference it must hold across every untreated period of every cohort, including cohorts not yet treated. No anticipation must hold there too, meaning units do not respond before onset. Under the fixed reference both are needed only between each treated cohort and the never-treated cohorts, from the reference period on. The fixed reference is the never-treated comparison of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) and Sun and Abraham (2021). The pooled default matches the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024). A test showed the difference. It changed only the early outcomes of a cohort not yet treated. The default att, the average effect on treated observations, moved from 1.8456 to 1.895. The fixed-reference att stayed unchanged. The help used to present the choice only as a trade of transparency against precision. That hid the fact that the identifying assumption differs.
items.decision: The author kept the pooled default and chose not to label it on screen. It places wooldid alongside its closest relatives, did_imputation and jwdid. It can be more precise, because it averages over more reference periods. The price is a stronger parallel-trends assumption. Flipping the default would change the numbers of every default run. He rejected four alternatives. One made the fixed reference at period -1 the default. One printed a note on every pooled run. One relabelled the plot's reference tick. One added a caution on the honestdid hand-off under the pooled reference. The author later saw that the help framed the choice only as transparency against precision. He then added the paragraph on the comparison group.
items.what_you_notice: Default results are unchanged. The help has a new paragraph on the comparison group. Three tools still require esfixedbaseperiod, because each needs a single omitted period. They are the adversarial test's p-value, pretrendpower() and the direct honestdid hand-off.

items.heading: Under a fixed reference, the pretreatment row is a placebo over the whole pre-period
items.what_changed: Under esfixedbaseperiod, the pretreatment row of the results table averages every pre-treatment period that can be estimated. It is not limited to the window requested with esprelength(), and it does not narrow when the window shrinks. The joint pre-trend test on the same run uses only the requested window. The help now says both things.
items.why: Under a fixed reference, every pre-period keeps its own coefficient. An average of all of them is therefore a well-defined placebo. A placebo is an effect measured before treatment, which should be zero if trends are parallel. Yet the row and the joint test can cover different periods and disagree on one screen. In one test, a shock confined to relative period -4 and earlier gave the pretreatment row a p-value of 5e-211. The joint pre-trend p-value directly below it was 0.82. The reader needs to know what each one covers to interpret both.
items.decision: The author chose to document the row as a placebo over the whole pre-period. The alternative was to restrict the row to the requested window so that it matched the joint test. That would have changed e(b), the stored estimates, on every fixed-reference run. It would also have needed special handling at esprelength(0).
items.what_you_notice: No number changes. The help entry for esfixedbaseperiod says what each of the two pre-period summaries covers.

items.heading: The conditions for matching did_imputation are stated in full
items.what_changed: The help's comparison with did_imputation now lists every condition for an exact match. The run must target the att and use the pooled reference. It must request no pre-treatment horizons and no controls. It must not use unconditionalse, the option for unconditional standard errors. In addition, i must identify units, or every unit within an i must be observed in the same periods. Adding the unit to fe() does not restore the match.
items.why: Under the pooled reference, requested pre-treatment horizons leave the reference pool. That shifts every post-treatment coefficient. did_imputation's own pre-trend option leaves its post-treatment estimates alone. did_imputation also uses unit fixed effects, while wooldid builds its cells on i. Suppose i is coarser than the unit and units within an i are observed in different periods. Then the two estimators genuinely differ. The two agreed to 4e-8 at esprelength(0). They differed by 0.048 at esprelength(4). They also differed with a coarse i on an unbalanced panel.
items.decision: The author ruled to state the esprelength(0) condition. He added the condition on the level of i later. Testing showed that balance within each i is enough. So the help asks only for that, which is weaker than a fully balanced panel.
items.what_you_notice: No result changes. A user checking wooldid against did_imputation now knows which settings must hold for the numbers to agree.

items.heading: The joint pre-trend test under clustering at or above i is computed, with a caution that its p-value is not calibrated
items.what_changed: jointtests reports a joint test that all pre-treatment horizons are zero. A cluster variable groups observations whose errors may be correlated. Sometimes the analytic cluster variable contains i, as when a run clusters on i itself. The test is still computed and printed there. A caution says its p-value is not calibrated. The caution names three remedies. They are permute(), bootstrap(), or a cluster() strictly finer than the cohort-by-period cells that leaves many clusters inside each cell. permute() is a permutation test that reassigns onset dates at random. bootstrap() re-estimates on resampled data. pretrendpower() uses the same statistic, follows the same rule and prints the same caution. v1.3 computed the test in every design without comment.
items.why: wooldid gives every treated cohort-by-period cell its own dummy variable. A cell dummy forces that cell's residuals to sum to zero. A cluster-robust variance allows errors to be correlated within a cluster. It is built from sums of residual terms taken cluster by cluster. When one cluster contains the whole cell, that sum is zero for the cell. The cell's own noise then never enters the variance. The estimated variance reflects mostly the noise of the control observations. It is too small, and so is the p-value. A true null was rejected 11 to 66 percent of the time at a nominal 5 percent. The rate stayed high with many cohorts and with large cells. With only a few clusters per cell, a finer cluster() leaves the test oversized too.
items.decision: The author first ruled for a hard refusal. That refused the test in exactly the design the help recommends elsewhere, clustering at i. did_imputation and Stata's estat ptrends report such a test without complaint. He then ruled to compute it with a caution. An earlier ruling would have suppressed the test only under pretrendpower(). He settled that conflict with one rule for one statistic in both places. He also ruled that the finer-cluster remedy must say it needs many clusters per cell, wherever it is named. He did not adopt an automatic switch to a bootstrap or permutation test.
items.what_you_notice: jointtests with clustering at i or coarser prints a p-value followed by a caution. The test needs at least two pre-treatment horizons in the window. Under esfixedbaseperiod with timetrends at the default reference period it needs three. timetrends adds a separate linear time trend for each cohort.

items.heading: New option pretrendpower() reports how much a clean pre-trend test is worth
items.what_changed: pretrendpower() takes power levels in percent, such as pretrendpower(50 80). Power is the chance that a test detects a violation of a given size. An estimand is the quantity an estimate targets. For each estimand type the option reports three things. The first is an estimate of the linear pre-trend slope, fitted through the reference period, with its standard error and interval. The second is the smallest linear pre-trend that each of two pre-tests would detect with that power. One pre-test is wooldid's joint test. The other asks whether any single pre-period coefficient is significant. The third is the bias such a trend would cause in the pooled estimate if it continued after treatment. The option requires esfixedbaseperiod and at least one pre-period coefficient. It is refused with impvalues, fastnose and permute(). impvalues is an alternative inference method built on cluster-by-cluster estimates. fastnose is a fast mode that computes no standard errors. Under bootstrap() the option uses the bootstrap covariance. Results go to e(roth_power_*) and companion scalars. att_it, att_i and att_itime are versions of the average effect that weight the cells differently. When only att_i or att_itime is requested, the att_it event study stands in for them.
items.why: Roth (2022) showed that conventional pre-tests often have little power. A pre-test that fails to reject is reassuring only if it could have detected a violation large enough to matter. The smallest detectable trend, and the bias it would imply, tell the user what a clean pre-test actually rules out. The line passes through the reference period because that is the one period normalized to zero. The pooled reference has no single such period, which is why the option needs esfixedbaseperiod. The bias is averaged over every post-treatment period the pooled estimate uses. The pooled estimate averages all of them, so a bias taken from the reported window alone would be too small.
items.decision: The author did not rule on most of the design. Those choices were made when the option was built, and measurements backed each one. The slope is estimated by generalized least squares, which weights the coefficients using their joint covariance. The option does not reuse the unweighted display line of the adversarial test. That line's naive interval covered 98.4 percent of the time at a nominal 95, and it was 2.6 times as wide. The joint test's detectable trend comes from the F distribution. F and chi-squared are both reference distributions for joint tests. F allows for the variance being estimated, while chi-squared treats it as known. A chi-squared shortcut was about 25 percent optimistic at 10 clusters. Taking the bias from the reported window alone understated it by 28 percent. The any-coefficient column is computed only up to four pre-periods. Its exact integration takes about three and a half minutes for one power level at six pre-periods. At seven it takes about 51 minutes. For larger designs the help points to Roth's pretrends package, which reads wooldid's stored event-study results directly. The author's own rulings on the option are three. He weighed removing it and kept it. Its joint-test power, weighted slope and implied bias have no counterpart in pretrends. He ruled that its existing departures from Roth stand and that only new work need follow Roth. He also dropped a proposed caution for designs with one observation per treated cell. The next item covers the last two rulings.
items.what_you_notice: A new option and new stored results. Under subgroups() only the overall event studies are analysed. Some pre-period coefficients can be exact combinations of others. The covariance is then rank-deficient, meaning some combinations of coefficients have no measurable variance. A caution then says the results describe only the independent coefficients and are not joint pre-trend evidence. This matters because the retained test can shrink to a single coefficient's t-test. In one case it discarded a coefficient with t = -11.7. When only att_i or att_itime is requested, a note says the bias column uses att_it's post-period weights and does not describe the requested estimand.

items.heading: pretrendpower()'s pre-tests are 5 percent tests whatever level() is, and the one remaining departure from Roth stands
items.what_changed: level() sets the confidence level of intervals. Here it moves only the slope's confidence interval. Both pre-tests whose power is reported are 5 percent tests. The any-coefficient test now uses the normal distribution for both its cutoff and its probabilities. The joint test still uses the F distribution with the regression's residual degrees of freedom, where Roth uses chi-squared. Residual degrees of freedom measure how much information is left over for estimating variance. Fewer of them mean heavier tails. A printed note says both pre-tests are at 5 percent under the normal reference whatever level() is. No caution was added for designs with one observation per treated cell.
items.why: A power calculation describes a test of a stated size. Size is the rate at which a test rejects a true null. The conventional pre-test has a size of 5 percent. When level() was first extended to the slope interval, it also changed the size of one pre-test and left the other alone. The two columns of one table then described tests of different sizes. At level(99) their order flipped, and at level(50) one column printed exactly 0. The any-coefficient column had also taken its cutoff from the t distribution while computing probabilities under the normal. Its stated 5 percent was then the size of no test anyone runs. At 9 degrees of freedom it was 2.4 percent. Using the normal throughout matches Roth. The joint test stays on F so that it powers the joint test wooldid actually prints. With few clusters the F is also closer to the true size. At three pre-periods and 15 degrees of freedom, a nominal 5 percent cutoff has a true size of 13.0 percent under chi-squared. Under F it is 7.8 percent. At 279 degrees of freedom both are close to 5 percent.
items.decision: The author first ruled to fix both pre-tests at 5 percent. He rejected making the joint test follow level(), which would depart from Roth's convention. He then ruled that the existing departures from Roth stand and that only new work should follow Roth. At that point there were two departures. The joint test used F where Roth uses chi-squared. The any-coefficient test used a t cutoff where Roth uses the normal. A later ruling moved the any-coefficient test to the normal throughout. The F reference for the joint test is now the one departure that remains. It stays because it powers the joint test wooldid prints and is closer to the true size with few clusters. He dropped a proposed caution for singleton-cell designs, meaning designs with one observation per treated cell. It would have fired on a large share of ordinary runs, since setting i to the unit is the default call. The existing rank-deficiency caution instead records the largest treated cell size in a hidden result.
items.what_you_notice: The any-coefficient column moved on runs with few degrees of freedom. Changing level() no longer changes either detectable-trend column. The printed note states the fixed size.

items.heading: The adversarial test is recalibrated, and its null is one line through the reference period with only its slope free
items.what_changed: The adversarial test asks whether all event-study coefficients, before and after onset, lie on one straight line in relative time. In v1.3 it fitted an unweighted line through the coefficients. It then treated the fitted values as known constants and ignored the line's own sampling error. Under the pooled reference it anchored the line on an invented zero. In simulation it rejected a true null 90 percent of the time at a nominal 5 percent. Pooled-reference runs printed p-values as small as 1e-165 that answered no question. The records classify this as a fixed defect. The p-value now comes from a minimum-distance test. It finds the line closest to the coefficients, measured by their full covariance. It then asks whether the coefficients sit further from that line than chance allows. A generalized inverse, a matrix inverse that skips directions with no measurable variance, handles degenerate cases. The reference distribution is F with the regression's residual degrees of freedom where those exist. The p-value requires esfixedbaseperiod. boottstat is the bootstrap that divides each replication by its own standard error. Under bootstrap() the p-value is a bootstrap quantity only with boottstat. Under permute() it is a permutation quantity. The line is now also forced through the omitted reference period, with only its slope estimated. The null is that every estimated horizon, pre and post, lies on that line. The numerator degrees of freedom rise by one. Under timetrends two periods are normalized to zero, so the null becomes that every coefficient is zero. The unweighted display fit in e(adversarial_line_*) keeps a free intercept.
items.why: Under a fixed reference, every coefficient is a difference from the reference period. A path that is truly linear therefore gives coefficients proportional to the distance from the reference period. That is a line through the reference point. The old test let the intercept float, so it could not see a shift that moves every coefficient by the same amount. An unusual or anticipating reference period produces exactly such a shift. Against it, of any size, the old test's power was exactly 5 percent. In one demonstration, a five-unit anomaly at every cohort's reference period pushed all coefficients near -5. Their t statistics ran from 40 to 68. The old test gave p = 0.75 analytically, 0.83 under boottstat and 0.90 under permute(). The new test gave 9.8e-57. The one-parameter null is a special case of the two-parameter one. So against every alternative the new statistic carries at least as much signal as the old. That follows from the mathematics of nested fits and holds without exception. Its one cost is an extra degree of freedom, worth 1.2 to 6.4 points of power at equal signal.
items.decision: The records treat the v1.3 behaviour as a defect, and the author's ruling chose the remedy. He ruled to fix both statistics and to confine the p-value to the fixed reference, with a caution under the pooled one. The choice of null was his own. He asked for a simulation before ruling and then adopted the one-parameter null. The old two-parameter test had the right size for the null it stated. He replaced it because it answered a different question from the one a fixed-reference event study asks.
items.what_you_notice: Every adversarial p-value moved twice, on the analytic path, under boottstat and under permute(). Pooled-reference runs no longer report one. The printed line says the coefficients and the reference period lie on a single line. The stored display line is given as a slope and an intercept at relative period 0.

items.heading: The adversarial test's clustering conditions are documented and left to the user
items.what_changed: wooldid does not check the number of clusters per cell before running the adversarial test. The help says the test is severely oversized unless many clusters span each treated cohort-by-period cell. Oversized means it rejects a true null too often. The help adds that clustering on i puts every cell inside one cluster. The guide gives the magnitudes. Where the condition fails, the help points to permute(), or to bootstrap() with boottstat. The bootstrapped p-value is still posted when each treated cell lies inside one cluster, although it carries no information there. The help does not say so.
items.why: The governing quantity is clusters per cell. The reason is the one given for the joint test. A cell inside one cluster adds none of its own noise to the variance. At a nominal 5 percent, the current statistic's size was 4.5 percent with six clusters per cell. It was 18.0 percent with two and 72.5 percent with one. The permutation version was 3.5 percent. Larger cells do not make up for too few clusters. Under a continuous treatment, also called a dose, the att family was sized at 5.0 percent. The family measuring average marginal effects of the dose was 40.2 percent with six observations per cell. With fifty it was 11.0 percent. When every cell lay inside one cluster, the bootstrapped p rejected 0 of 200 true nulls. It also rejected 0 of 40 planted breaks that the analytic test caught 35 times. So it never rejects there, whatever the truth. That measurement covers only this one geometry.
items.decision: Calibration work produced a mechanical decision rule. It recommended a run-time gate at about six clusters per cell and 180 clusters overall. The author chose documentation only and left the judgement to the user. That includes the cell-size question under a continuous treatment. For the bootstrapped p-value when every cell lies inside one cluster, he chose to change neither code nor help. He was offered withholding the statistic and documenting the limit, and he rejected both.
items.what_you_notice: No gate and no new caution. The help warns about clustering. A user who clusters at i and relies on bootstrap() with boottstat gets an adversarial p-value that will not reject.

items.heading: An adversarial test that cannot run cautions and continues, and a test with no p-value fails outright
items.what_changed: The test may be requested when the window holds fewer than one pre-treatment and one post-treatment horizon. Under timetrends it needs three coefficients. The sample may also lack those horizons. In either case the test is now dropped with a caution, and the run continues. In five cases no p-value can be formed. They are the pooled reference, a degenerate covariance, bootstrap() without boottstat, too few usable bootstrap replications, and too few usable permutations. In each of them the test now fails outright. No line is printed or stored, and a caution says the test failed and why. adversarial with fastnose is still refused.
items.why: The original defect was that a requested test could vanish without a word. A caution fixes that. A fitted line with no p-value offers no inference at all. Earlier cautions said the line was still reported. That invited users to read it as if it were a test.
items.decision: The author first ruled to refuse a run whose window was too narrow. Refusing broke 121 of 501 test configurations. Each carried adversarial as one option in a grid, the way a user setting options from a macro would. He amended the ruling to a caution. On line-only output his rule is that a test with no p-value has failed and should say so. The alternative was to keep the line beside a caution saying no p-value was computed.
items.what_you_notice: Runs that used to stop, or drop the test in silence, now continue with a caution. Pooled-reference runs no longer post line matrices. No p-value, estimate or standard error moved.
sources: review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md s4 rulings (card #25 and siblings; two more line-only paths)

items.heading: A caution when the adversarial test's covariance is rank-deficient, with its degrees of freedom stored
items.what_changed: Sometimes the covariance behind the adversarial test is rank-deficient. Its rank is positive but incomplete, so some combinations of coefficients carry no measurable variance. The test then runs on the directions the generalized inverse keeps. On analytic runs a caution gives the rank and the degrees of freedom the test used. The numerator degrees of freedom are stored in e(adversarial_df_*).
items.why: Dropping the directions the covariance cannot measure gives the standard generalized-inverse Wald test. A Wald test measures how far estimates sit from the null, scaled by their covariance. This one has the right size when the covariance is right, and its only loss is power. But the user had no signal that part of the hypothesis went untested. pretrendpower() already cautioned in the same situation, and this makes the two consistent.
items.decision: One proposal was to refuse the test when the covariance is rank-deficient, as the alternative method does. The author judged the reduced test statistically sound. He chose to keep it and disclose it.
items.what_you_notice: A new caution on rank-deficient designs, and a new stored degrees-of-freedom result. No p-value moved.

items.heading: The adversarial test keeps its name and placement, with no added reading guide
items.what_changed: No change. The adversarial p-value still prints beneath the joint pre-trend test under the same name. The help still calls its null adversarial toward finding pre-trend violations. No sentence was added to say that a genuine treatment effect will also reject it.
items.why: The help states the null correctly. Every horizon lies on one line through the reference period, with the best-fitting slope. Because the slope is fitted, a linear trend that carries on after treatment is part of the null. That is the sense in which the test is adversarial. A rejection means no single line fits the whole path. A real break at onset is one way that happens.
items.decision: The author kept the label and the placement. He declined a printed reading in the output. He also declined a short help paragraph on how to read the result. Both were raised twice.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing changes.

items.heading: altmethod_adversarial is kept, and it is now an error without adversarial
items.what_changed: altmethod_adversarial projects a line from the pre-period coefficients and the reference period. It then tests whether the post-period coefficients follow it. It now counts the full uncertainty of the projected line. Specifying it without adversarial stops with an error instead of doing nothing. It requires esfixedbaseperiod and at least one pre-period coefficient beyond the reference.
items.why: It answers a narrower question. It asks whether the post-period path continues the pre-period trend. In v1.3 it left out the variance of its forecast, so it too rejected too readily. One of its p-values moved from 1e-22 to 3.7e-6 once corrected. In the calibration work it was the better-sized of the two statistics at every boundary measured. The one case where it met the size target and the main test did not sat at the edge of the band fixed in advance. The calibration report marked that claim provisional. A modifier that silently does nothing when its parent option is missing suggests a test was run when none was.
items.decision: The author considered removing the option and kept it, citing its narrower question and better size. The error without adversarial follows the package's convention for modifiers used without their parent option.
items.what_you_notice: A call with altmethod_adversarial but no adversarial now stops with an error. The alternative p-value moved with the recalibration.

items.heading: A subgroup horizon that cannot be estimated is dropped with a caution, and that subgroup's line test is skipped
items.what_changed: margins is the Stata command that turns the regression into averaged effects. When it marks a subgroup's event-study horizon as not estimable, wooldid drops that horizon from that subgroup's event study. A caution names it. The subgroup's other horizons and every other subgroup are unaffected. If no horizon of a subgroup can be estimated, that subgroup's event study is skipped with its own caution. A subgroup that loses its pretreatment average row is recorded in hidden results and cautioned. For a subgroup that lost a horizon, the att and att_it adversarial tests are skipped with a caution. That holds on the analytic path and under permute(). v1.3 either stopped after estimation with a bare invalid-name error, or reported an estimate of zero with every standard error missing.
items.why: margins marks a result as omitted when the design leaves it unidentified. The marker is the only signal that separates a real estimate from a number margins computed anyway. So it has to be read. A horizon that cannot be estimated has no estimate to report. The subgroup's other horizons remain valid, so dropping one horizon is better than refusing the whole run. The adversarial test assumes the coefficients sit on a complete grid of relative periods. With a horizon missing, possibly from the middle, the line fit no longer means what the test's name says.
items.decision: The author ruled that the run should proceed, and later that it should disclose which subgroups lost rows. He rejected reporting the row with blank cells. He ruled that dropping should be the one rule on every route. On the route that reads the omission marker, that is what happens. One route lacks the marker. It is the default cell-collapse path under safety(off), where a non-estimable pre-period estimate can come back as zero up to rounding error. The test suite's records still show that zero being carried there, and the records do not show the drop being built on that path. Under permute() he ruled to skip the adversarial test, as the analytic run does. Computing it on the reduced grid was the alternative.
items.what_you_notice: Runs that used to crash now finish, with cautions naming the dropped horizons. The subgroup's event-study tables, estimates and stored matrices stay aligned. The adversarial tests for average marginal effects have no such check.
sources: review_process/changes_review_2026-09-22.md s4 rulings (adversarial p under permute() for a subgroup whose pre horizons were dropped)

items.heading: New option simultaneousbands draws a band that covers every horizon at once
items.what_changed: simultaneousbands builds a simultaneous band at level() for each event study. The band covers all of the event study's horizons at once with that probability. Without bootstrap() it is simulated from the event study's analytic covariance. It uses 10,000 draws on a fixed internal seed and then restores the user's random-number state. With bootstrap() it is taken from the replications. The printed table keeps its pointwise intervals. The band's endpoints are stored in e(esband_*), with the critical value in e(esband_crit_*). The plots draw the band as a dashed pair, which narrows to zero at the reference period like the pointwise shading. The option is off by default. It is refused under permute(). Under fastnose, or when an event study has fewer than two horizons with a usable variance, it is skipped with a caution.
items.why: A pointwise 95 percent interval covers one horizon with 95 percent probability. A reader who scans the whole event study for no effect anywhere before onset is making a claim about all horizons at once. Pointwise intervals do not support that claim. A sup-t band does, following Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Moller (2019). It widens every interval by one common factor. The factor comes from the distribution of the largest standardized deviation across horizons. Before this, nothing in wooldid supported that kind of claim. A simultaneous band belongs to the whole event study and to no single row. So it goes on the plot and in stored results, and the table is left alone.
items.decision: The author first made the band depend on a wider study of the covariance matrix. That study found the band needed only the event-study covariance already captured, so the dependency fell away. He ruled to build both the analytic and bootstrap bands. They are off by default so that no existing figure changes. They appear on the plot and in stored results. Under permute() the tool for many horizons at once is the permutation step-down, covered next. The permutation engine shows only permutation quantities.
items.what_you_notice: A new option. When it is on, the event-study plots show a dashed band and new stored results appear. The printed table is unchanged.

items.heading: The permutation step-down is opt-in, and pre-treatment horizons form their own family
items.what_changed: Under permute(), a step-down procedure adjusts each horizon's p-value for the fact that many horizons are tested at once. It works from the largest studentized deviation, meaning a deviation divided by its own standard error. It used to run on every permute() run with two or more post-treatment horizons. It now runs only when permstepdown is specified. The procedure now also runs over the pre-treatment horizons. Those are stored and reported as a separate family in e(perm_stepdown_pre). The computation itself did not change. With permstepdown, a run reproduces the earlier stored results exactly.
items.why: The step-down added two footer lines and up to sixteen stored matrices to runs whose authors wanted only p-values. Pooling pre-treatment and post-treatment horizons into one family would enlarge the family. Every post-treatment adjusted p-value would then change. The two families also answer different questions. One asks about effects after onset, the other about pre-trends. The pre-treatment family carries a caveat that its footer states. In staggered designs, where cohorts start treatment at different dates, the reassigned onset dates spread the permutation distribution of pre-period statistics too wide. So its adjusted p-values are conservative in a way the post-treatment family's are not.
items.decision: The author ruled on all three parts together with the bands. The step-down became opt-in. The pre-treatment horizons became their own family. The engine stays permutation-only. It was not extended to the bootstrap, even though the Romano and Wolf (2005) step-down is itself a bootstrap method. The simultaneous bands give the bootstrap its tool for many horizons at once.
items.what_you_notice: permute() runs no longer print or store step-down results unless permstepdown is given. With it, a separate pre-treatment family appears, with its own footer line.

items.heading: The analytic band uses the same t law as the pointwise intervals, has no floor, and cautions under clustering at i
items.what_changed: Where the regression reports residual degrees of freedom, the analytic band's draws follow a multivariate t distribution with those degrees of freedom. The pointwise intervals use the same law. When the regression reports no residual degrees of freedom, as under poisson, the draws are normal. The critical value is the simulated quantile itself, with no floor. When horizons are almost perfectly correlated, the band can therefore come out narrower than the pointwise interval. When cluster() is at the level of i or above, a caution says the analytic band is too narrow. It names bootstrap() as giving a valid band. That is the approved wording. The bootstrap band's coverage was measured only with a cluster() strictly finer than i. The help elsewhere no longer claims that bootstrap() repairs a cell that lies inside one cluster.
items.why: The pointwise intervals use the t distribution. A band simulated from the normal could sit inside them with few clusters and cover too rarely. The analytic band is the pointwise standard errors scaled by one common factor taken from the same covariance. When a cluster contains a whole treated cell, those standard errors are understated. The band inherits that in both its width and its critical value. Without a caution, the guide's list of pre-trend tools made the band look safe in exactly the design where it covers too rarely. In one measurement on a 10-cluster design the band covered about 90 percent of the time at a nominal 95. The pointwise intervals held 95.
items.decision: The program first gained a floor at the pointwise t quantile. The author had it removed the same day. He preferred that users see when the band approach is not working as expected. A floor would have given a more sensible number of a fundamentally different kind. He ruled to add the caution under clustering at i. It names bootstrap() as the remedy because permute() refuses the band. He saw the 10-cluster coverage figure and left the help silent on it.
items.what_you_notice: Analytic bands widened on runs with few degrees of freedom. A band narrower than the pointwise interval can appear, and it signals that the approach is struggling. A new caution prints on runs that cluster at i or coarser. It fires on the common design where i is the unit and the run clusters on the unit.
