items.heading: The bootstrap band matches the run's intervals and never edits a standard error
items.what_changed: With bootstrap() but no boottstat, the band scales each replication's largest deviation by the spread of the bootstrap draws. Under boottstat it divides by each replication's own standard error. That makes it a percentile-t band, one built from studentized replications. Some replications produce effectively no variance, because every standard error they report falls below 1e-8 of the outcome's scale. Those replications are left out of every studentized result. That covers percentile-t p-values and intervals, the bands, subgroup contrasts, and the joint, equality and adversarial tests. Their sampled values are kept in e(bootdist_se) and in bootsave(). Cautions report how many replications were excluded, and how many had some standard error below 1e-5. The counts are stored in e(boot_novar) and e(boot_sesmall). If one horizon lacks a usable standard error, the bootstrap band refuses the whole event study. The analytic band drops only that horizon.
items.why: Under boottstat every other interval on the run is percentile-t. A band on a different scale would not be comparable with the intervals beside it. A studentized statistic divides by a standard error. A few collapsed replications had ordinary numerators and denominators 33 to 120 times too small. They had blown one band up to 3.85e14. Leaving out draws that carry no variance fixes that without inventing numbers. The bootstrap critical value is a maximum over the horizons, taken replication by replication. A horizon that cannot supply a denominator in every replication changes what that maximum is taken over. That argues for refusing the whole band. Dropping the horizon would also be defensible.
items.decision: The author first had one construction for both bootstrap displays. He then ruled for percentile-t under boottstat, so the band sits on the same scale as its neighbours. He rejected outright a proposal to replace small replication standard errors with a floor value. In his view a standard error must never be edited by rule of thumb. It would have been the only such edit in the program. He ruled to exclude replications with no variance and to report the count. He accepted the stated limit. On a nearly degenerate design with no failed replications, the band is still unusable. No rule applied one replication at a time can fix that. The different handling of an unusable horizon in the two bands has not been ruled on.
items.what_you_notice: Under boottstat the band is wider or narrower in line with the percentile-t intervals. Absurd band widths from collapsed replications are gone. Two new cautions and two new stored counts. A bootstrap run can print no band at all where the analytic run would band most horizons. Only a generic caution says so.

items.heading: The event-study vector and its full covariance are stored for honestdid, lincom and test
items.what_changed: For each event-study estimand type, wooldid now stores three results, with versions per subgroup. e(b_es_*) holds the coefficient vector, labelled pre# and post#, with the reference omitted. e(V_es_*) holds its full covariance, including genuine terms between horizons, taken from the margins call that produced them. e(numpre_*) holds the number of pre-periods, which honestdid needs. The help includes a honestdid example. The covariance is withheld with a caution when no horizon has an identified variance, typically under timetrends. It is also withheld for the average-marginal-effect families when treated cells lie inside single clusters. Under fastnose the vector is stored and the covariance is not. The caution about no identified variance no longer prints under fastnose. Under impvalues neither is stored.
items.why: Before this, e(V) was diagonal. Sensitivity analysis in the style of Rambachan and Roth (2023) was impossible without re-estimating. So were Roth's pretrends and any test or lincom across horizons. A test across horizons needs to know how the horizons move together, which standard errors alone do not say. The margins call already computed that covariance and threw it away. Fast mode computes no variance by design, so a caution that none was identified told the user nothing.
items.decision: The author asked for the full block to be kept. For fastnose, the help claimed the vector was stored. He chose to make that claim true instead of correcting the sentence. He later ruled to silence the no-variance caution under fastnose. It still prints when a real variance is degenerate.
items.what_you_notice: New stored results after any event-study run, and a worked honestdid example in the help. A fastnose run no longer repeats the no-variance caution once per event study.

items.heading: e(V) now carries each event study's own covariance block, and says so
items.what_changed: On analytic runs with an event study, each event study's covariance block is written into the matching diagonal block of e(V). Every covariance between two event studies, or between an event study and a pooled estimate, stays zero. The hidden result e(wdid_vcvstate) reads analytic-blocks. e(wdid_vblocks) and e(wdid_vblockn) name and count the blocks written. A row whose variance is not identified keeps its missing marker on the diagonal. Only its off-diagonal entries are zeroed. The help says e(V) is for display except within one event study. No footer prints.
items.why: All of an event study's horizons come from one margins call, so their joint covariance already exists. Leaving it out of e(V) was a gap in the accounting. No estimate was missing. With it included, a test or lincom across the horizons of one event study on the posted e(V) is valid. The rest of the matrix is genuinely unknown. The delta method approximates a variance through a linear expansion. Some estimand types share no common expansion that could link their variances. A pooled effect is also a combination of its own horizons. So those cells stay zero.
items.decision: The author was sceptical and first asked for a study of whether a full covariance matrix was feasible. It found the general matrix blocked, so he ruled to include only the event-study blocks. He first ruled to zero the whole row and column of an unidentified horizon. He then confirmed keeping the missing marker on the diagonal. A zero there would make an unidentified standard error print as 0 instead of missing. He chose help text and a stored marker over a printed footer.
items.what_you_notice: Off-diagonal entries between horizons of the same event study are no longer zero. No diagonal entry moved. The hidden result e(wdid_vcvstate) says what e(V) is on each run.

items.heading: The conditions for a correct honestdid hand-off are documented, and wooldid does not police them
items.what_changed: The help lists what a correct direct hand-off to honestdid requires. The run must use esfixedbaseperiod at the default reference period of -1, and it must not use timetrends. It needs at least one pre-period and one post-period coefficient, consecutive horizons, and a covariance with no degenerate rows. The help warns that other layouts give honestdid the wrong timing without any error. e(es_ndegen_*) counts degenerate horizons and is stored only when some exist. The help also states two conditions every user of e(V_es_*) inherits. First, a treated cell inside one cluster adds none of its own variation. Second, when i is the unit, each treated cell is one observation, and the covariance carries only control-side variation. The honestdid example passes parallel(0), so honestdid does not start extra Stata processes. The example also explains that an empty robust confidence set is a finding about the data. The recipe for lincom and test posts the matrices with dof(`=e(df_r)').
items.why: honestdid reads the coefficient vector by position, so it cannot tell when the layout is wrong. In one measurement honestdid accepted a covariance with a zeroed post-period row. It returned a confidence interval identical to the clean run. Its own return code is therefore no guard, and the user needs to know which of wooldid's results to check. Without dof(), lincom and test fall back to the normal distribution. That is narrower than the table when clusters are few.
items.decision: The author ruled to document the conditions. He also ruled to pin honestdid's behaviour in a test, so a change in a new honestdid version would be noticed. He rejected withholding e(numpre_*) when degenerate rows exist. He reasoned that wooldid's hand-off need not guard against cases honestdid does not guard against itself.
items.what_you_notice: No behaviour changes at the hand-off. The help and the example say what must hold. e(es_ndegen_*) appears only when the covariance has degenerate rows.

items.heading: New event-study composition table e(escomp)
items.what_changed: e(escomp) has one row per reported horizon. It gives the number of cohorts, units, clusters and observations, and the summed weight. It also gives each horizon's share of the weight under both event-study weighting schemes. Versions per subgroup are stored too, along with scalars describing the reference pool and the treated sample. The table prints under summarystats.
items.why: When different cohorts contribute at different horizons, an event-study profile can jump even with no change in any cohort's effect. Such a jump can look like a pre-trend. In one test dataset a switch in composition read as a worsening pre-trend with p = 0.021. Flat columns in the table rule composition out. Moving columns show it could be the cause, though they do not prove it. The table is a diagnostic aid and performs no test.
items.decision: The author added the table as a diagnostic. He approved skipping it inside bootstrap and permutation replications, where it would only add run time.
items.what_you_notice: A new stored table, printed when summarystats is specified.

items.heading: New option anticipation() moves the effective onset earlier
items.what_changed: anticipation(#) treats the effective onset as the recorded onset minus #, before relative time is built. This matches the shift() option of did_imputation. Relative period 0 is then # periods before the recorded onset. The help advises raising espostlength() by # and requesting an event study. It explains how too small and too large a value each show up, and advises using the smallest value that can be defended. The shift is stored in e(anticipation).
items.why: If units respond before the recorded onset, the reference period and the pre-period horizons are contaminated. Parallel trends then fails through no fault of the comparison group. Shifting the onset moves the response into the treated periods. Too small a value leaves anticipation in the reference period, which shows in the pre-period horizons. Too large a value keeps the pre-trends clean but pulls the pooled estimate toward zero. The first post-period horizons then fall before any response and read near zero. Only an event study shows either problem.
items.decision: The option came from a set of new features the author approved. Its design follows did_imputation's shift() convention so that results line up with that package. The convention came with the build, and the author did not rule on it separately.
items.what_you_notice: A new option and a new stored result. Horizons are relabelled relative to the shifted onset.

items.heading: Poisson results stay on the log scale, and the options that left it are removed
items.what_changed: Under poisson every reported effect, including every event-study horizon, is a difference in linear predictions. Take a binary treatment without interactive controls, which are controls allowed to change the treatment effect within a cell. There each cell's effect is the log of the ratio of expected outcomes with and without treatment. Under contreat(), the continuous-treatment option, the reported quantities are slopes in the dose on that scale. poisexpresults, which reported differences in predicted counts, is gone. So are semielasticity and the eydx and eyex elasticity types. For the continuous treatment only dydx and dyex are accepted. Under poisson their tables and plots are titled as semi-elasticities and elasticities respectively.
items.why: On the log scale, the plain operators of margins already are the elasticities. dydx gives the change in the log of expected y per unit of the dose, which is the semi-elasticity. dyex gives the elasticity, the percent change per percent change in the dose. The removed types took a log of a log. The reported semi-elasticity then depended on the units of y. Multiplying y by ten moved it from 0.142 to 0.040. On the count scale, the delta-method standard error of the att left out the variance of the fixed effects. The regression absorbs those effects and never reports them. It was about 23 percent off on a realistic count panel. The error did not shrink with sample size, and nothing in the output said so. On the log scale, differences cancel the absorbed effects, so the variance is complete. The earlier titles had semi-elasticity and elasticity reversed.
items.decision: The author first remapped the affected types to the log scale with a caution. He then removed them. He judged that rescuing the count-scale features would take too much, especially as some of the problems sit upstream in the ppmlhdfe package. ppmlhdfe is the Poisson regression package wooldid calls. Repairing poisexpresults would have meant putting the fixed effects into e(b) through a refit with explicit dummies. He ruled to leave the plain operators of margins alone and to relabel the titles under poisson.
items.what_you_notice: Calls naming poisexpresults, semielasticity, eydx or eyex now stop with an error. Poisson dose-effect tables carry corrected titles. The reported att is on the log scale and is not the average treatment effect in levels. Exponentiating it does not recover one.

area: How the program talks to you, and what was removed
title: How the program talks to you, and what was removed
intro: This part covers how wooldid tells you what it did. It covers the safety() switch, the errors and cautions the program prints, its two documents, the redisplay of stored results, and a fast mode for trying out specifications. It also covers the options that were removed, and the few that were kept after being considered for removal. Two ideas run through these changes. A user should never get a different estimate from the one they asked for without being told. And an option earns its place only if it does something useful that nothing else in the package does.

items.heading: safety() now has a stated meaning: switching it off accepts a risk, never a wrong number
items.what_changed: The help and the usage guide now describe three outcomes for a questionable specification. A refused run stops with a named error. A result reported without inference keeps its point estimate. Its standard error, p-value and interval are shown blank, never as zero. A cautioned result is computed in full, and a line of text names the risk and the remedy. safety(off) turns some refusals into cautions and skips some checks. About forty-five refusals hold whatever safety() is set to.
items.why: Some checks guard against an estimate that may be unreliable. An informed analyst can reasonably choose to accept that risk. Other checks guard against option combinations known to produce a wrong or meaningless number. No analyst gains from receiving such a number. A user who switches safety off should know which kind of check they are giving up. A missing standard error is shown blank because a zero would read as perfect precision.
items.decision: The author ruled that the full list of what safety() does must be published before anyone considers narrowing the option. The alternative was to leave it as v1.3's single undocumented switch. The list he asked for shows where the code draws the line. safety(off) cannot lift any screen on option combinations or on allowed values. It cannot lift the check for missing packages, or poisson's requirement of an outcome that is never negative. It cannot lift any conflict with fastnose, the fast mode described below.
items.what_you_notice: Chapter 12 of the usage guide lists each check by what safety(off) does to it. safety() now accepts only on or off. In v1.3 any other value, including a typo such as safety(of), was quietly treated as on. It now stops the run with an error.

items.heading: Where the safety(off) line falls: five checks that now always hold, and two left switchable
items.what_changed: Five situations are now refused whatever safety() says. The first is impvalues with a cluster() that is finer than i or cuts across it. impvalues requests the Ibragimov and Muller method explained below. The second is bootstrap(bayes) with att_it, att_i or att_itime. These are the cell-weighted estimands, which give each cohort-by-period cell equal weight. The other three concern subgroups under permute(). They are a unit whose subgroup changes over time, a subgroup that varies within a unit-by-period cell, and a unit labelled on some rows and missing on others. A treated unit whose i code is above 2,147,483,647 is also refused by name. Outside permute(), a unit that switches subgroup or is only partly labelled is still refused by default. safety(off) still lets it through, with a caution.
items.why: In each of the five cases, a run without the check gives a wrong number. The Ibragimov and Muller method estimates the effect separately in each cluster. It then measures uncertainty by the spread of those estimates. That needs each cluster's estimate to be separate and independent. With clusters finer than i, each cluster's estimate is a reweighting of the same regression coefficients. Their spread then badly understates the uncertainty. Because the cell-weighted estimands weight every cell equally, part of their sampling variation comes from which cells appear in a sample. The Bayesian bootstrap gives each cluster a random weight in each replication, but it never drops a cluster. So it misses that part of the variation. Under permute(), every cluster can be treated in some replication. A unit whose subgroup is not fixed, or is labelled on only some rows, can then enter a replication's treated group. It is counted by its share of weight, even when the observed run never touches it. The observed run's screens look only at treated units. So under permute() the screens run over every unit and cannot be lifted. The two switchable cases are different in kind. A unit that switches subgroup and is let in counts toward each subgroup by the share of its sample weight carrying that label. That is a known distortion a user can choose to accept. att_i and att_itime then no longer weight units equally, and the help says so.
items.decision: The author chose to make the five cases impossible to lift. Before, safety(off) let each of them through. He left the two subgroup screens outside permute() switchable. That matches his own message text, which tells users they may specify safety(off). He kept the within-cell subgroup screen beside the split-unit screen, although the second catches most of what the first does. For very large i codes he first chose to renumber units internally. He chose a plain refusal once that change proved much larger than first estimated.
items.what_you_notice: Runs that used safety(off) to get past any of these five cases now stop with an error. The bootstrap(bayes) caution for cell-weighted estimands is gone, because the combination is now refused.

items.heading: contreatwithin no longer switches off every check
items.what_changed: contreatwithin estimates dose effects from treated units only. In v1.3 it set safety to off for the whole run. Now it relaxes only the checks that require an untreated comparison group. These are the drop of periods with no comparison unit, the scan for effect terms dropped as collinear, and the checks on the range of relative time. A term is collinear when other variables in the model already explain it fully, so the regression drops it. The relaxed setting also still turns the refusal of contreatwithin with the byTime control type into a caution. And it lets makecfxplots draw the plots for the estimands other than att. Everything else follows the safety() value you typed. That covers the data checks, the subgroup rules, the dose-slope check, the variable-count check, and the bootstrap and permutation routines.
items.why: contreatwithin identifies dose effects from variation among treated cohorts only. The data need not contain any untreated units. So relaxing the checks that insist on one is correct. Choosing that design says nothing about whether the data are sound. A user who never typed safety(off) should still learn that treatment onset varies within a unit. They should also learn when the model will exceed Stata's limit on the number of variables.
items.decision: The author ruled to restore the variable-count check under contreatwithin. He also ruled that the effective safety value be settled before any message that depends on it prints. The variable-count check is itself new in this version. As first built, it read the relaxed setting. So a contreatwithin user who typed no safety() lost it. A run that exceeded the variable limit then failed late with Stata's unexplained error r(907), in place of an early named error. The alternative was to leave contreatwithin switching everything off, as v1.3 did.
items.what_you_notice: A contreatwithin run can now stop on a data check that v1.3 would have skipped. safety(off) still skips them.

items.heading: Changes to what is estimated are announced, with three exceptions under safety(off)
items.what_changed: espostlength sets how many periods after treatment the event study reports. With subgroups() and a pre-treatment event-study window, wooldid raises espostlength from 0 to 1. That announcement now prints under safety(off) too. Only the explanation beneath it is silenced. Three other adjustments still print their caution only under default safety. The adjustment itself happens under either setting. First, periods with no comparison unit in the sample are dropped. Second, treated cells with no dose variation are dropped. Third, a requested pre-treatment period is folded into the reference period when the panel is too short to separate them.
items.why: safety(off) exists to let a run past a screen. It was never meant to hide what was estimated. A window that gains a horizon the user never asked for has a different target. The user needs to know that to read the results correctly.
items.decision: The author ruled that the espostlength announcement prints under any setting. The help states the general rule that a run which changes your specification says so. The reference-period fold was put to him on 2026-09-13, with a recommendation to let its caution print under safety(off) as well. What was recorded is that the silent behaviour was kept, and the code did not change. The two sample drops were never put to him. All three stay silent under safety(off). The usage guide lists them among the cautions safety(off) suppresses.
items.what_you_notice: Under safety(off) the espostlength line still prints. The dose-cell drop is still recorded in e(contreat_ndropcells), even though no caution prints. The help and chapter 12 of the guide state the disclosure rule without exception, and these three cases break it. Either the rule's wording or these three cautions will need to change, and that choice is the author's.

items.heading: New checks on the data under default safety
items.what_changed: wooldid now stops with a named error when treatment onset is not constant within a unit of i, and it names an offending unit. i is the variable that groups the data into the units whose treatment timing the model follows. wooldid also checks that subgroups do not vary within unit-by-period cells. It checks that the customweightmultiplier() variable is never negative, and that lattice values are whole numbers of zero or more. It prints a caution when i takes more than 100 distinct values. It stops before estimation when the model would need more variables than Stata's maxvar setting allows. maxvar is Stata's cap on the number of variables in memory. And it adds a line of diagnosis when a run dies with Stata's own error r(907), the error for too many variables. The refusal of negative weights was already in v1.3.
items.why: Nothing else catches an onset that varies within a unit. Each row is then placed in event time on its own, so one unit is split across cohorts. Test runs showed a 41 percent shift in one horizon's estimate, and a pre-trend of the wrong sign, with no error. A pre-trend is the set of estimated effects before treatment, which should be near zero. The most common costly choice is to set i to the individual unit. wooldid builds one term for each cohort-by-period cell, and runtime grows faster than the number of those cells. Setting i to onset cohorts and putting unit fixed effects in fe() keeps the permanent differences between units in the model at far lower cost. Stopping early on the variable count saves a long run that would otherwise fail late with an unhelpful message.
items.decision: The author approved the caution about a fine i and the variable-count check. The alternative for the variable limit was to let Stata fail on its own. safety(off) skips all of these checks.
items.what_you_notice: Data with inconsistent onset now stop with error r(459) instead of running. Runs with a fine i print a caution recommending fe() and a coarser i.

items.heading: No check was removed to save time
items.what_changed: The checks that safety() controls were timed. They cost between two and five percent of a run. None was removed. The two checks that scan the whole sample now run once per call. Before, they ran again in every bootstrap or permutation replication. The usage guide says the checks are cheap. It says switching them off can be worth it once a specification is settled. It adds that this is no reason to switch them off while a specification is still being developed.
items.why: Most of these checks stand between the user and a wrong number that would otherwise appear with no error. A check of that kind is never redundant, however rarely it fires.
items.decision: The author set a three-part test for removing a check. It must cost real computation. It must guard against something rarer than about one run in a hundred. And it must duplicate a failure that Stata would report later anyway. The core checks that the model can be estimated stay whatever they cost. Almost nothing met the third part. Most checks stop a silent wrong number, which Stata would never report. One part of the variable-count check was recorded as meeting the test, and it is left for his ruling. He asked for the findings to be documented first. Then the one change that removes no warning was made. The two whole-sample checks now run once, in place of once in every replication.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing changes in the output. Long bootstrap and permutation runs no longer repeat the whole-sample checks in every replication.

items.heading: A requested test that cannot run is dropped with a caution, neither refused nor silently skipped
items.what_changed: The adversarial pre-trend test asks whether all the event-study estimates could lie on one straight line through the reference period. The event-study window may be unable to support that test. It may have been requested with no horizon before treatment, or none after. Or the data may leave too few horizons. In each case the test is dropped and a caution says why. The joint pre-trend test asks whether all the pre-treatment estimates are zero together. When every treated cell sits inside a single cluster, that test is still computed. A caution explains that its covariance is degenerate, meaning it cannot measure uncertainty in some directions. This holds both under jointtests and under pretrendpower().
items.why: A test that vanishes without a word is the real problem. Refusing the whole run would break the way applied researchers run robustness checks. They often apply one set of options across many specifications in a loop. A caution reports what did not happen and keeps the rest of the results.
items.decision: The author first ruled to refuse. Measurement showed that refusing would stop 121 of 501 existing test specifications that had run before. All of them carried adversarial across a grid of windows. He amended the ruling to a caution. For the joint pre-trend test he chose one rule for both places the statistic appears. The alternative was to suppress it under pretrendpower() alone.
items.what_you_notice: Scripts that set adversarial or jointtests across many windows run to completion. They print a caution where a test could not be computed. The usage guide states that no accepted option is a silent no-op, meaning an option that is accepted and then does nothing.

items.heading: A test with no p-value now reports no partial result
items.what_changed: Beside its p-value, the adversarial pre-trend test reports the straight line fitted to the event-study estimates. On five paths the test could produce the line but no p-value. The line was still stored in e(adversarial_line_*). Now no line is stored on those paths, and nothing about a line prints. A caution says the test failed and names the reason. The reasons are a pooled reference period without esfixedbaseperiod, and a degenerate covariance. Others are bootstrap() without boottstat, which bootstraps t-statistics, and too few usable bootstrap or permutation replications.
items.why: A line with no test beside it invites a reader to judge the pre-trend by eye. Nothing then tells them how much of the line is noise. A test that cannot produce a p-value has failed, and the output should say so.
items.decision: The author ruled that a test with no p-value has failed. No line is posted, and the caution says the test failed. He approved the wording of each caution. He then applied the same rule to the two paths that run through the bootstrap and permutation routines. The alternative was to keep the line under a caution saying the p-value was unavailable.
items.what_you_notice: Scripts that read e(adversarial_line_*) find it absent on runs where the test has no p-value. No p-value, estimate or standard error changes.

items.heading: Messages follow one convention, and the author rewrote the errors
items.what_changed: Every message that stops a run begins 'Error:' and is shown in Stata's error colour. Every caution begins 'Caution:' and is shown as plain text. Two informational notes remain. One of them is the diagnosis printed when Stata itself reports error r(907). The word 'Warning' is gone. v1.3 printed two reference-period 'Warning' lines in error colour, and they are now cautions. The author rewrote the error messages himself. Most now fit on a single short line that says what is wrong and what to do.
items.why: A user scanning a log needs to see at once whether a run stopped or only raised a flag. v1.3 mixed three words and two colours with no consistent meaning. Messages are also the program's main way of telling a user that an estimate should not be trusted. The econometrician who designed the estimator is best placed to judge what a user needs to hear, and in how few words.
items.decision: The author rewrote every error message. The cautions were shortened under his instruction and set before him for review. Since 2026-09-21, no new error, caution or note is added without his wording. A few messages that deletions forced are marked for his check. Some shortened errors lost their explanation of why the check exists. That explanation moved into a comment in the code beside the check, where a maintainer will find it. The alternative was longer messages that explain the reasoning at run time.
items.what_you_notice: Errors are shorter. Of the 200 error messages, 133 were reworded and one was deleted. Fourteen that ran over several lines now fit on one.

items.heading: Fewer and shorter cautions, with the false and textbook ones removed
items.what_changed: Forty-three cautions were cut to three parts. They say what happened, what it means and what to do. None of their conditions changed. Fourteen notes and five cautions were deleted. One was the generic bootstrap line saying inference is unreliable with very few clusters. Another was the note printed above the gteffects table. Two others claimed the histogram outputs used the analytic covariance.
items.why: Some cautions repeated textbook econometrics. One example is the fact that clustered standard errors are poor with few clusters. Such a caution tells a working applied economist nothing new, and it buries the cautions that matter. What should remain is what departs from their expectations. These are the places where wooldid is unusually sensitive. A false caution is worse than none. The histogram draws point estimates only, so no covariance is involved. The caution about few treated clusters is specific to this design, and it still prints.
items.decision: The author asked that users not be overwhelmed by cautions, and that textbook material leave the runtime output. He marked each deletion himself. Conditions were left alone, so the pruning changed no behaviour. A few protective clauses were restored where shortening had removed a remedy the user needs. One deleted caution, about covariates in the bootstrap, went because the problem it described was fixed.
items.what_you_notice: Logs are shorter. Each remaining caution still names the option or stored result it concerns. It fires in the same situations as before.

items.heading: A failed write of the replication draws no longer throws away the run
items.what_changed: bootsave() and permsave() write the bootstrap or permutation draws to a file. Such a write can fail, for example because the folder is read-only or the disk is full. The run now still finishes. It prints its tables and posts the return code in e(boot_save_rc) or e(perm_save_rc). A caution prints below the tables. Before, the failure stopped the run before any table printed, although every result had already been computed.
items.why: A bootstrap or permutation run can take hours, and the draws file is a by-product. Losing the inference because a side file failed to write wastes the whole run. The return code keeps the failure visible to a script that runs quietly. Placing the caution below the tables keeps it from scrolling out of sight.
items.decision: The author asked for this so that users can still see their results when the rest of the run succeeded. Each save routine checks again after the replications whether a file has appeared under the name since the run began. He left that check fatal, accepting that such a run is lost. A stale file that exists before the run is refused before the replications start, as before. A failure to write the plot files late in the run is also still fatal.
items.what_you_notice: A run whose save fails ends with a caution and a nonzero e(boot_save_rc) or e(perm_save_rc). It no longer ends with an error.

items.heading: A caution when the matrices of draws are too large to store
items.what_changed: When a run completes more than 10,000 replications, the matrices of draws are not posted. These are e(bootdist) for the bootstrap, and e(permdist) and its companions for permutation. A caution now says so and points to bootsave() or permsave(). Exact permutation enumerates every possible assignment of treatment. It is now allowed up to 65,534 assignments, where it used to stop at 10,000. 65,534 is the largest number of rows a Stata matrix can hold.
items.why: A user who reaches for the draws after a long run should learn at the end of that run that they are missing. Otherwise the first sign is a failed command later. The enumeration limit comes from the size of a Stata matrix. It says nothing about the data, so safety(off) cannot lift it.
items.decision: The author first considered an error that safety(off) could lift. He then chose to set the limit at the matrix ceiling, which nothing can lift. On the bootstrap side the alternative was to stay silent. He approved that caution's wording. The permutation caution's wording still awaits his approval.
items.what_you_notice: Exact permutation runs with between 10,001 and 65,534 assignments now run. Runs above 10,000 replications print a caution about the missing matrices.

items.heading: Four cautions added on 2026-09-25, where an estimate means less than it appears to
items.what_changed: Four cautions were added on 2026-09-25. The first concerns lattice(), which splits the dose into bins. A bin of a treated cell with no dose variation borrows its dose slope from another bin of the same cell. The ame, the average marginal effect of the dose, then includes those borrowed slopes. The second concerns contreatwithin in periods with no untreated reference rows. There one treated cell's level effect is set to zero. The att, the average effect of treatment on the treated, then depends on that choice there, and the ame is the result to rely on. The third concerns simultaneousbands, a band that covers all event-study horizons at once. Built from the analytic covariance with cluster() at or above i, the band is too narrow. bootstrap() gives a valid band. The fourth concerns an event-study covariance that is rank deficient, meaning some combinations of horizons have no measured uncertainty. The adversarial test then uses only the directions that remain, and the caution prints the degrees of freedom it used.
items.why: Each caution flags a result whose meaning quietly differs from what a user would assume. A borrowed slope is not that bin's own effect. An att that depends on a normalisation is not identified by the data. For the band, the regression fits each treated cell its own coefficient. That coefficient makes the cell's residuals sum to zero. The cluster-robust variance is built from each cluster's sum of residuals. When the whole cell lies inside one cluster, that sum is zero for the cell's coefficient. So the variance cannot see the cell's own noise. A band built from it covers the truth less often than stated. A test on a rank-deficient covariance has fewer degrees of freedom than the number of horizons suggests.
items.decision: The author approved each text. He ruled out a fifth check, a screen for doses outside treated cells. Another caution was considered, saying conventional OLS standard errors are understated in the same contained-cell situation. It was tested by simulation first. The reported standard errors matched the simulated spread, a ratio of 0.999, against 0.549 for robust errors. That caution would have been false, so it was not added.
items.what_you_notice: These cautions appear only in the situations described. e(adversarial_df_*) records the degrees of freedom the adversarial test used.

items.heading: Treated cells with no dose variation now leave the sample, with a caution
items.what_changed: Under contreat(), a treated cohort-by-period cell whose dose takes a single value is dropped from the estimation sample. wooldid prints a caution with the count of dropped cells. The count is stored in e(contreat_ndropcells), and the dropped rows are counted in e(N_dropped). A cell whose dose is zero throughout is never dropped. Nothing is dropped on a side of treatment onset where no cell has dose variation. The check does not run under contreatcontrols(untreatedZero).
items.why: A dose slope needs dose variation within the cell. Without it, the slope term drops out of the regression as collinear. The ame then averaged in a zero at that cell's full weight, which pulled the ame toward zero. One test gave 0.72 against a true value of 1.00, with a p-value near zero and only a generic caution. Dropping the cells makes the ame an average of slopes the data actually identify.
items.decision: The author chose to drop the cells through the same checks that already drop periods with no comparison unit. He approved the caution. His ruling exempted only the all-zero cells under contreatcontrols(untreatedZero). The alternatives put to him were to report no ame at all, or to average over the remaining cells and report the share left out. A third was to document the problem only. As built, cells with zero dose throughout are kept under every control type. A block of pre-onset cells with no dose variation anywhere is kept whole. The literal rule stopped a design the help recommends, setting the dose to zero before onset, with an error inside margins. That departure from his ruling is recorded for him to confirm.
items.what_you_notice: In designs where some cells had a constant dose, the ame can move away from zero. The att is now estimated on the same reduced sample. safety(off) keeps the drop but silences the caution.

items.heading: Other new cautions where a result could mislead
items.what_changed: Five more cautions were added in this version. Under permute(), clusters whose onset falls after the last period are treated as never treated in the estimation. They are now permuted as never treated too, and a caution counts them. cfxplotnose skips standard errors on the dose-effect plots to save time. It is now dropped with a caution under permtstat, permtci or boottstat, which build their statistics from those standard errors. Before, every plot cell's inference came back blank with no message. Under poisson, the ppmlhdfe routine can drop the pooled dose control when the dose's level is large next to its spread. The ame then goes wrong silently, and a caution now says so. Under contreatcontrols(), a reference group whose dose barely varies was refused below 1/100,000 of the sample standard deviation. Between that and 1/1,000 a caution now prints, as it already did for byCohort. Under bootstrap() with cluster(), a caution notes a unit of i that falls in two or more clusters. It now prints only when att_i, att_it or att_itime is in the run, since only their standard errors miss variation then.
items.why: Each flags a case where the output looks normal but the number, or its inference, is off. Several produced confident wrong answers with no message at all. With the dose shifted by 300 in one poisson test, the ame was .52 against .24, 6.5 standard errors off. In the reference-group band, one test reported an att of -150 against a true 2.56. A late-onset cluster permuted as its own onset group was being treated differently from the estimation it was testing.
items.decision: The author ruled on each case and approved each caution's text. For the dropped poisson dose control he chose to detect and warn. The caution is skipped when unit fixed effects really do carry the dose, because the drop is then correct. For the reference-group band he chose a caution, matching the byCohort screen. For the two-cluster caution he chose to print it only where it applies. The counts e(boot_reid) and e(boot_nstraddle) are still stored on every run.
items.what_you_notice: These cautions appear only in the situations described. No estimate changes. Plot cells that came back blank under permtstat, permtci or boottstat now carry their replication inference. Under permute() with late onsets, the count of possible assignments and permsave()'s onset columns change.

items.heading: permute() has its own caution about few treated clusters
items.what_changed: When fewer than six clusters are ever treated, permute() prints its own caution. It says the test then rests on onset having been assigned exchangeably across clusters. It adds that a few atypical treated clusters can make the test reject too often. The bootstrap's few-cluster cautions were not copied across.
items.why: Exchangeable here means any cluster was as likely as any other to receive a given onset. The cluster bootstrap and the permutation test lean on different assumptions. The bootstrap treats clusters as random draws from a population. It fails with few or unusual treated clusters. The permutation test treats the actual assignment of onsets as one of many equally likely assignments. It fails when treated clusters differ from the rest, for example in how noisy their outcomes are. A caution copied from the bootstrap would name the wrong risk. Few treated clusters do not by themselves make the possible assignments few. Their number is stored in e(perm_npossible).
items.decision: The author ruled that the two methods should not be made to match for its own sake. Each difference should have a stated reason. He chose a caution written from the permutation test's own way of failing. On 2026-09-25 he approved its current wording, which names the exchangeability risk. An earlier wording said the sampled draws would repeat, which does not hold in general.
items.what_you_notice: Runs under permute() with fewer than six ever-treated clusters print this caution. The help's permute() entry states the same risk.

items.heading: The help file was cut back to usage, and describes only the current program
items.what_changed: The help had grown from about 11,500 words in 2024 to 46,900. It was rebuilt from the 2024 text to about 19,700 words. It later gained about 1,600 words of econometric corrections. Each option added since 2024 has a compact entry. The entry says what the option does, when it applies, when it is refused and when to turn it off. Statements about what earlier versions did were removed. The comments in the code now describe what the code does, leaving out how it came to be.
items.why: A user opens the help to find out how to run the command. The test for what stays is departure from expectations. It keeps the places where wooldid needs more clusters, or behaves differently, than an applied econometrician new to it would expect. Textbook material, testing detail and internals belong elsewhere. History is noise to a user. To a maintainer it invites changing working code back toward an old design.
items.decision: The author chose to restore the 2024 text and add to it. The alternative was to compress the long version in place. He ruled that backward compatibility is not a goal for the help. One trace remains. The elasticity entry still says the eyex and eydx forms were removed.
items.what_you_notice: The help is less than half its former length. bootstrap() and permute() have their own subsections. The surprises specific to wooldid remain, in a sentence or two each. These include clustering at or above i, the p-value floors and the cell collapse.

items.heading: A long usage guide for advanced users and AI agents, with a generated list of every message
items.what_changed: A separate guide of about 73,000 words ships with the package, and the help links to it. Its chapters open with decision rules. They cover what level to choose for i, and what level to cluster at. They cover when to bootstrap and when to permute, and which pre-trend tools are reliable when. They also cover the continuous-treatment control types, how to make runs faster and what safety() controls. Chapter 14 lists every error and caution with the full set of conditions under which it prints. It is generated from the program's code and regenerated whenever a message changes.
items.why: The detailed advice that no longer fits a help file is still valuable. It helps most someone setting up many runs, or an AI agent writing them. It warns against the common default of setting i at the individual unit. A hand-kept list of several hundred messages drifts away from the code. Generating it keeps it accurate. The full conditions tell a user why a message printed without reading the program.
items.decision: The author asked for this second, longer document, and asked that it leave out internal testing detail. The alternative was to keep everything in one help file.
items.what_you_notice: net get wooldid copies the guide to the working directory. The help's header and its Bugs section link to it.

items.heading: The help now tells users to cluster at the level where treatment is assigned
items.what_changed: The help states the default variance. Without cluster(), the linear model reports conventional OLS standard errors. It reports robust ones with sampling weights or under poisson. None of these allows for correlation within a unit over time. The help says the short examples leave out cluster() only for brevity. The first example now clusters by unit, with i as the onset cohort. The help ties the cluster level to the level at which treatment is assigned. It no longer claims that bootstrap() or permute() repair standard errors for cells that sit inside one cluster. Only a finer cluster() does.
items.why: Outcomes in a panel are correlated within a unit over time. Standard errors that ignore this usually overstate precision. A help file that shows unclustered examples, or recommends a remedy that does not work, leads users to report standard errors that are too small. The bootstrap resamples whole clusters. So a cell inside one cluster is always resampled whole, and its own noise stays invisible.
items.decision: The author reviewed these corrections and kept them, including the changed first example and the edits on the simultaneous band. The alternative was to revert them to keep the help shorter.
items.what_you_notice: Example 0 clusters by unit. The cluster() entry gives the rule with an example. A state policy studied on county data needs cluster(state).

items.heading: Typing wooldid alone redisplays the last results
items.what_changed: After an estimation, typing wooldid with nothing after it prints the stored tables and diagnostics again, line for line. This works after estimates restore and with no data in memory. Plots are not redrawn, and cautions from estimation are not repeated. Disclosures stored with the results, such as the fast-mode note, are repeated. In v1.3 a bare wooldid was an error.
items.why: This is how Stata's estimation commands behave. It lets a user recover the tables without paying again for a long bootstrap or permutation run.
items.decision: Only a completely empty command line triggers the redisplay. Stata's usual test for a redisplay would also have caught wooldid, update. This way that command, and mistyped options, still reach wooldid itself. Results stored under a different version of the display are refused, so they are never shown wrongly.
items.what_you_notice: wooldid alone works after estimates restore. Options on the redisplay line are refused.

items.heading: A failed call leaves your previous results in place
items.what_changed: A wooldid call may fail at any stage, including during or after a bootstrap or permutation loop. The results that were in e() before the call are then restored, e(sample) included. Typing wooldid alone then redisplays those earlier results. Internal settings used during the call are cleared when it ends, whether it succeeds, fails or is interrupted. In v1.3 a failure after the first stage left wooldid's internal regression, fitted on temporary variables, in e().
items.why: Stata's estimation commands leave the previous results alone when they fail. A user might run esttab, lincom or test after a failed call. Without the restore they would act on wooldid's internal scaffolding, or on half-built results, without knowing. Internal settings left over from a debugging session once changed a later bootstrap table with nothing printed. Results must depend only on the command typed.
items.decision: The author ruled to hold the caller's results and restore them on every failure. The earlier design refused any redisplay after a failure, because e() might hold partial results. Once e() is restored, that refusal only blocked valid results, so it was dropped. He also ruled to clear the internal settings at the end of the call, where the earlier design cleared them at the start. A diagnostic setting is meant to be placed just before the call it applies to.
items.what_you_notice: After an error, e() and the redisplay show your last successful results, or whatever was there before the failed call.

items.heading: Stata's bootstrap and jackknife prefixes work with wooldid
items.what_changed: bootstrap _b: wooldid and jackknife _b: wooldid now run to completion. Typing wooldid alone afterwards shows the prefix's own table, as regress does. The help says that wooldid's cluster() must name the prefix's cluster variable, and that the bootstrap prefix does not allow weights. It says svy is not supported, and names the bootstrap() option as the supported route to bootstrap inference.
items.why: After a prefix, e(V) holds the prefix's covariance. Redisplaying wooldid's own analytic tables would show standard errors that differ from the ones posted. The header would not say so, and that is misleading inference.
items.decision: The author ruled to show the prefix's table. The alternative was to redisplay wooldid's analytic tables, as it did before.
items.what_you_notice: The prefixes work, and the redisplay after them shows the prefix's standard errors.

items.heading: fastnose: point estimates only, for trying out specifications
items.what_changed: fastnose runs every margins call without computing variances. Tables keep their shape, with standard errors, p-values and intervals shown as missing. The header says standard errors were not computed. e(V) is not posted, so test and lincom refuse. The help asks users to re-run the chosen specification without fastnose before reporting results.
items.why: Nearly all of a run is spent on the delta-method variance inside margins. That is the calculation that turns the regression's covariance into standard errors for the averaged effects. When a user is comparing specifications, point estimates are enough. Test runs were typically two to four times faster. One poisson event study ran over 265 times faster.
items.decision: The mode is off by default and must be asked for. The output says plainly that standard errors were not computed. So a table without standard errors cannot be mistaken for a full run.
items.what_you_notice: A new option, fastnose, and a header line reading 'Standard Errors: not computed (fast mode)'.

items.heading: fastnose shows the same rows as a full run, and refuses options whose whole output is a variance
items.what_changed: fastnose is refused with unconditionalse, pretrendpower(), boottstat, permtstat, permtci, permanalyticse, adversarial and jointtests. adversarial and jointtests are accepted under permute(), where the run is already in fast mode. With impvalues or bootstrap(), fastnose prints a caution and is ignored. Fast mode still drops the event-study horizons a full run would find cannot be estimated, so the rows match.
items.why: A fast run is useful only if it shows the same estimates as the full run, without standard errors. Otherwise a specification search is misled by rows the real run would drop. Options whose entire output is a statistic built from the variance are refused, so they never print blank. impvalues already runs margins without variances, and the bootstrap replications already run in fast mode. So asking for fast mode on top changes nothing. boottstat is refused because each replication needs its own standard error to form its t-statistic.
items.decision: The author ruled to refuse fastnose with permanalyticse, whose only purpose is to show analytic standard errors. The alternative was to print them blank. For impvalues and bootstrap() he turned the refusal into a caution. The option is then cleared, so the run is identical to one without it. He also ruled that the caution saying no horizon has an identified variance should not repeat on fast runs, where it says nothing new.
items.what_you_notice: fastnose with impvalues or bootstrap() no longer stops the run. Typing fastnose under permute() is accepted.

items.heading: Table tools show the real permutation results, with no invented covariance
items.what_changed: By default a permute() run skips analytic standard errors, so it posts no e(V), the covariance matrix. esttab is a widely used command that builds tables from stored results. Without e(V) it printed an empty standard-error row. Its footer still said standard errors were in parentheses, and it wrote that claim into .tex and .csv files. Every permute() run now posts e(p), e(ci_l) and e(ci_u). esttab reads these first, so it prints the permutation p-values and intervals. No covariance is posted. Under fastnose without permute(), nothing of this kind is posted. The help warns that esttab then prints an empty row.
items.why: A covariance of all zeros would let table tools run. It would also state false precision almost everywhere it was read. esttab would print intervals of zero width, and commands that now refuse would print a standard error of zero. Posting the p-values and intervals the permutation actually produced fixes the tables without inventing any number. test and lincom still refuse, because they need a covariance that does not exist.
items.decision: The author first ruled on a condition. If fast mode broke table tools, wooldid should post an all-zero covariance that anyone inspecting it would see is false. Measurement showed that fast mode did break them, silently. It also showed the zero covariance would look true on nearly every surface. He then ruled to post e(p) and the interval, and nothing else. Later he extended this to every permute() run. Before, under permanalyticse or permtstat, esttab switched to analytic p-values while wooldid's own table showed permutation ones.
items.what_you_notice: esttab tables of permute() runs show the same p-values and intervals wooldid prints. Where e(V) exists, esttab's standard error and t columns stay analytic.

items.heading: Removed: oldsyntax
items.what_changed: v1.3's oldsyntax option renamed the onset-period event-study row from post0 back to contemp. It is gone, and a call that names it stops with an error. Runs that did not use it give identical results.
items.why: It existed only for do-files written before v1.3 renamed that row to work with event_plot. Keeping it meant carrying a second naming scheme through the row labels and the covariance matrices. The bootstrap and permutation routines already refused it.
items.decision: The author asked for its removal as a simplification. The alternative was to keep it as a compatibility option.
items.what_you_notice: Do-files that use oldsyntax must drop it and refer to the onset row as post0.

items.heading: Removed: cleanmatrices
items.what_changed: v1.3's cleanmatrices option ran clear mata and matrix drop _all around the call. It is gone. The help now tells users whose sessions keep failing after a reghdfe crash to type those two commands themselves. It warns that they also remove the user's own matrices and Mata objects.
items.why: The recovery is two commands a user can type, choosing what to lose. The option also wiped wooldid's own compiled routines in the middle of a run. That caused a real crash and required defensive code throughout the program.
items.decision: The author chose deletion. Earlier he had ruled to refuse the option with permute(). He reversed that once the crash proved to occur only when the program was loaded from a do-file, not when it was installed.
items.what_you_notice: Do-files naming cleanmatrices stop with an error. The Bugs section of the help gives the manual recovery.

items.heading: Removed: emptycellsoverride
items.what_changed: v1.3's emptycellsoverride option turned off wooldid's use of Stata's set emptycells drop. It is gone. wooldid always uses that setting during a run, and restores the user's own setting when it exits.
items.why: It changed no estimate or standard error, and it made the run about five times slower. It mattered only for reading the raw regression printed under verbose. A user who wants that regression can re-run the command that verbose prints, under set emptycells keep.
items.decision: The author chose deletion. The alternative was to keep it as a way out of a global Stata setting that wooldid changes.
items.what_you_notice: Do-files naming emptycellsoverride stop with an error. Nothing else changes.

items.heading: Removed: suppresssgprimaryeffects
items.what_changed: v1.3's suppresssgprimaryeffects was a speed option. It skipped the estimates for each subgroup and reported only the differences between subgroups and the test of equality. It is gone. Every subgroups() run now reports each subgroup's own estimates.
items.why: The estimates for each subgroup now come from the same calculation as the differences. So the option saved only part of the run, 11.8 seconds against 6.6 on one example. It split the code into about twenty branches. It also hid a serious defect. The guard against degenerate subgroup differences did not work when the option was on. Seeing each subgroup's effect beside the difference also guards against reading a difference without its levels.
items.decision: The author chose deletion. The defect was repaired before the option was removed.
items.what_you_notice: Do-files naming the option stop with an error. The same call without it returns everything it did before, plus the estimates for each subgroup.

items.heading: Removed: poisexpresults, semielasticity and the eyex and eydx elasticities
items.what_changed: These v1.3 options are gone. contreatelasticitytype() now accepts only dydx and dyex. Under poisson, results are reported on the linear index, the scale on which the model is linear. There dydx is already the semi-elasticity of the expected outcome and dyex its elasticity, and the tables are titled that way.
items.why: The removed forms divide by the model's predicted outcome. reghdfe's prediction leaves out the absorbed fixed effects. So the denominator was wrong, and so were the answers. The two estimation routines disagreed by 65 percent on one test design, and by 13 percent under timetrends. Under poisson the log link makes a derivative of the linear index a proportional effect on the expected outcome. So the semi-elasticity and the elasticity are still available as dydx and dyex. What is gone is poisexpresults' reporting of effects as differences in expected counts.
items.decision: The author chose to remove the options outright. The alternative was to repair the calculation. He removed the expected-count scale too, although it was the one path on which the dividing forms were correct.
items.what_you_notice: Do-files naming semielasticity, poisexpresults, eyex or eydx stop with an error. Poisson results are no longer available as differences in expected counts.

items.heading: Removed: permrawp, the permutation p-value that leaves out the observed assignment
items.what_changed: permrawp reported the absolute-value permutation p-value as a plain share of the draws, without counting the observed assignment. It is gone, and so is e(perm_rawp*). permabsp remains as the absolute-value convention. The option existed only during development and was never in a release.
items.why: Under a permutation test the observed assignment is one of the possible assignments, so it belongs in its own reference set. Counting it is called the add-one form. It keeps the test valid, meaning it never rejects more often than its stated level. The plain share rejects too often when draws are few. It could also print a p-value of exactly zero, which no permutation test can support. Under exact enumeration the two are equal. On sampled draws the plain share can be recovered from permabsp and e(perm_n), when a match with ritest or Stata's permute is needed.
items.decision: The author had admitted the option so users could reproduce the number ritest prints. He reversed that in favour of the conservative convention.
items.what_you_notice: Development do-files naming permrawp stop with an error. The error for giving both permside() and permabsp now names only those two options.

items.heading: Other options that existed only during development
items.what_changed: Several options added during this cycle were removed before any release. bootalpha() chose how the Bayesian bootstrap weighted clusters. bootstrap(bayes) now always draws one weight per cluster, on equal terms. ties half-counted bootstrap draws exactly equal to the estimate. e(perm_lb_*) and e(perm_ub_*) duplicated e(perm_bandlo_*) and e(perm_bandhi_*). fastcollapse and fullprecisionslow were replaced by a single option, nofastcollapse.
items.why: The only other setting of bootalpha() weighted each cluster by its number of rows. On panel data that understates standard errors badly, and panels are what wooldid is for. Rubin's Bayesian bootstrap with one weight per cluster is the standard form. Exact ties between a continuous statistic and its estimate essentially never occur. Results were identical with and without ties, even with five clusters. The perm_lb and perm_ub names read like confidence bounds. They held quantiles of the null distribution, meaning cut points of the statistic's spread when treatment has no effect. The two collapse options read as opposites but controlled different things. Their one use, asserting that the collapse happened, is now met by a caution when it is skipped.
items.decision: The author chose deletion in each case. Users who need the row-count weighting of bootalpha() can use bayesboot. For the duplicate results he reversed an earlier plan to keep them with a deprecation notice, since no released do-file can depend on them. For the collapse options he rejected a hidden alias, so that an old do-file fails loudly and never runs something different.
items.what_you_notice: Nothing changes for users upgrading from v1.3. Do-files written during development that name these options stop with an error. A skipped cell collapse is announced by a caution.

items.heading: Removed: salvaged standard errors for the ame when every cell sits inside one cluster
items.what_changed: Sometimes the covariance of the ame was entirely zero because treated cells sat inside single clusters. wooldid used to re-estimate the model with regress, with the fixed effects written out as dummy variables, to salvage some standard errors. That fallback is gone. wooldid still detects the all-zero variance. It prints a caution that no standard error is identified, naming the reason and the alternatives.
items.why: The zero variance is a symptom. When a cell lies inside one cluster, the cluster-robust variance cannot see its noise. Re-fitting with explicit dummies does not change that. So the salvaged standard errors had no sound basis. The slow solve over hundreds of redundant dummies also delayed the user's discovery that the specification needed a finer cluster() or a different inference method.
items.decision: The author ruled to remove the fallback. It had been adopted earlier as part of a larger package, where its cost was never weighed on its own.
items.what_you_notice: Such runs now report the ame without a standard error, with a caution. Before, they took much longer to report a number.

items.heading: Kept after being considered for removal: permside(), permanalyticse, altmethod_adversarial and permtci
items.what_changed: These four options remain unchanged.
items.why: permside() is the only way to put a one-sided permutation p-value in the printed column. That also puts it in e(p) and in tables made with esttab. permanalyticse is the one-call way to get analytic standard errors beside permutation p-values. It also supplies the covariance that the honestdid sensitivity analysis needs. altmethod_adversarial tests whether the post-treatment estimates lie on the line projected forward from the pre-treatment ones. That is a standard test, and its null hypothesis differs from the primary test's. permtci reports a symmetric interval built from the permuted t-ratios and the observed standard error.
items.decision: The author kept all four. The alternatives were to have users read one-sided p-values from stored results, or run the analytic specification separately. Another was to use honestdid with no allowed departure from the pre-trend.
items.what_you_notice: No change.

items.heading: level(): wooldid checks the value itself and restores your setting after every call
items.what_changed: A level() outside 10 to 99.99, or with more than two decimal places, stops with wooldid's own named error. The session's confidence level is restored after every run, including a failed one.
items.why: When wooldid passed the value straight to Stata's set level, Stata refused many legal values. The number was rendered with digits it never had. An illegal value reached Stata's own message late in the run. wooldid now checks the range and the two-decimal precision itself. It passes Stata a value Stata will accept, so the interval columns are labelled for the level in force. A level left changed by a failed call would silently change the interval width of later commands. So it is restored on every exit.
items.decision: The author chose to add wooldid's own refusal. The alternative was to leave level handling to Stata.
items.what_you_notice: Illegal levels stop with a clear error, and later commands keep your confidence level.
